The win moves United level with Liverpool in the WSL, with both teams three points off the European places.

Sports.title: Let there be blanks instead of Manchester City’s name on trophies: there was no honour there | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
At half-time in the 2014 League Cup final, Sunderland led Manchester City 1-0. Yaya Touré equalised with a casually brilliant 30-yard clip 10 minutes after the break, and City went on to win 3-1. City, we now know from the independent commission, were at the time involved in a prolonged and calculated act of cheating, while Touré, the leaks in Der Spiegel suggested, was being paid via a dual contract to disguise exactly how much City were spending. Although precise details were left to the appendices, the commission’s report refers to payments “not recorded in an employment contract … but instead recorded in a consultancy agreement”.

Had Sunderland won, they would not merely have ended a 41-year wait for a trophy but would have qualified for the following season’s Europa League. It’s possible, of course, that the strain the extra games placed on the squad would have led to relegation in 2015, rather than the familiar trope of sacking a manager, in this case Gus Poyet, midway through the season, and surviving thanks to a bump under his successor, Dick Advocaat.

But it’s also possible that the greater exposure brought by European football, the surge of positivity engendered by unfamiliar and unexpected silverware, may have led to Premier League consolidation, stability and semi-regular European qualification.

Should Sunderland feel cheated? Of course they should, just as those who came second behind Lance Armstrong should feel cheated; just as Liverpool and Arsenal should feel cheated over the League Cup finals of 2016 and 2018; just as Stoke should feel cheated over the 2011 FA Cup final; just as Manchester United should feel cheated over the Premier League titles in 2012 and 2018 and Liverpool should in 2014; just as every club who played in the same competitions as City between 2009 and 2018 should feel cheated. But does that mean the 2014 League Cup should be taken from City and awarded to Sunderland?

These are two different questions, and it’s probably best to deal with the latter first – and this, unfortunately, is where subjectivity is unavoidable. I can’t speak for other Sunderland fans but, personally, I wouldn’t want it.

Perhaps this comes from never having seen my club win a major trophy. If it happens, I want it to be pure. I want images that will be remembered down the generations, like the highlights of 1973 – Ian Porterfield’s goal, Jim Montgomery’s save and Bob Stokoe’s celebratory skip across the pitch in mac and trilby.

I want the surge of adrenaline when a goal is scored, the agonised wait of injury time, the rush of the final whistle. I want tears and hugs and community and togetherness, all the things my dad’s generation banged on about. I want to get drunk and sing on a train. I don’t want to find out via an alert on my phone 12 years after the fact as I unpack the dishwasher.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City’s Yaya Touré equalises against Sunderland in the 2014 League Cup final. Photograph: Eddie Keogh/Reuters

Others may feel differently but the arithmetic of trophies won seems far less important than the experience of winning and the memories and sense of comradeship it provokes. Glory denied cannot be rectified a generation later by an independent commission, no matter how august.

Awarding rivals league titles seems even less satisfactory. In the 2017-18 season, for instance, the league was effectively over by the end of January with City 15 points clear.

As City went on to amass 100 points, there was little point in the four sides behind them – Manchester United, Liverpool, Chelsea and Tottenham, who were separated by five points – exerting themselves to try to rein City in.

Their priorities changed. United, Chelsea and Spurs all reached the FA Cup semi-finals. Liverpool got to the Champions League final. In those circumstances, why would any of them have prioritised the league? To award United, who finished second, the title, would seem not just empty but arbitrary.

That, though, does not mean City should not be stripped of those titles. They won them unfairly; why on earth should they be allowed to keep them? (And yes, something similar could be said of Chelsea, but that’s an argument for why Chelsea should also have been stripped of titles, not for why City should not be).

How can those trophies be left in the record books for future generations unquestioningly to see? How can City stand as the fourth-most successful side in league history when so much of that success was achieved by cheating?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The argument will be made that City’s players strived hard for those trophies. But so did players for those other teams, the ones who weren’t cheating. And how much easier to win in a deep squad full of high-grade players, drawn to City by the money they were offering, money whose source, the independent commission concluded, had been disguised in contravention of Premier League regulations.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City with the League Cup in 2014, one of seven major trophies won between 2009 and 2018. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Euphoric memories cannot be expunged, but it is for City fans (and players and coaching staff and directors) to decide what to do with them. If they still want to exult in Sergio Agüero’s 94th-minute winner to claim the 2012 Premier League title, nobody can stop them. But the rest of the world knows what it was based on, that as the rest of the Premier League played to regulations voted in by the clubs themselves, City did not.

That would mean that there was no Premier League champion in 2012, 2014 or 2018, no FA Cup winner in 2011 and no League Cup winner in 2014, 2016 or 2018 (and it does not seem unreasonable to wonder, when all this is done, whether there might be more to be investigated after 2018). If there are blanks on the roll of honour, let them be; there was no honour there.

Let the spaces stand as testimony to what those seasons were. Let them stand as a memorial to the years when a foreign entity tried to subvert English football, when a foreign entity took this country’s greatest cultural mode, and all the passion and all the feeling, all the sorrow and all the joy, all the love it has entailed, and tried to twist it for its own political ends. Let them stand as a warning of the dangers of laissez-faire capitalism, when everything, no matter how beloved, could be sold off to the highest bidder.

And let them stand as a monument to a Premier League that finally – belatedly? – took action, to a process that maintained its independence, to an institution that, at no little risk to its own wellbeing – a risk that has not gone away – in the end preferred justice and fairness and decency over grubby deals with the rich and powerful.

Let the years without a champion stand for ever vacant, both as a rebuke and as a tribute. Sometimes, emptiness can be the most eloquent statement of all.

Sports.title: Manchester City whistleblower ready to help UK authorities in return for protection
Sports.content:
Rui Pinto, whose leaks helped to trigger the Premier League’s investigation into Manchester City’s financial affairs, is prepared to help authorities in the UK with their legal case in exchange for protection from threats, the Guardian understands.

Despite the crowdfunding campaign launched on Friday to fund a new life after leaving the protection of the Portuguese police, the whistleblower’s priority remains to cooperate, provided adequate security arrangements are in place.

In addition to the sporting ramifications of the case being conducted against City by the Premier League, British authorities could also decide to extend the inquiry. That has already occurred in Portugal in relation to some of the documents disclosed by Pinto. City were found guilty of more than 100 charges by an independent commission that unearthed “sham” contracts to boost income artificially by £900m, an investigation that was prompted by Pinto’s leaks of thousands of private documents.

City confirmed on Friday the club will appeal against the tribunal’s verdict.

With detailed knowledge of the documents, individuals and companies involved in the case – as well as documents that may have been overlooked during the investigation – Rui Pinto is willing to continue as a protected witness in another country, it is understood.

Just days before his arrest in Budapest in January 2019, the 37-year-old Portuguese national was negotiating entry into a witness protection programme in France, an initiative that was halted by the Portuguese authorities.

If it is confirmed that Rui Pinto will no longer be a protected witness in Portugal, he will be free to cooperate with authorities in other countries from 10 October. He has cooperated sporadically with French, German and Belgian authorities. The UK could now be added to that list, should it wish to do so.

Pinto’s potential contribution in the UK could extend well beyond the City furore. The hundreds of millions of files he gathered as part of Football Leaks and Luanda Leaks are not solely in the possession of the Portuguese authorities.

Between his arrest in Hungary and his extradition to Portugal, French authorities travelled to the Hungarian capital and copied the contents of all the electronic devices in the whistleblower’s possession. Rui Pinto was later acquitted of 241 counts after a second trial in Portugal in April this year.

The documents can now be shared between countries as part of international cooperation between nations with bilateral ties, including the UK.

Rui Pinto is now waiting to find out what his future holds. His defence protested against the decision of ending the protection, accusing Portugal of “state terrorism”. The whistleblower’s lawyers said they had appealed against the decision and had sought to establish how the risk assessment had been carried out but had received no response.

The hacker says he wants to leave Portugal for a secret location. At the time of writing, more than €19,000 (£16,530) had already been raised by a crowdfunding campaign.

Sports.title: Celtic fans throw tennis balls at club owner Dermot Desmond during golf tournament
Sports.content:
Celtic’s principal shareholder Dermot Desmond had tennis balls thrown towards him during his visit to the Alfred Dunhill Links golf tournament at St Andrews in a protest from fans.

The 76-year-old – who has been criticised by supporters for an apparent lack of progress on the pitch – was taking part in the pro-am event on Saturday when the disruption happened on the green of the 15th hole.

Tennis balls with pictures of Desmond’s face crossed out were thrown on to the green, with Desmond then escorted off the course by security.

The Celtic Fans Collective later released a statement on X, which included video and pictures of the protest, calling for change at the top of the club.

View image in fullscreen Dermot Desmond is driven away from the course after the fans’ protest. Photograph: Stuart Wallace/Shutterstock

“Dermot Desmond has essentially been allowed to run Celtic Football Club whilst using his wealth to hide from supporters and accountability,” the statement said. “Fans took the chance today to send a message that this arrangement cannot continue.”

Martin O’Neill’s side – who claimed the Premiership title ahead of Hearts after a final-day decider last season as part of a domestic double – currently sit top of the table, two points clear of rivals Rangers.

Celtic, though, lost the last three games before the international break, including two defeats by Rangers, one at Parkhead, and were also beaten 3-1 at home by Ferencvaros in their opening Europa League fixture.

Sports.title: ‘Portugal’s greatest symbol’: Bruno Fernandes backs Cristiano Ronaldo despite walkout
Sports.content:
Bruno Fernandes has said Cristiano Ronaldo remains “the greatest symbol” of the Portugal team, despite his decision to walk out on the squad this week.

Ronaldo said on Wednesday he had left the team camp after the Portugal coach, Jorge Jesus, said he would not start against Denmark. Portugal went on to win the Nations League contest 4-2 without him, and Ronaldo’s international future remains in doubt.

Manchester United midfielder Fernandes called for unity after a tumultuous few days in which Portugal fans’ opinions have been split over Ronaldo’s decision, and the future for their country’s leading goalscorer and most capped men’s player.

“Regarding Cristiano, I had a conversation with him, and what I told him, and what I repeat here, is this – the most important thing is that, regardless of what happens, Cristiano Ronaldo will never cease to be the greatest symbol of our national team, of our football, and of the country, for what he has done not only in Portugal but throughout the world,” Fernandes told reporters on Saturday.

“He has a reserved place not only among the best of all time, but also in the hearts of all Portuguese people, and the most important thing is that we stop dividing things,” Fernandes added. “There are no divisions in the national team, it is one and will remain so, despite any noise that may come from outside.”

“We are outside of this controversy, but what I ask is that the country does not divide itself, does not make choices, that it respects all sides At the same time, Cris is and will be the biggest icon of our national team, he deserves everyone’s respect, regardless of who likes him more or [who likes him] less.”

Portugal beat Norway 2-1 in Oslo last Sunday with Ronaldo an unused substitute, then prevailed 4-2 in Copenhagen after his departure from the squad, with Fernandes wearing the captain’s armband. The Nations League holders face Norway again on Sunday, this time in Porto.

Jorge Jesus, who managed Ronaldo at Saudi side Al-Nassr before taking the national team job, said the 41-year-old was a “symbol of Portugal,” adding that there would be time to speak about him after the Norway game.

“I’m going to focus on the team, on the opponent which is Norway, one of the five best teams in Europe. That’s the problem right now,” said the 72-year-old coach.

Sports.title: Bruno Fernandes reveals talks with Cristiano Ronaldo after star, 41, stormed out of Portugal camp amid rift with manager Jorge Jesus - and tells feuding pair to settle their issues 'behind closed doors'
Sports.content:
Manchester United and Portugal midfielder Bruno Fernandes has revealed he has attempted to hold clear-the-air talks with Cristiano Ronaldo amid his rift with national team manager Jorge Jesus.

Ronaldo, 41, landed in Madrid in the early hours of Thursday morning after flying from Copenhagen, where Portugal faced Denmark on Thursday, on his private jet. He had been seen leaving the Parken Stadium in the Danish capital on Wednesday after missing a third consecutive training session.

Ronaldo later confirmed in a statement on Instagram that he had left the team's camp because of comments made by Jesus in his press conference.

The Portugal boss said the captain would not start the Denmark clash, just days after sitting on the bench for the entirety of the 2-1 win in Norway, but insisted there was no issue between the two.

Ronaldo's future is now unclear, but team-mate Fernandes is now doing his best to try and salvage the relationship.

'To put an end to this matter once and for all, I don't need to speak with my colleagues,' Fernandes said. 'We know how to manage our situations.

Bruno Fernandes (right) has held clear-the-air talks with Cristiano Ronaldo (left) after the latter stormed out of the Portugal camp

'We have a situation that has nothing to do with the players, and our most important role is to deliver results.'

He continued: 'I had a conversation with Cris. What I told him is that the most important thing, regardless of what happens, is that he will never cease to be the greatest symbol of our national team and country, for everything he has done in Portugal and around the world.

'He has a reserved place not only among the best of all time, but also in the hearts of the Portuguese people.

'We cannot divide ourselves; the national team is one, and all parties should resolve their issues behind closed doors. I think that's how it will be, and that everything will end well on both sides.

'We are out of the matter; we spend a lot of time playing cards and are outside the controversy surrounding this issue, but I ask that the country not be divided, not make choices, and accept all sides.

'Cris will always be the greatest icon of our national team, of world football, and deserves the respect of all Portuguese people, regardless of who likes him more or less.'

Jesus, meanwhile, who took over from Roberto Martinez after the World Cup, oversaw a 4-2 win for his side on Thursday night, and insisted he remains in control of the team – with full faith from the players.

'I don't have a group in my hand. I have a group that believes in the coach's ideas,' he said. 'They believe in my ideas and, because they have a lot of individual quality, things become easier.

'If that's having a group in my hand, then I do, because they go hand in hand with me and my ideas.'

Portugal boss Jorge Jesus insists he is in control of his players and has a 'clear conscience' amid his feud with Ronaldo

Ronaldo said: 'After the national team coach's press conference, and following a conversation with the President of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team training camp.

'In due time, I will tell all Portuguese people the truth about the reasons that led to my departure from the national team, to which I have always dedicated myself.

'Now is the time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates.'

This week, he also liked a post on social media which saw Felipe Melo say: 'I see a grotesque difference in the players’ treatment with Cristiano Ronaldo in relation to Argentina players with (Lionel) Messi.'

Jesus, though, who also managed Ronaldo at Al-Nassr, insists his conscience is clean.

'It's not difficult for me to focus,' he added. 'You know what's difficult for me? It's not understanding what's going on inside. It's not knowing how to train my players. That's what's difficult for me. The rest... zero.

'What's important is what we have to do. The things that happen don't separate the group, they haven't separated us and they won't separate us.'

Sports.title: Chaos as Ireland manager is forced to end press conference early after 'verbal attack' from Israeli journalists - who accused players of racism - as tension grows ahead of crunch second meeting
Sports.content:
Chaos as Ireland manager is forced to end press conference early after 'verbal attack' from Israeli journalists - who accused players of racism - as tension grows ahead of crunch second meeting

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson was forced to end his press conference early after his players were accused of using a racist term to describe Israel players by an Israeli journalist, one day before the two nations are set to meet again in Nations League action.

The first Ireland-Israel tie earlier this week became football's most politically charged match amid calls for the Republic to boycott the fixture due to the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

While the fixture went ahead, Ireland's players voted to wear black armbands to honour civilian lives lost in the conflict, lower their heads during the Israeli national anthem, and fail to exchange pennants as is custom during international ties.

Second goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu personally boycotted the match on ethical grounds with QPR defender Jimmy Dunne named as the third-choice 'keeper on the team-sheet due to UEFA regulations.

Hallgrimsson has borne the brunt of questions around the fixture beyond football matters, but Irish press officers were forced to intervene in Backa Topola after he was first seemingly asked to comment on the Flydubai incident, which saw a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv diverted amid an alleged hijacking by a co-pilot with 'extremist views'.

'What do you say about the people you support, the ideology is based on murder, just this week one of them tried to kill 100 Israeli passengers, 27 children. Innocent children and thousands of others,' the first journalist managed, before being pulled up by Ireland's press officer Kieran Crowley.

Incredible scenes at Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference this morning, which came to an abrupt end when it was disrupted by an Israeli journalist making bizarre and unfounded allegations against Irish players. pic.twitter.com/WsunljS1lE — Off The Ball (@offtheball) October 3, 2026

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson ended his press conference early after an Israeli journalist accused his players of racism

Amid widespread calls for the fixture to boycotted from Irish fans, Ireland played the match but performed a number of gestures before the match

'We are only concentrating on football questions today,' said Crowley, before a second journalist asked a far more incendiary question.

The second Israeli journalist alleged that Ireland players had called their Israeli counterparts 'monkeys', prompting an immediate response from Crowley, who said: 'That is completely untrue. That is completely untrue'.

The press officer then attempted to take the microphone from the journalist who insisted that he was doing 'his job' and told him 'you cannot take it' in an attempt to keep hold of it.

'They are not lying about it,' the journalist insisted, while a representative close to Hallgrimsson called an end to the press conference and for the Irish media to follow him out for a separate media huddle.

'You've just broadcast a lie,' he said to the second journalist, who continued to state that he was entitled to ask the question in the open press conference.

Earlier in the press conference, it was confirmed that the Irish federation (FAI) had begun an internal investigation into allegations that their own player Adam Idah had been subject to racist abuse during the first tie from Israel fans.

An Israeli television reporter is believed to have then followed the manager into the hall to demand further access beyond UEFA's pre-match agreement, but was blocked by a member of Ireland's security team.

No UEFA delegate was present for the press conference.

Hallgrimsson later described the interruption to Irish media as a 'verbal attack'.

The Israeli players had previously spoken out against their opponents following the first tie, with captain and West Ham star Manor Solomon alleging that Ireland had 'said nonsense (to them) during the game.'

'If I say what I think about them, I'll probably be banned for a few games so I don't want to say. Of course they hate us and we don't like them,' he continued.

'I believe in ourselves that we can do it. I know who I'm with here, I know the players and the team, we will get out of this and get revenge for this.

'I'm already looking forward to the next game against them, it's going to be completely different. What they did with the anthem? I'm not interested in them, we have a country that is ten times better than theirs, stronger, an amazing country with amazing people.

'We are proud to wear the national team's shirt and be Israelis. We are proud of our country and our soldiers. (The Irish) can play all their tricks. We are Israelis and love the country. And that will always be the case.'

Sunday's match will be played in the small Serbian town behind closed doors, but the fixture had initially been scheduled to take place in Dublin.

It was later moved after the threat of a boycott grew and after a friendly with Qatar in May was stopped twice when tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown onto the pitch.

While the match will be shown by RTE in Ireland, the broadcaster will again cut back its screening of the game with no studio punditry, no advertising and only using commentary from an international feed.

Sports.title: Watching Lee Carsley's England's U21s is a breath of fresh air and they will embrace the target on their backs in pursuit of a historic Euros three-peat next summer
Sports.content:
England men's U21s qualified for next summer's European Championships with a game to spare after their goalless draw against Slovakia.

The reigning champions are seeking their third consecutive European crown under manager Lee Carsley and sealed qualification undefeated, winning seven and drawing two of their nine fixtures.

They now head to Ireland next week, with Carsley saying emphatically at full time that he 'definitely' does not plan to mix things up in a bid to secure a perfect record.

Daily Mail Sport football reporter Tara Anson-Walsh was at Stoke City's Bet365 Stadium to bring you the things we learned…

Most importantly, get the job done

Carsley can sleep easy tonight knowing the first obstacle has been cleared on the road to a historic Euros three-peat with England's U21s.

Qualification? Check. Goals? Plenty of them. Fun? Well, based on England's journey through this qualifying campaign, it certainly looks like it.

Carsley can sleep easy tonight after England U21s secured qualification for next year's Euros

England found the back of the net 22 times in their previous eight qualifying matches, and the beauty of this side is that goals can come from virtually anywhere.

Against Kazakhstan last week, centre backs Josh Acheampong and Max Alleyne got on the scoresheet before Middlesbrough striker Will Lankshear sealed the victory.

With four goals scored in three of their previous four matches, confidence was sky high. 'Every time I step on the pitch I believe I'm going to score,' Lankshear said after that game.

There was something slightly ironic, then, that England's first match without a goal was the one that simultaneously secured their place at next summer's tournament.

In front of 8,313 fans at Stoke City's Bet365 Stadium, England knocked on the door all evening but simply could not find a breakthrough.

Lankshear came closest. Fresh from scoring on his debut, the Middlesbrough striker twice escaped his marker at the back post but could not keep his headers on target.

There was frustration at full time after 16 shots at goal failed to find the back of the net, but Carsley was quick to remind his squad that qualification was the priority.

'They were very frustrated at the end of the game, but I made the point to them that to play in a major competition it's the story of a season, not just one game,' he said.

'They've put themselves in a great position now to do something no other country has done before in terms of potentially winning the tournament for a third time, so it's exciting times.'

Carsley leads the charge

It is worth a quick reminder that England went 39 years without winning this tournament before retaining it at the first time of asking last year.

The quality and depth of young talent available to Carsley is jaw-dropping, but the England boss has also played a significant role in creating the environment that allows those players to flourish.

Carsley's importance to this team's success cannot be overstated, though he would probably be the last person to say so.

Asked last week how he maintained continuity despite the constant turnover that comes with Under 21 football, he instead praised the mentality of his players, particularly their ability to stay ready even when they might 'think it's not going to be their day'.

Will Lankshear had been freescoring before drawing a blank against Slovakia in Stoke on Friday

City's Lewis and his team-mates knocked on the door all night but could not find the net

Watching Carsley's England is a breath of fresh air. The shackles are off, and this is a team that wants to dominate possession, move the ball quickly and attack.

England had 69 per cent possession against Slovakia and registered 16 shots to their opponents' four. Against Kazakhstan, they enjoyed 81 per cent of the ball. Before that, they recorded 74 per cent possession against Moldova.

They have dominated this qualifying group from start to finish, with a 1-1 draw against Andorra and this one against Slovakia the only mild blemishes on an otherwise outstanding campaign.

No wonder they are embracing the target on their backs heading into next summer.

England tie up loose ends thanks to Alleyne

Slovakia, sitting second in the group, should have posed a sterner test than bottom-placed Kazakhstan.

But unlike against Kazakhstan, where England conceded twice through lapses in concentration and Carsley admitted they would need to 'play better if we're going to be a serious team', they were far more assured against a stronger Slovakian side.

At the heart of that defensive display was Max Alleyne.

The Burnley centre-back, on loan from Manchester City, delivered another assured performance and the numbers backed it up.

Four tackles made and four tackles won. Four interceptions. Six of eight duels won. Eleven recoveries.

'He was outstanding,' Carsley said. 'There was once or twice in the first half where they counterattacked, one-v-one and Max cleaned it up. We shouldn't be in that position, but it was only because of Max's outstanding attributes that we got away with that.

'I thought Max, Ash (Phillips), Josh (Acheampong) and Rico (Lewis) were outstanding tonight. The concentration is something that we have to be better at in terms of Under 21s.

'Generally, when they perform with their senior teams, they've got older, more experienced players around them that are constantly talking them through the game. But they really stood up for themselves tonight. As forward-thinking as we were, I thought we were solid at the back.'

Sports.title: It's a disgrace that a case as seismic as City's is STILL shrouded in secrecy - we don't even know who was on the panel that found them guilty: OLIVER HOLT
Sports.content:
This is the top flight of English football now, this faceless parade, this feast of redaction, this lawyers’ jamboree, this case without end, this land of double-speak and deflection and filibuster and prevarication and delay and uncertainty, this wrangle still cloaked in such absurd levels of secrecy, threat and paranoia that it makes the trial in The Trial look transparent.

The interminable, impenetrable battle between the Premier League and Manchester City, one of its member clubs, has been a ludicrous, ruinous shambles of a process that has brought only ridicule and shame on the English game. Amid its agonising and its navel-gazing, its threats and its suspicion, it has forced a league that was once supposed to be the envy of the world to its knees.

There is no prospect of it rising to its feet any time soon, either. Football still does not even know the identities of the three members of the commission that handed down the initial judgments. Those ruled that Manchester City were guilty of all the charges of financial misconduct that had been levelled at them by the Premier League back in the mists of time.

The top flight is a cast filled with bad actors and a medium laden with foul tribal abuse and so some degree of anonymity while the case was ongoing is understandable but to preserve the mystery now has allowed City and their acolytes to attempt to provoke disquiet about their possible allegiances.

City have referred to the independent commission as a ‘Premier League commission’ and its judgment as an ‘opinion’. Speculation has been allowed to form that perhaps one of the panel members was a supporter of a rival team. It is standard disinformation but the conspiracy theories could be easily dispelled if the process were more transparent.

There is precedent, after all. After City and the Premier League went to arbitration in October 2024 over the league’s Associated Party Transaction rules, the hearing took place behind closed doors at the International Dispute Resolution Centre in front of a three-member tribunal made up of former High Court judge Sir Nigel Teare, former Supreme Court Justice Lord Dyson and Monckton Chambers’ Christopher Vajda KC.

Pep Guardiola smiles at the Premier League trophy but his successes are now tainted

The interminable battle between the Premier League and his former club Manchester City has been a ludicrous, ruinous shambles of a process which some have taken to poking fun at

Yet the transparency of that example has not been followed here. It is hard not to feel that much of the bitterness of the case, the inflamed tensions it has created throughout the game and the grave damage it has done to football in this country would have been diminished if the proceedings had taken place in open court and been held up to the light.

The scale of the secrecy surrounding the case has felt unnecessary and self-defeating from the start. No one knew when the hearings were taking place or if they were taking place or if evidence was still being given or which witnesses were being called or when verdicts might be close. Other cases are held in camera, of course, but this is a row about football, for goodness’ sake.

The lack of transparency that has dogged it all the way through has spawned all manner of other conspiracy theories and continues to undermine it even now. Much of the judgment that has been released publicly is redacted. The judgment speaks of witnesses accused of lying to the commission but sheds no light on who they are.

Kyle Phillips, a partner at one of the United Kingdom's leading law firms, Howard Kennedy, told ESPN earlier this week: ‘It's very difficult to read because a lot of it is redacted and there's no evidence or appendices that they keep referring to… Although the panel's names are redacted, you'd expect them to be experienced lawyers.

‘There will be a fuller balanced judgment that we don't have sight of: that's the problem, so we can't assess the language that's used from that perspective. But you would think everything they said is supported somewhere by their evidential findings, and that they have got good grounds for making the points that they have.’

When it was put to Phillips that the commission referred to witnesses in support of City’s evidence about the source of their sponsorship funding and that they had been found to have given false and dishonest evidence, he pointed out: ‘Yes, but we don't know which witnesses are accused of that, do we?’

The first trial of Manchester City is over and their owners have been found guilty of all of the most serious charges. Now it is about to begin all over again because they have appealed - and it may be that their punishment is announced within 30 days, and then rescinded if an appeal is successful, and no one knows when football might be able to breathe anew.

‘The Club’s firm position,’ City’s statement said on Friday as they revealed they had lodged their appeal at 7pm on Thursday, ‘is that on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.’ It is time, they declared, for Round Two.

Richard Masters, chief executive of the Premier League, gives Pep Guardiola a league winner's medal during his time at Manchester City

Lord David Pannick KC (right) has represented Manchester City before in their fight against the Premier League over accusations of financial wrongdoing

The Premier League’s interminable pursuit of City, which became our game’s closest approximation to Jarndyce v Jarndyce since its inception in February 2023, appeared to reach a conclusion a little over a week ago when it was announced that the club had been found guilty of the vast majority of charges levelled against it. Now, it has got a second wind.

The case is still couched in so many uncertainties and concealments that it has continued to sow confusion and distrust. This was supposed to be the case that restored faith in the Premier League as a competition but instead it feels as though the game is running out of control and lurching towards chaos. It feels as if football is lost in the murk somewhere and we are no closer to getting it back.

That level of concealment creates a vacuum which City try to fill. City and their chief executive, Ferran Soriano, continue to bleat about the ‘irrefutable evidence’ they possess that proves their innocence in all of this and yet it appears from what we know of the judgment of the Independent Commission, which ruled on the charges, that the irrefutable evidence has already been refuted.

Germane to that is evidence that City believe proves their principal sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government and not the club’s stated owner, the Abu Dhabi United Group. City are thought to be ready to argue in their appeal that the money received by Etihad, the state airline, came directly from the Abu Dhabi government and that state-owned entities are allowed to sponsor clubs under Premier League rules.

Others are deeply sceptical about that argument. City claim not to be state owned but the problem with state ownership is that lines become blurred very quickly and grow so opaque that, just like so much with this case, it is almost impossible to tell where one entity begins and another ends.

If City are really not owned by Abu Dhabi, then why is Abu Dhabi so enraged and threatened by the verdicts handed down by the independent commission? Bloomberg reported on Friday morning that United Arab Emirates officials had warned the UK government that the severity of any punishment of City could harm the relationship between the two.

The report said the City affair may undermine ‘their appetite for future grand-scale commitments in Britain, and that the UAE consider the Premier League’s actions to have an influence on the bilateral state relationship’. If feels like quite an over-reaction if City are not state-owned.

The layers are not being peeled away. They are multiplying. What now? That is still a question with no easy answer. A new anonymous three-person independent panel will be appointed to hear City’s appeal but that will run separately to the process of punishing City for the guilty verdicts in the initial judgment.

Manchester City's Enzo Fernandez and Rayan Cherki may lead the team to victory over Liverpool at Anfield on October 11 but how much importance should we attach to that result?

It is impossible to run a sport with that kind of uncertainty hanging over it. City could be hit with a penalty that relegates them. But then they might win the appeal which would invalidate the initial verdicts

Once the sanction is decided, there are then 30 days to announce it. But there is no timetable for how long it will take to arrive at the chosen punishment. Some experts have said they think it is possible there could be an announcement of punishment before the end of the season. Others have said it could be up to five years.

It is impossible to run a sport with that kind of uncertainty hanging over it. City could be hit with a penalty that relegates them. But then they might win the appeal which would invalidate the initial verdicts. Which would then invalidate a sanction already visited upon them. It’s chaos, which is exactly what City’s chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak always promised it would be.

And somewhere in the middle of all this wreckage, fans will still turn up to watch men playing football. But they will not know what to believe. If City beat Liverpool at Anfield on October 11, for instance, and go further clear at the top of the Premier League, how much importance should we attach to that result?

Fans will not know whether the result of the game they are watching will mean anything by the end of the season. Nor will the players. Nor will the managers.

Nor will the television companies who pay billions of pounds to broadcast something that may be a sham. They will not know whether what they are watching is real. Or whether these matches are ghost games soon to be declared invalid.

And in that miasma of gloom and uncertainty, sport starts to die.

Sports.title: Imperious Jude Bellingham cements his status as the future of Thomas Tuchel's team: Real Madrid star a class above as England humiliate old foes Croatia in seven-goal thrashing, writes IAN LADYMAN
Sports.content:
The Croatians here by the Adriatic did their best to make this rivalry feel the way it used to. They filled this tiny little stadium with thousands of schoolkids to get round the fact this was supposed to be a behind closed doors game.

In the crowd on the far side some of the children even held up a banner.

‘It’s not coming home,’ it read, in reference to a familiar Croat poke at perceived English arrogance.

They even had a familiar face on the touchline. After an absence of 14 years, Slaven Bilic – architect of his country’s most famous victory over England at Wembley in 2007 – was back in charge of Croatia.

But out there on the grass, out where it mattered, Thomas Tuchel’s brilliantly enterprising and energetic England humiliated, embarrassed and shamed their opponents on a quite remarkable night for both nations.

They outplayed them, out thought them, out ran them and frankly ruined them. They won by seven when it could have been a dozen.

Children in the stands. Men against boys on the field. What a night for Tuchel’s team.

So, yes, this seems to be a rivalry that’s now over. Dismantled 4-2 by England at the World Cup in June, Croatia fielded eight of that line up here, including 41-year-old Luka Modric. But this is a Croatia team on the wane. England, despite last weekend’s defeat to world and European champions Spain, are suddenly trending spectacularly in the right direction.

Bellingham was head and shoulders above the rest and has cemented his position as the player around whom the future of this England team will now surely be built

England were magnificent, with this probably their best football under Tuchel

The presence of more than 6,000 children – along with endless parents and coaches – seemed a little bit like a V-sign to UEFA. It’s in the regulations but even so. This game was supposed to be played in an empty stadium because of alleged far-Right behaviour by Croat supporters.

This in no way felt like a punishment and all that can be hoped is that the Croatian youngsters enjoyed their evening out watching the likes of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane and Anthony Gordon.

England were, it must be said, absolutely fabulous. Magnificent, even. This was probably their best football under Tuchel and for some long while prior to that. Yes, Croatia were woeful with a back line so square Kane could have parted his hair with it.

But they are the 14th ranked team in the world so still England had to play their football and they did so with a hunger and a tempo that made a mockery of the fact this four-game international period was supposed to be a test of their physical and emotional capacity.

Bellingham was once again head and shoulders above the rest and over the course of games against Spain, Czech Republic and now Croatia, the 23-year-old has cemented his position as the player around whom the future of this England team will now surely be built.

There were outstanding performances from Kane, Anthony Gordon, Bukayo Saka and, on his first start, Bournemouth’s Alex Scott. But it was Bellingham who ran this game, easing his way through the Croatian midfield imperiously as though he owned it.

His first contribution of note was to free Gordon down the inside left channel in only the third minute.

That was to become a pattern and though Gordon was denied by goalkeeper Dominik Livakovic on that occasion, he was given no chance five minutes later when Bellingham released Kane down the other side and the England captain drove his 88th international goal high into the roof of the net with his right foot.

Livakovic had conceded four against Spain earlier in the week and here the story of the night was set astonishingly early.

Croatia were no match for England in central areas – in terms of appetite as much as anything – while their back four was pierced monotonously by England’s deep runners.

The Croatians filled this tiny little stadium with thousands of schoolkids to get round the fact this was supposed to be behind closed doors game

MATCH FACTS Croatia (4-2-3-1): Livakovic 7; Stanisic 5 (Kramaric 75mins 6), Vuskovic 6, Gvardiol 6, Perisic 5; Modric 5 (Jakic 57mins 6), Kovacic 5; Ivanovic 5, Sucic 5 (Pasalic 45mins 5), Baturina 5 (Vlasic 45mins 5); Musa 5 (Matanovic 45mins 6) Booked: Kovacic Manager: Slaven Bilic 3 England (4-2-3-1): Pickford 6; Quansah 7, Konsa 6, Guehi 6, Hall 7 (Lewis-Skelly 79mins) 6; Scott 7.5 (Garner 70mins 6), Anderson 7.5 (Gibbs-White 70mins 6); Saka 8, Bellingham 9, Gordon 8 (Eze 70mins 6); Kane 8 (Rogers 70mins 6) Goals: Kane 8 & 53, Bellingham 21, Gordon 39, Saka 45 & 68, Rogers 88 Manager: Thomas Tuchel 8 Referee: Sven Joblanski (Ger)

Gordon was denied twice more in the ninth and 25th minutes – the second from point blank range – but in the middle of that he played his part in setting up England’s second. A Saka cross to the far post was slightly overhit but when Gordon pulled it down, he was criminally given all the time in the world to ease it square to Bellingham to tap it in.

Already there was a sense of inevitability about the game and indeed the result. Croatia showed no sign of a response. There were other near misses – one from Kane and a shot over from Elliot Anderson – before Jarell Quansah and Bellingham laid on simple finishes for Gordon – at last – Saka as half-time neared.

Around this time there was also a moment of vague comedy at the other end. Having finally mustered some impetus of their own, Croatia seemed set to at least score a goal but when Manchester City’s Mateo Kovacic rounded Jordan Pickford eight yards out, he somehow sliced the ball wide.

With the game over by half-time, England could enjoy themselves. This was probably the first time Tuchel’s team had played without pressure since before the World Cup. Tuchel resisted the temptation to make changes at half-time while Bilic, perhaps understandably, did not. He made three.

His team were helpless, though. Helpless and hopeless. What was particularly embarrassing was that the goals kept coming the same way. Only eight minutes had gone in the second half when Anderson crossed low from the right and Kane slid the ball in at the far post. It seemed that the only ones here who couldn’t see the repeat patterns were the players in the red and white squares.

The sixth goal arrived with 22 minutes left as the Croatian defence presented the ball to Kane who presented it to Saka who slammed it in. On the touchline, Bilic was nowhere to be seen by now. He had taken refuge on the bench, seeking in vain some kind of shelter from the worst night of his life.

By the time he reappeared with three minutes to go, it was to see England substitute Morgan Rogers roll in number seven. That made this Croatia’s record ever defeat and by now many of the children in the stands had disappeared.

Homework must have felt preferable.

Sports.title: Give me my medal! 'Greedy b*****d' Paul Scholes disagrees with Wayne Rooney after Man United legend said he would NOT accept title if Man City are stripped of trophies
Sports.content:
Give me my medal! 'Greedy b*****d' Paul Scholes disagrees with Wayne Rooney after Man United legend said he would NOT accept title if Man City are stripped of trophies

Paul Scholes has responded to his former Manchester United team-mate Wayne Rooney after the latter said he wouldn't accept the 2012 Premier League title if Manchester City were stripped of it.

Since the bombshell legal verdict that found Man City guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges made against them by the Premier League, there has been much debate over how City's illustrious period from 2009-2018 should be judged.

Rio Ferdinand and David De Gea have publicly called for the 2011-12 prize to be added to their medal collection but Rooney said Man United do not 'deserve' to be awarded it.

Now Scholes has weighed in. The midfielder uploaded a punchy Instagram story in response to Rooney saying: 'Keep hearing ex-team-mates saying they want trophies taking off them but they don't want their medals... f*** that I'm a greedy b*****d I want my medal.'

Rooney took to his YouTube show, Stick to United, to explain that if City were to lose their titles he would not want a Premier League winners' medal for the 2011-12 campaign in which United only missed out on the title on goal difference.

'I have heard Rio has come out saying about getting another Premier League medal... I wouldn't really feel comfortable accepting another Premier League medal, if I'm being honest,' he said.

'I don't think we deserve it, we didn't do enough that season to win the league. I think we were six or seven points clear with four or five games to go and we threw it away.'

Paul Scholes (left) and Wayne Rooney (right) won five Premier League titles together

'I've seen everything that has come out over the past few days and listening to people and I was putting myself in a Man City player's shoes... they're players, they're doing everything they can to try and win the Premier League title and in their mind they have done it, if those players have no understanding of what is going on above them, if that happened to me... I would be absolutely devastated.

'It might happen, they might take them [medals] away, but I wouldn't want it [a medal] because I don't think as a team we deserved it that year because obviously we didn't finish first.

'So when I see team-mates saying "I want a medal", I'm happy with the five I've won. I wouldn't want this one. Should they get it stripped for what the owners have done? Yeah maybe, but I wouldn't feel comfortable accepting it.'

Scholes already has eleven Premier League winners medals in his trophy cabinet with him and Rooney winning five top-flight titles together.

Man City confirmed they have lodged an appeal against the guilty verdict on Friday.

In a statement, they said: 'The club’s firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.

'The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

'We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete.'

Manchester City beat rivals Manchester United to the 2011-12 title thanks to Sergio Aguero's dramatic winner against QPR

New Premier League rules state that a hearing must be held within 12 weeks of an appeal being lodged, with a decision due within 30 days of the hearing, which can only last five days, concluding.

Daily Mail Sport reported on Thursday that City will attempt to prove their innocence by arguing that the government of Abu Dhabi – rather than the club’s owners – part-funded ‘sham’ sponsorship.

Sports.title: Something on your mind, Mateo? Man City star Kovacic misses OPEN GOAL in Croatia's clash with England
Sports.content:
Manchester City midfielder Mateo Kovacic sensationally missed an open goal while playing for Croatia against England – with fans wondering whether club issues were playing on his mind.

Kovacic, 32, has played for City since 2023, but now finds the club engulfed in a war with the Premier League that has seen them found guilty of the vast majority of their financial charges.

City are appealing the verdict, but it emerged on Friday night that one of their main defences surrounding sponsorship from Etihad could be in tatters due to the brand previously stating they are state-owned.

And those issues could have played into Kovacic's international form as he missed a golden opportunity on Saturday.

The midfielder found himself around eight yards from goal with a pretty much empty net to pass into, but sliced wide.

He had won the ball off club team-mate Elliot Anderson, rounded Jordan Pickford, and only had to roll the ball into the net – but failed.

A STUNNING miss from Mateo Kovačić 🫣



The Man City man rounds the keeper and misses an open goal. pic.twitter.com/YfPuDehwYf — ITV Football (@itvfootball) October 3, 2026

Manchster City midfielder Mateo Kovacic missed a sitter while playing for Croatia against England on Saturday

'Kovacic missed an empty net after all that work,' one fan wrote on X. 'These City players look traumatised by the 114 charges.'

Another posted: 'These City cheats are literally quivering in their boots whilst playing knowing what they all are.'

England manager Thomas Tuchel had previously admitted the Three Lions' City players are nervous about their futures.

While City stress their innocence and have appealed the decision, Tuchel admitted that Marc Guehi, Elliot Anderson and Nico O'Reilly are naturally anxious.

The trio have been inundated with calls and messages over the past week, with O'Reilly now having flown back to Manchester for treatment on an injury.

'Are they worried or are they concerned? I think that would be a very human reaction if you don't know what's going on for the club that you signed,' Tuchel said.

'They're still young. They're ambitious. They're told they are totally innocent and don't know what's going on.

'We speak about it at dinner and at a table of eight or 12 people. Of course, we speak about it at breakfast.'

Kovacic's club face a potentially significant punishment after being found guilty of financial breaches against the Premier League

Tuchel claimed that the news around City being found guilty of the vast majority of charges had represented a 'distraction' before then clarifying that the City trio had been focused in meetings and training sessions.

'It's a big topic in camp,' he added. 'We had some time off between the matches and it is a big subject. How can it not be a topic? We talk with them but only briefly.'

The German did also suggest that he would continue considering picking players in the event that they are relegated from the Premier League as a punishment, should an appeal fail.

'I would always try to pick the best team for the camp, occasion, tournament,' he said. 'I will never rule that out because they don't play in the top flight in their country. We need to look at it case by case.'

Sports.title: Roy Keane makes huge 'greatest of all time' prediction on England star after Croatia masterclass
Sports.content:
Roy Keane makes huge 'greatest of all time' prediction on England star after Croatia masterclass

Jude Bellingham starred for England against Croatia as they ran out 7-0 winners.

View 2 Images Roy Keane lavished praise on Jude Bellingham. (Image: ITV Football)

Roy Keane believes England and Real Madrid star Jude Bellingham can become 'one of the best in the world '. The 23-year-old scored and assisted three as Thomas Tuchel's side inflicted Croatia's heaviest-ever defeat with a 7-0 rout.

‌



‌



England continue to bounce back from their disappointment against Spain as they followed up the win over Czechia earlier this week. Captain Harry Kane netted twice while Bukayo Saka also scored two with Anthony Gordon, Morgan Rogers and the Birmingham City academy graduate chipping in.

‌



Bellingham is continuing to prove his importance to the Three Lions and he has received glittering praise from the former Manchester United midfielder.

‌



England player ratings as brilliant 9/10 star leads the way in Croatia thrashing READ MORE :

Keane said: "The way he's progressing as a player, there's so much to come. At this moment in time, he's an amazing footballer, the package, the power.

"There's so much to come from him, his leadership skills, his hunger and desire out of possession, he's such a young player, his desire to get into the box, he's making it so easy. Before the game, we were thinking (about) Croatia, they made them look like Gibraltar-type of team.

"Outstanding in every aspect, I think Bellingham can go on to be one of the greatest players of all time.

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

"Of course, if he avoids injuries but his attitude with England recently, I've praised him a lot but what he's doing out of possession lifts the players in the team, playing for Real Madrid doing brilliant things, that will inspire the players. He's a huge leader for them."

Bellingham provided assists for three different scorers, teeing up Kane for the opener then providing Saka to make it four on the stroke of half-time.

‌



The midfielder general played his part in the seventh as he provided Rogers with his second international effort to round off the scoring.

View 2 Images Jude Bellingham was sensational as England thrashed Croatia

The Real Madrid star has began shouldering more and more responsibility for England, popping up with key moments during the route to the Euro 2024 final and during the summer at the World Cup.

Article continues below

Saka said during a post-match interview with ITV: "He was amazing tonight to be fair.

"He deserved [England] player of the year and he probably deserves man of the match tonight as well.

"He was special. Happy to play with him and happy to have him in the England team."

Sports.title: Unstoppable Jude Bellingham is a future Ballon d'Or winner and can be England's best ever
Sports.content:
Unstoppable Jude Bellingham is a future Ballon d'Or winner and can be England's best ever

England faced off against a player who has already been crowned the world's best player, but in Jude Bellingham, the Three Lions have a player ready to take the crown

View 3 Images Jude Bellingham was sensational as England thrashed Croatia

This was the passing of the baton from one of football’s all-time greats to a future Ballon d’Or winner.

‌



‌



Jude Bellingham stamped his quality all over this emphatic, sensational and thrilling England victory. One goal and three assists and easily the best player on the pitch.

‌



Bellingham also put Luka Modric in the shade as England had too much speed, threat and thrust for Croatia who crumbled in the Stadion HNK Rijeka.

‌



Modric, now 41, was one of the best players in the world, won the Ballon d’Or himself in 2018 but was given the complete run-around by Bellingham and Co.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



Bellingham, 23, has the capacity and potential to be England’s best-ever player. Clearly, he needs a trophy to prove it but, with performances like these, the trophies must follow.

Real Madrid star Bellingham was just unstoppable and the only shame was that only 100 England fans were in the stadium to see it.

What an absolute farce. UEFA banned Croatia fans because of racist chanting but they still let in 6,342 school kids. So much for behind-closed-doors. Mind you, Croatia were probably thankful otherwise the crowd would have turned on them.

‌



England were brilliant but Croatia were dreadful. Absolutely dreadful. Slaven Bilic has come back for a second stint and might be wishing he had not. This team has had its day.

View 3 Images Luka Modric and Bellingham shake hands before Croatia vs England

By contrast, England were bright, full of ideas and super slick. A new-look midfield partnership of Elliot Anderson and Alex Scott - both 23 - were excellent. Declan Rice might actually have a job on his hands to get back in.

‌



The last time Scott and Anderson played together was when they helped England’s under-21s win the European Championships. They have a lovely understanding which carried on into the seniors.

Scott was making his full debut after coming on as a substitute in the Czech Republic and is quickly showing England do have ball-playing midfielders who have possession in their DNA.

Of course Harry Kane scored. England’s Captain Marvel is chasing down 100 goals. Thomas Tuchel said this week he would only need 13 games to get 13 goals. Well, here were another two ticked off the list.

‌



Kane is up to 89 from 124 caps and only needs one more appearance to equal Peter Shilton’s record of 125. Even at 33, he is getting better with age.

The interesting thing is - and this has gone unnoticed in some quarters - is that Bellingham played alongside Kane at the World Cup and they have quickly formed a lethal partnership.

View 3 Images Bellingham was sensational in England's win over Croatia

‌



They teamed up together for England’s first goal. It only took eight minutes for them to open up Croatia’s lame defence.

Bellingham’s exquisite through ball put in Kane who took the ball in his stride and then smashed it into the roof of the net.

The second goal followed soon enough. Jarell Quansah and Bukayo Saka combined, Gordon supplied the pull back and that was touched in by Bellingham.

‌



England made it 3-0 before half time. Quansah whipped in a curling cross and there was Gordon running in at the back post to head home.

Croatia were having a stinker. Mateo Kovacic missed one of the biggest sitters you will ever see after a rare Anderson mistake. Clearly, the Manchester City midfielder might have other things on his mind.

‌



England made them pay. Bellingham’s low cross set up Bukayo Saka who fired in to make it 4-0. This was embarrassing. That made it one goal and two assists for Bellingham. Incredible.

It was 5-0 after 53 minutes. Anderson’s low cross was turned in by Kane. England made it 6-0 after 68 minutes. Kane’s assist set up Saka who smashed his second goal into the roof of the net.

Worse followed. Bellingham provided another assist and England substitute Morgan Rogers raced through, rounded the keeper and slotted in to inflict Croatia’s biggest-ever defeat.

Article continues below

The poor kids might not come back while the 100 England fans began chanting: “Are you Scotland in disguise?”

Sports.title: Former West Ham winger scores debut goal just five hours after completing transfer
Sports.content:
Former West Ham winger scores debut goal just five hours after completing transfer

The forward has been on the lookout for a club throughout the summer

View 2 Images Anthony Scully of Exeter City celebrates scoring a goal to make the score 1-0 (Image: Kieran McManus/Shutterstock)

Former West Ham United youngster Anthony Scully made an immediate impact with his new club - just hours after sealing the transfer. The 27-year-old has been searching for a new club over the summer.

‌



‌



The winger left Shrewsbury Town at the end of his contract back in July. After just over three months without a club, he signed a three-year deal with League Two side Exeter City on Saturday morning.

‌



He was named in the starting lineup for the league game against Rotherham United. In a day to remember, he ended up scoring what turned out to be the winning goal for his new club in a 1-0 home victory.

‌



Mikel Arteta given triple Arsenal injury boost as three stars return to training READ MORE :

The goal brought an end to a month-long League Two goal drought for the Grecians. It also secured just their second win of the league season.

Scully came up through the youth team at West Ham, but failed to make a first-team appearance for the Hammers. He completed a move to Lincoln City in 2020, and has also spent time with Wigan, Portsmouth, Colchester (loan) and Shrewsbury.

Speaking about his decision to move to Exeter, Scully said: “I'm only 27, and I'm coming into the best years of my career, so the next move for me was the most important football-wise.

‌



View 2 Images Anthony Scully of Exeter City scores a goal to make the score 1-0 (Image: Kieran McManus/Shutterstock)

“I want to be playing for a side and playing for a manager that has a style of football that suits me as a player, so that's why I held off from a few other options to hope that it would come. When Exeter came calling it was perfect.”

Manager Matt Taylor outlined what Scully would bring to the team. “Anthony is a player we’ve come across before and I’ve got strong memories of his energy, his ability on the ball and his enthusiasm for attacking moments,” he said.

‌



“He’s 27, has a strong pedigree and still has a lot to offer. He had other opportunities available to him, but he sees this as a good fit for himself, as much as we see it as a good fit for him.

Sports.title: England batter Croatia as Harry Kane underlines Ballon d'Or credentials - 5 talking points
Sports.content:
England filled their boots against Croatia in a staggering Nations League rout over their familiar but out of sorts opponents in Rijeka.

It took just eight minutes for England to take the lead in absolutely ruthless fashion, which was a sign of things to come. A stray pass from Josko Gvardiol was picked off and Jude Bellingham slid the perfect ball into Harry Kane, who found the top corner.

Bellingham made it 2-0 with a tap-in from Anthony Gordon's pass from the byline and the Barcelona forward should have put England three up inside 25 minutes, only to put his close-range effort straight at Dominik Livakovic.

It hardly mattered. Minutes later, Jarell Quansah put in a peach of a cross and Gordon stooped at the back post to head in his third goal in as many Nations League games. Mateo Kovacic passed up the chance of an open goal after Elliot Anderson was caught on the ball before it got even worse for the hosts.

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Bellingham picked out an unmarked Bukayo Saka after a flowing counter-attack to make it 4-0 before half-time. Slaven Bilic made three substitutions at the break, but it made no difference, with Kane netting from Anderson's cross early in the second half to continue the rout.

Saka added his second as Croatia's performance turned from terrible to farcical before the Arsenal winger spurned another simple chance for a hat-trick. Bellingham put a one-on-one chance wide but made up for it by completing a hat-trick of assists with a through ball for Morgan Rogers to make it 7-0.

‌



Here are the talking points from a remarkably one-sided affair.

1. Deadly Kane

It's hard to find anything new to say about England's captain, so in the absence of a unique thought I'll stick to reiterating what's already been said, yet is still worth repeating. Harry Kane is dynamite.

The way he took the opening goal underlined how he's mastered his craft. After Marc Guehi intercepted his Manchester City teammate Gvardiol's pass, Kane was already positioning himself in between the two Croatia centre-backs. He then took a perfect touch from Bellingham's pass and, without hesitating, picked out the top corner with his next touch.

‌



That was his 88th goal in 124 appearances. He added his 89th in the second half and is entirely deserving of the Ballon d'Or later this month.

View 5 Images Harry Kane opened the scoring early on (Image: Carl Recine/Getty Images)

2. Croatia get schooled

The match was played in an odd atmosphere - and that wasn't just down to England's utter dominance from kick-off. A loophole in UEFA's rules meant that 6,000 children were allowed to attend, despite Croatia - in theory - playing the game behind closed doors as punishment for racist and discriminatory fan behaviour during last year’s Nations League.

The rules state that “children up to the age of 14 (duly accompanied) from schools and/or football academies can be invited to the match free of charge”. They turned up to watch their team get schooled in Rijeka.

‌



While England were fluent and red-hot, the home defending was shambolic. The amount of space Slaven Bilic's side gave up made things very easy and gave the 100 travelling fans something to cheer.

View 5 Images Croatia's young supporters watched a shambolic display from their side (Image: MARKO PERKOV / AFP via Getty Images)

3. Spanish influence

The game was over by half-time and all four of England's goals had a Spanish influence. One of the talking points around the first Nations League game was whether the Three Lions should copy Spain's blueprint, or forge their own.

Well, they are benefiting from the country either way, with Gordon and Bellingham at the centre of their strategy under Thomas Tuchel. Everything Gordon touches turns to gold right now in an England shirt - and the confidence boost his move to Barcelona has given him shouldn't be underestimated.

‌



Bellingham, meanwhile, has been on fire for club and country of late. He ended the game with three assists and one goal to go with his three goals and three assists in seven La Liga games for Real Madrid this season. Tuchel's front four is now set in stone, with Kane, Bellingham, Saka and Gordon accounting for 26 of the team's last 30 goals.

View 5 Images Jude Bellingham ended the first half with a goal and two assists (Image: Michael Regan/The FA via Getty Images)

4. Bad night for Trent

Trent Alexander-Arnold was man of the match in the 2-0 win over Czech Republic on Tuesday but was forgotten by Saturday night. When the team sheet was given in his absence raised a few eyebrows, while Tuchel's explanation for picking Quansah only made it worse.

"There is a lot to defend on the side," the England manager said, basically confirming the long-held and widespread belief about Alexander-Arnold: that he isn't secure enough in defence. The fact that Quansah didn't have much defending to do and registered an assist with a Trent-like cross no doubt solidified Tuchel's thinking.

‌



With Reece James an established Tuchel favourite and Quansah considered a safer bet, Alexander-Arnold might have to wait a long time for another chance.

View 5 Images Jarell Quansah got an assist to cement his place in the pecking order at right-back (Image: MARKO PERKOV / AFP via Getty Images)

5. Scott sparkles

England were so good that the fact Declan Rice was sat watching the game at home on the sofa was completely forgotten. The Arsenal midfielder is the spine of Tuchel's team, yet his withdrawal has proven to be a blessing in disguise, allowing the manager to take a look at other options.

Having seen Myles Lewis-Skelly in previous games, Bournemouth's Alex Scott got the nod in Croatia. While it was the front four who took the headlines, Scott looked completely at home on his first start for his country, with his confident, smooth playing style fitting nicely into England's intensity. He won the ball back high up the pitch on a few occasions and set the ball rolling for Kane's opener with a crisp pass into Bellingham.

‌

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta given triple Arsenal injury boost as three stars return to training
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta given triple Arsenal injury boost as three stars return to training

A group of Arsenal players who weren't selected by their countries during the international break are training at London Colney, including three Gunners stars who've been injured

View 2 Images Mikel Arteta has welcomed back three players (Image: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

Arsenal stars Ben White, Cristhian Mosquera and Piero Hincapie have all returned to training in a timely boost for Mikel Arteta. The trio had each been out of action and were unavailable for international duty.

‌



‌



But they were all spotted training at London Colney as the remainder of Arteta's squad prepare for when the Premier League returns next weekend. Arsenal host Leeds in the early kick-off on Saturday, October 10.

‌



The Gunners are hoping to bounce back from their first defeat of the season last month, as they were hammered 3-0 away to Brighton. With William Saliba out because of a long-term injury, Arteta will be pleased to have defensive reinforcements.

‌



Both White and Mosquera have been out with hamstring injuries, missing one and five games respectively. Hincapie was on the bench against Brighton amid his recovery from a muscle problem but is now back in training, as seen in footage shared by Arsenal.

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



It's not all good news on the injury front, though. Christos Tzolis picked up an injury in Greece's 2-2 draw at home to the Netherlands on Thursday and reportedly faces three weeks out.

Meanwhile, Saliba is understood to be targeting a return in November. Arteta recently stressed the need to be patient, saying: "He is in rest mode at the moment.

"He had to do almost nothing, an aggravated injury, so it's going to take some time to heal. We know that."

‌



The Arsenal manager will need to make use of the depth in his squad during their upcoming run of nine games in 27 days. The reigning Premier League champions begin by welcoming Leeds to the Emirates before hosting Lille in the Champions League three days later.

View 2 Images Ben White, Cristhian Mosquera and Piero Hincapie were all seen training (Image: Arsenal)

‌



Trips to Nottingham Forest and Bayern Munich come next prior to a home game against Everton. Arsenal resume their Carabao Cup campaign at Fleetwood Town before facing Liverpool, Slavia Prague and Hull City.

Arteta wants his players to use their loss at Brighton to fuel another winning run, having claimed victory in each of their first six games in all competitions this season. "We need to feel the pain," the Gunners boss said.

"Today we need to take this lesson very, very seriously because it's going to happen. I think we need to look at it in isolation first and get the learnings and then we can put it into the overall picture."
