World.title: Canada scores a dairy win on U.S. soil as farmers grumble about Trump's trade war
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On the most elite stage in the world of competitive dairy, a Canadian teenager and her "favourite cow" scored two major wins while on U.S. soil.

Never heard of competitive dairy? Let me assure you, it's a really big deal. One win — let alone two — at the World Dairy Expo in Madison, Wisc., can be life changing for farmers and their cows.

It can boost the value of an animal by tens of thousands of dollars. Future offspring can become more valuable too. And of course, there's an element of national pride, especially when Canada and the U.S. are locked in a trade war.

Alyson Doiron, a 16-year-old high school student from Cap-Sante, Que., glows as she poses for photos with her aforementioned favourite cow — Arolene Dempsey Ella, who goes by "Ella" for short, was the five-year-old cow awarded the top prize at the International Junior Holstein Show.

"She's an easy cow to work with. We love her so much," Doiron told CBC News.

Doiron cheered and cried as she was given the prestigious honour on Ella's behalf, at the Expo on Sunday. Even though this is a global gathering, the actual competitions are between animals from Canadian and American farms, due to health and safety regulations.

"This means a lot to me," she said with a nod to her home province. "It just proves that in Quebec, the [cow] show is really really strong," she said.

The win on Sunday was just the start of a very big week for Doiron and Ella.

Sore point for some Americans

In the arena where the cows are judged, Canadian, American and Mexican flags hang in the rafters. It is a reminder, as constant as the smell of manure, that cross-border competition and co-operation are valued in this space.

"I think it's important for us to be here," said Brian Carscadden, the executive senior manager and part owner of Blondin Sires, a Quebec-based dairy company that has milk production and artificial insemination operations.

"If you think of the Westminster Dog Show, it's not unlike that. If you can win that, you've got a dog that's worth some money. It's the same here with your cow."

Carscadden and his team drove more than 1,500 kilometres from St. Placide to Madison, with 25 cows in trailers in tow. He says his business has not been affected by the trade war yet, and that it does not come up often in conversations at the Expo.

"There's jokes here and there," from his American friends, he said, along with "the odd snide remark … that makes things interesting."

Brian Carscadden, executive senior manager of the Quebec-based dairy company Blondin Sires, says there have been 'jokes here and there' about the trade war from his American friends at the Expo. (Katie Simpson/CBC)

"I always advise my Canadian colleagues that it's not our country, it's not our politics, don't talk about it."

Americans at the Expo are far more direct.

The trade war is a sore point for some, including voters who are connecting dots between U.S. President Donald Trump's broad economic agenda and increases in the cost of living.

"There is no lowering of grocery prices, no lowering of gas prices. I mean obviously it's all going higher and it makes me struggle," said Paula Lawver.

She's a single mom from a farming community in Indiana, and is at the Expo with a group of students from her son's high school. She describes herself as a conservative voter with conservative values, but does not consider herself a Republican.

She calls the dispute with Canada "nonsense," and says it will influence her vote in the midterm elections this November. Lawver says she will not support candidates in favour of tariffs and trade wars.

Retired farmer Gary Craugh, seen here with his wife Pam, says both Canada and the U.S. have been 'childish' during the trade war. (Sylvia Thomson/CBC)

Seth Muck, a farmer from New York state, says he too may reconsider how he votes in the midterms.

He says in the past he's voted "hard, hard Republican, hard conservative." But after feeling the impact of Trump's global trade agenda, he's considering backing candidates with a "bit more moderate-type agenda."

Muck says his cash crops and farm inputs have been affected the most, noting that the price of fertilizer is double what he paid last year. Though he still holds out hope that economic conditions could improve.

"Perhaps it's going to take a bit … like ripping off a Band-Aid," he said.

Even among those willing to be more patient with Trump and his economic vision, CBC News did not find any Americans at this Expo supportive of the heated rhetoric that has upended the Canada-U.S. relationship.

"I think it's needless, pointless and childish. Both sides," said Gary Craugh, a retired farmer from Wisconsin.

WATCH | Ottawa warned not to 'interfere': 'You will pay': Trump adviser warns Canada not to 'interfere' with U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:54 White House trade adviser Peter Navarro warned Canada not to 'interfere' with U.S. midterm elections in border states such as Maine and Michigan by lobbying against the Trump administration's tariffs. Navarro said Canada would 'pay even more dearly' for doing so.

Another retired farmer from Wisconsin, John Galgowski, says he's baffled by it all.

"I throw up my hands and go, 'Why are we doing this?'"

Galgowski does not support the Trump administration, and says the way the country has been run since Trump returned to office has only reaffirmed his position.

"It's just bad times," he said.

The way these voters described their experience is very different from how the Trump administration is framing the moment.

About 120 kilometres from the Expo, in Milwaukee, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer hosted a gathering of G20 trade ministers, where he unapologetically advocated for the "America first" trade agenda, arguing that the strategy is working.

"American workers and their families are better off now than they were before President Trump took office," Greer said as he read from prepared remarks.

Greer's defence of the Trump administration's policies suggests there are no plans to change course anytime soon.

Which means the trade war with Canada is poised to grind on.

Ella's big day

Even if the country-to-country tensions won't go away, Canada did score one more win at the World Dairy Expo.

On Friday, Doiron proudly paraded Ella in front of the judges on the arena floor, competing for one of the week’s largest titles: Supreme Junior Show Champion.

Doiron poses with Ella, her cow, at the World Dairy Expo in Madison, Wisc., on Monday. The Quebec teen and her five-year-old cow were awarded Supreme Champion of the Junior Show on Friday. (Katie Simpson/CBC)

It's a moment that almost didn’t happen. Doiron says she helped raise Ella, but when her parents unexpectedly sold the cow, she was devastated.

"I was so mad at my parents, because she was just the cow I liked," she said, recalling the way she loved all of Ella's spots as a kid.

Doiron was determined to be reunited with her favourite cow, and when the opportunity arose, she re-purchased Ella, despite objections from her parents. "I need to bring this cow home," she told her mom.

The reunion was clearly meant to be.

In front of a packed arena, Doiron and Ella’s big moment finally arrived — the cow was named Supreme Junior Show Champion, a victory for all of Canada.

World.title: Internal documents show why Ottawa is worried about the Alberta referendum, even if the province votes to stay
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Internal federal documents offer insights into how Ottawa is assessing the economic fallout from the possibility of Alberta separating from Canada and becoming an independent state.

The documents from Finance Canada and the Justice Department also shed light on the consequences being considered from the uncertainty caused by Alberta separatism.

Finance Canada briefing notes, released to CBC News through access to information legislation, detail the federal government has been quietly studying the impact of a possible $18-billion fiscal shock, corporate head office flight and a mass exodus of Albertans to neighbouring provinces if Alberta exits the federation.

It also flags that federal pension laws are "flawed" and might not be up to the task of dealing with the possibility of Alberta exiting the Canada Pension Plan.

Much of the documents were redacted but still shed light on a range of outcomes the government is considering this fall.

The documents are dated June 2026.

Alberta's Oct. 19 referendum asks voters whether the province should remain in Canada or hold another vote at a future date to leave. Up until now much of the analysis of the economic hit of Alberta potentially separating has focused on the impact on the province instead of Canada as a whole.

Although polling indicates more Albertans want to remain in Canada than leave, the documents show even the possibility of a separation referendum could cause economic harm to Canada and the province.

Exodus of business headquarters

The analysis invokes the 1995 Quebec referendum which resulted in Quebecers voting to remain in Canada by a tight margin.

Data from bond and equity markets showed that vote coincided with "tightening in financial conditions both provincially and nationally," it states.

Businesses, it notes, delayed "investment decisions pending greater clarity regarding future economic arrangement."

Citing data from the Conseil du patronat du Québec during the late 1970s and early 1980s, it states that 263 major corporate head offices, including Sun Life, left Montreal.

"Lingering uncertainty in Alberta could trigger a similar exodus of headquarters, especially for non-resources sector companies," the documents state.

Under the heading "interprovincial population outflow," it notes that in 2021 Alberta saw nearly 17,500 net workers with post-secondary degrees move into the province — and suggests highly educated and highly skilled workers would leave an independent Alberta in large numbers.

CBC News asked Finance Canada for more details about the department's work studying the impact of the Alberta referendum.

Instead, the Privy Council Office responded with an emailed statement which said the federal government is "conducting its own study of various third-party economic analyses" on the potential costs of Alberta's separation from Canada.

"Alberta is an integral part of Canada and contributes significantly to the prosperity of Albertans and Canadians. Alberta is stronger as part of a united Canada," wrote Privy Council spokesperson Mélany Gauvin.

15% of national GDP

The analysis is also a reminder of how much the Albertan economy provides for the rest of Canada.

Between 2022 and 2024, Alberta's net fiscal contribution averaged roughly $18 billion annually.

With the province accounting for $475 billion in annual economic activity, Alberta represents 15 per cent of national GDP over the last decade.

Over the same time period the province also accounted for 31 per cent of Canada's exports. Most of this came from energy.

WATCH | Ranchers weigh in on separation: Stability or a fair shake: Ranchers' perspectives on separation | Duration closed caption 2:24 With just weeks to go until the referendum, CBC News reached out to ranchers in southeast Alberta to ask how they'll vote and what the end result could mean for their livelihoods.

University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe has completed a similar analysis on the impact of separation. Tombe, who is part of the federalist group Lead Not Leave, notes that in 2024 Ottawa collected more than $19 billion than it spent in the province.

An independent Alberta would get to keep that money but Tombe's report found it would be quickly eaten up by NATO defence commitments, expenses related to assuming federal operations and falling revenues from a shrinking economy.

In an interview with CBC News, Tombe said although Canada stands to lose a lot from Alberta leaving, the real loser would be his province.

"Without doubt, it would be Alberta that would experience the largest economic disruption as a result of separation," Tombe said.

Canada Pension Plan impacts

Tombe has also done some number crunching on the impact of Alberta exiting the Canada Pension Plan.�

The CPP was established in 1966 as a measure to provide retirement income to older Canadians and to make up for gaps in private pensions.

The plan has opt-out provisions and a formula to transfer assets, but the internal document notes the federal government's independent overseer of the CPP, the chief actuary, is concerned about the wording and payout formula set out in the federal law that governs the pension plan.

"In addition to the legislation being open to interpretation, the chief actuary has indicated that the formula it sets out is flawed," the documents state.

When the CPP and the legislation that came with it was set up in the 1960s, its assets were invested in provincial bonds.

But now the fund is invested in infrastructure like airports, equities and other global bonds — making divesting Alberta's share complicated.

"I would anticipate that if a province were to want to exercise their right to withdraw that the Supreme Court would have to make a ruling on what the language in the act ultimately means," Tombe said.

World.title: Canada bet billions on an EV boom. Was it too much, too soon?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal and provincial governments bet billions on the rapid rise of the electric vehicle industry. But major EV and battery projects in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia have since been delayed, cancelled, suspended, substantially changed — and in one case, gone bankrupt — as automakers and suppliers adjust to weaker-than-anticipated demand.

The latest is Volkswagen's massive PowerCo battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont., where production has been pushed back two years to 2029, because of "evolving market demand."

The setbacks are raising questions about whether Canada bet too big on how quickly the EV market would grow. Critics say demand may never reach the levels needed to support the scale of battery production governments sought to attract, while others argue these are temporary delays in the decades-long shift toward electrification.

A million batteries, but for what?

Grieg Mordue, a former Toyota executive and retired McMaster University professor who studied the auto industry, says the St. Thomas plant illustrates two problems with Canada's EV investment strategy: scale and location.

When the project was announced in 2023, PowerCo said the plant would eventually make enough battery cells for roughly one million EVs a year.

Mordue says that seemed inefficient since Volkswagen's major assembly operations are in the southern United States and Mexico, meaning batteries produced in St. Thomas would have to travel long distances to reach the vehicles they're intended to power.

A person handles an electric vehicle battery on display at the EV & Charging Expo in Toronto. Ottawa and the provinces have committed billions of dollars in public support to attract EV and battery manufacturing. (Oksana Shtohryn/CBC)

Europe isn't the obvious destination either, he says, because Volkswagen (VW) already has battery production capacity there.

Even together, VW's North American plants don't produce enough vehicles to provide an obvious market for a million batteries a year.

"They got a million batteries," he said. "What are they going to do with them?"

VW and its PowerCo subsidiary did not respond to a request for comment.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford speaks at a news conference announcing the St. Thomas plant in 2023. (Kate Dubinski/CBC)

VW has said the plant remains a cornerstone of its North American battery strategy and is continuing construction even as it pushes production back.

VW also said the delay will allow it to incorporate newer battery technology and scale production as demand develops.

It could also have an upside for taxpayers, Mordue said — in the form of a smaller subsidy bill.

Much of the support promised to Volkswagen is still tied to how many batteries the plant produces. With production now set for 2029, and with those incentives scheduled to start declining in 2030 and ending in 2032, Mordue said governments will likely pay "a whole lot less" than the original maximum.

Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada said in a statement that the federal government has so far contributed $700 million to the construction of the St. Thomas battery plant, noting Ontario is responsible for one third of the $13.2 billion governments have agreed to in production subsidies.

" The government remains engaged with PowerCo on their updated timelines," the statement said.

Ontario's Ministry of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade did not respond by deadline.

A bet on the long-term

Still, others argue that looking at today's EV demand misses the time scale on which investments such as St. Thomas were made.

A sign marks the entrance to General Motors' CAMI Assembly plant in Ingersoll, Ont. The plant was converted into Canada's first full-scale EV plant in 2022, but production was suspended in 2025. (Denis Babin/CBC/Radio-Canada)

"These investments are meant to last 50 to 70 years or more," Joanna Kyriazis, director of policy and strategy at Clean Energy Canada, told CBC News.

She said the current slowdown should be seen as growing pains in an industry that is still transitioning, rather than evidence Canada built too much battery capacity.

There are signs Canada's EV market may already be recovering after a slowdown.

New registrations of battery-only EVs rose 37.4 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, compared with the same time last year, according to Statistics Canada. When hybrids are included, Canadians registered 58,811 new zero-emission vehicles during the quarter, up 26.7 per cent.

Kyriazis says the investments are about keeping Canada relevant as the global auto industry undergoes a historic shift from gasoline-powered vehicles.

An electric vehicle's charging port is displayed at the 2026 Canadian International AutoShow in Toronto. Despite government subsidies for producers and consumers, electric vehicles accounted for 11.7 per cent of new light-duty vehicle sales in Canada in the first three months of 2026. (Michael Charles Cole/CBC)

"It's not a question of maintaining a place in the North American auto industry. It's: is Canada going to have an auto industry that survives in the 21st century at all?" she said.

"There's a clear direction that the global auto sector is going and if Canada wants to have a competitive auto sector into the future, we've got to be able to make and sell competitively priced electric vehicles and the parts that go into them."

Kyriazis says the potential market for these batteries also extends beyond electric vehicles. As electricity grids expand, batteries will increasingly be needed to store power and help balance supply and demand.

The St. Thomas site and a NextStar plant in Windsor, she said, "were looking at a short-term strategy of building batteries that would be used for grid-scale storage while EV [uptake] in North America started to sort of even out."

Kyriazis argues the current U.S. retreat from electric vehicles could prove temporary and that Canada shouldn't base a decades-long industrial strategy on policies that could change again under a future administration.

There is evidence the EV battery bet may have been early rather than fundamentally misplaced. The wider justification for building domestic battery capacity hasn't disappeared either.

China produced more than 80 per cent of the world's battery cells last year, according to the International Energy Agency, leaving governments in North America and Europe to build domestic supply chains in an industry that remains heavily concentrated in Asia.

Will buyers catch up?

University of Guelph economics professor Ross McKitrick is less convinced that time will solve the problem. He said EVs have an established market, but argues governments built their policy around expectations of demand far greater than what has so far emerged.

"What the government's been trying to do is force that market into existence," he said. "The numbers just don't add up."

McKitrick points to the billions governments offered manufacturers to build EVs and batteries, while simultaneously offering consumers incentives to buy the vehicles as evidence the industry wasn't able to sustain itself on the scale governments envisioned.

In a 2024 paper published in the Canadian Journal of Economics, McKitrick warned that if Canada's EV sales requirements rise faster than buyers' willingness to purchase them, it could hurt automakers and the wider economy.

Ottawa scrapped EV sales requirements in 2026 and is moving to repeal the broader federal mandate. It announced replacement emissions standards in February with consultations on the proposed regulations running until Oct. 29.

Electric vehicles still account for a minority of new vehicle sales in Canada, despite years of government incentives aimed at encouraging consumers to buy them.

Electric vehicles accounted for 11.7 per cent of new light-duty vehicle sales in Canada in the first three months of 2026, according to Transport Canada, down from a peak of 15.4 per cent in 2024.

"At this point, it's a niche market," McKitrick said. "Some households like the product and are willing to pay for it."

World.title: Woman, 2 children dead after serious collision near Foam Lake, Sask.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A serious collision near Foam Lake, Sask., Friday afternoon has left three people dead.

On Friday afternoon, a truck was attempting to pass a semi and collided with an SUV on a grid road about nine kilometres west of Foam Lake, RCMP said in a Saturday news release. Foam Lake is about 150 kilometres northeast of Regina.

A 40-year old woman, an eight-year old girl and a five-year old girl, all from Foam Lake, were in the SUV and were declared dead at the scene by EMS.

An adult man was also in the SUV and was taken to hospital by STARS with serious injuries, the release said.

The driver of the truck was taken to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, and two passengers were also taken to hospital. One passenger had non-life-threatening injuries, according to EMS, while the other had serious injuries, according to STARS, the release said.

The semi driver not not report any physical injuries to police and his semi was not damaged.

RCMP say 40-year-old Kelly Knopf from Sumter, South Carolina, was arrested and charged with three counts each of dangerous operation of a vehicle causing death and dangerous operation of a vehicle causing bodily harm.

He is scheduled to appear in Yorkton Provincial Court on Monday.

Wadena/Foam Lake RCMP continue to investigate with the assistance of a Saskatchewan RCMP collision reconstructionist.

World.title: Sliding student scores spark fresh calls to revisit how we're teaching math
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Earlier this week, Kendra Corbett stood at a blackboard breaking down an addition question for her Grade 3s, laying out step by step how to determine the answer and occasionally testing out suggestions her students called out.

A little later, she split her class into groups. Some youngsters played math games while others worked on an assignment using base ten blocks — manipulating the small plastic cubes, bars and squares (denoting units of one, 10 and 100, respectively). Corbett settled in with a handful of kids for a focused lesson on ordering numbers from least to greatest. All the activities allowed for practice learning three-digit numbers.

"We assume kids come in knowing what numbers actually mean. If they can count to 10, that doesn't necessarily mean they understand what 10 represents," said Corbett, a teacher in Upper Grand District School Board in Orangeville, Ont., some 60 kilometres northwest of Toronto.

"If they don't have the foundation of knowing what numbers actually mean and understanding of magnitude, then they're really going to struggle later on."

Knowledge and understanding of math rests on building blocks that students usually start developing in primary school. But with recent international and provincial assessments warning about sluggish and waning math skills among Canadian students — a slide that pre-dates the pandemic — some experts say we should revisit how we teach math and pay numeracy the same attention literacy has received in recent years.

What worries Canadian mathematician John Mighton are the changes happening over time, specifically the growth in students who are slipping to lower levels — where some can only handle basic math or are considered below functional numeracy — and the wider impact of that trend.

"That's a real threat to our country, to our economy, even to our political system. How can you think your way through problems that involve risk or probabilities or science if you can't do the simplest math?" said Mighton.

A Grade 3 student uses base ten blocks to help visualize three-digit numbers. (CBC)

"It's a tragedy that we think math is not as important as it as and that we're not doing something about it."

Back in 2002, Mighton founded JUMP Math, an education charity that's grown to work with students and teachers in K-8 schools across Canada and abroad.

Teaching novices a new concept takes a different approach than teaching those already fluent in a topic, he says, yet much math instruction of the past 20 years has treated kids like experts before they're ready.

"From day one, you're given a lot of rich problems … highly contextualized, lots of complexity, lots of language. People don't feel they're really giving kids math unless they're doing that kind of problem," Mighton said.

Mathematician and educator John Mighton, left, seen with colleague Dana El Assi, says some math education tends to confuse the goal with the means to reach it. (Jessica Wong/CBC)

"We mistake the end where we want to get kids to — we want them to be great chess players, great problem solvers — with the means to get them there," he said.

"Guide kids more, scaffold more, give more practice, build foundational knowledge, so the kids can become experts …When you do that, kids become much better problem-solvers."

LISTEN | Deep debate about teaching math: The Current 25:25 Are your kids learning math the RIGHT way?

Building a solid foundation and then strong reasoning and problem-solving skills are especially important amid the rise of artificial intelligence, he says.

"It's a dangerous idea that kids are just going to be able to deal with all the challenges that are coming from AI … if they don't have any domain-specific knowledge, particularly in mathematics.

"You're going to be so easily fooled and misled and you'll make disastrous decisions if you don't understand the math."

Not a return to rote learning

As with the recent shift toward more explicit, structured and phonics-led literacy teaching, there's a growing call for more systematic, teacher-led, direct instruction in math.

That doesn't mean rote learning, Mighton says, but does mean relying on evidence-based practices. He encourages teachers to use screenings, for instance, and regular low-stakes assessments to help them to make adjustments that propel students' progression.

WATCH | Building skills and confidence: How to build math skills and student confidence: Mighton | Duration closed caption 2:00 Mathematician John Mighton on teachers drawing from the science of learning to help students bridge gaps and build math knowledge, why that doesn't mean a comeback for rote learning and why knowing math is vital for kids.

There's a wealth of research about how children learn — on their attention spans, their ability to absorb information, barriers to that, and more — yet that research doesn't always translate into classrooms nor into the training that aspiring and working teachers receive, says neuroscientist Daniel Ansari, a professor of psychology and education at Western University in London, Ont.

He also advocates breaking up math learning into multiple, simplified steps, because it helps developing minds more readily pick up information.

"Sometimes teaching can assume that children start out as experts and they are required immediately to focus on their understanding, explaining their answers. And these sorts of things can overwhelm their cognitive systems and thereby prevent information making its way into long-term memory," he said.

Ansari says educators can absolutely strike a "balance between explicit instruction and letting children discover things working by themselves," but adds teachers must keep in mind what's developmentally appropriate and what learners are ready for.

Western University professor Daniel Ansari says the wealth of research about how children learn doesn't always reach students or their teachers. (Western University)

Take timed practice — a.k.a. those "mad minute" sheets with rows of addition, subtraction, multiplication or division questions to be answered as quickly as possible — as an example.

Introduced too early, it overwhelms cognitive capacity, Ansari says. But once students have some time to learn and a bit of practice, "mad minutes serve as a way of increasing and deepening their fluency — and then it can also become something really fun."

Rather than touting a "back to basics" mentality, Ansari instead suggests we consider "how can we improve things further, pick some things that we maybe discarded too early? Keep some things we're doing right now, but reassess some others."

Back in Orangeville, Upper Grand K-12 math lead Ashley Kozak has overseen a multi-pronged plan to improve early math learning. It includes central math facilitators, creating new teaching resources, employing an early math screener and, for the schools with the greatest need, sending in support teachers to deliver focused tutoring.

Updated math training for Grade 1 and Grade 3 teachers and principals has also boosted educator confidence, Kozak says, adding the board saw improvement in its latest EQAO results.

While she loves seeing kids' "a-ha" moments when visiting math classes, she says it's even better seeing students confidently approach the next questions.

"It's more than memorization. It's about problem-solving. It's about making those connections," she said. "Seeing that ... makes me feel like 'OK, we got this. We can do it.'"

World.title: U.A.E. says co-pilot on FlyDubai plane that nearly crashed attacked captain with cockpit's crash axe
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The co-pilot suspected of stabbing the captain of an Israel-bound FlyDubai flight before passengers and others stopped the attack is an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami, three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf and Western diplomat, said on Saturday.

The United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said Saturday that the co-pilot attacked the captain with the cockpit's crash axe and tried to take control of the plane in a "terrorist attack."

"Investigations into the incident involving FlyDubai flight FZ1073 found that the co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist attack," Prosecutor General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said in a statement carried by the U.A.E.'s state news agency.

The prosecutor general's comments were the first by Emirati investigators to describe the incident as an attempted terrorist attack. While Emirati authorities and the airline have not publicly identified the co-pilot, Israeli officials have previously said he is an Omani national.

All three people who identified the co-pilot spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. The Gulf diplomat said investigations are underway to establish whether he acted as a "lone wolf or has any connection with any extremist groups."

The co-pilot, who officials said nearly crashed the sharply plummeting flight with more than 170 people aboard, was barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, a separate person familiar with the matter said.

The co-pilot was then hired by the U.A.E.-based airline FlyDubai, the person said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. It was not immediately clear to what extent he was vetted when he was hired. Oman's barring of him was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

An official says the co-pilot was born in the U.A.E.

How the co-pilot managed to be working in the cockpit on Wednesday morning is a central question for investigators. Israel says it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don't maintain diplomatic relations with it. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations.

There was no immediate comment from the U.A.E. government or Oman Air. Oman's government has said nothing publicly in response to repeated questions since the incident.

FlyDubai said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still under investigation and that it was not in a position to comment further, a spokesperson said on Saturday.

The co-pilot was born in the U.A.E. and his mother is Syrian, according to another regional official with knowledge of the investigation.

WATCH | FlyDubai pilot tells Indian PM how he managed to open cockpit door: 'I can't let anyone die': FlyDubai pilot tells Indian PM how he managed to open cockpit door | Duration closed caption 5:33 Capt. Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a FlyDubai flight, described how he fought for his life in the minutes after his co-pilot stabbed him and the plane began a steep descent. He spoke with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a video call broadcast live on television news channels.

The official confirmed that the co-pilot worked with Oman's national airline but was removed from flying because of concerns that he showed signs of extremist views. He was later moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, the official said.

Security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot's motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss details of the investigation.

U.A.E. senior diplomatic adviser Anwar Gargash on Friday called the attack a "dangerous terrorist act" in a post on X. The incident is a test for the U.A.E government, which has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has also bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.

A social media account was deleted the day of the flight

Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot's background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone "Islamist radicalization," but provided no evidence.

WATCH | How FlyDubai Flight 1073 survived impossible odds: How FlyDubai Flight 1073 survived impossible odds | About That | Duration 2:58 Andrew Chang breaks down what we know about the apparent attempt to hijack a FlyDubai flight bound for Tel Aviv and how the plane landed safely despite all odds. Images provided by The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images

The captain, who was badly wounded, has said he used his remaining energy while being stabbed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed alarmingly unusual sounds to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilize the plane. It made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

Investigators have not publicly identified the object used to stab the captain or said whether it was carried onto the plane or came from inside the aircraft.

Both the captain and co-pilot were later taken to the U.A.E. as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating.

An Israeli government official confirmed that Israeli investigators would take part alongside Emirati authorities in the U.A.E.-led investigation.

The aircraft dropped about 16,625 feet in just over 30 seconds while flying over Saudi Arabia on its journey from the U.A.E. to Israel, according to flight-tracking data from Flightradar24. The route is popular among Israeli travellers. Most passengers aboard the plane were Israeli nationals.

Once crew and passengers intervened, the plane landed safely in Saudi Arabia.

World.title: Hudson Williams wore this cardigan. Then the Indigenous designer's business went viral
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Canadian actor Hudson Williams stepped out wearing a piece by Canadian Indigenous designer Justin Jacob Louis on Wednesday, Louis didn't expect to go viral.

In fact, he nearly forgot it was happening.

The Samson Cree Nation-born designer was spending National Day for Truth and Reconciliation away from work. He was with his family, unplugged and out paddling on the lake.

And then he checked his phone.

"There was, like, a whole bunch of sales and the social media was lighting up and I was just like, 'What is going on? Did something happen?'" he said in an interview with CBC News.

"I realized that, like, every cardigan had sold out. At that time, there was like $12,000 in sales in a matter of an hour. And I was like, 'What the hell?'"

WATCH | Designer speaks about viral sweater worn by Hudson Williams: How Hudson Williams sold out an Indigenous-designed cardigan | Duration 0:47 On National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Heated Rivalry star Hudson Williams wore a cardigan by Indigenous designer Justin Jacob Louis to the Kate Spade New York Global Summit on Women's Mental Health. Within hours of his appearance, the sweater sold out online — with Louis saying the surge in sales across his website amounted to two to three months' worth in just two days.

The Heated Rivalry star wore Louis's blue-and-black journey knit cardigan to the Kate Spade New York Global Summit on Women's Mental Health, along with an orange ribbon on his chest marking National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

For Louis, seeing his work worn that day by a prominent Canadian actor made the moment "pretty special."

"There was intention and genuine interest in supporting us behind it, so that made it more meaningful for me," Louis said.

The cardigan, which costs $350, was designed by Louis, founder and creative director of Section 35 and the Justin Jacob Louis label. And it made its way to Williams as part of a last minute request.

How they connected

Louis said someone from Williams's team initially contacted him by email and over Instagram about the actor's interest in buying the piece — just last weekend.

Shipping it from his warehouse wasn't feasible within the timeframe, but he happened to have the right size at his studio in the Fraser Valley in Chilliwack, B.C.

Someone from Williams's team drove from Vancouver to Louis's studio that Sunday to pick it up.

From left: Jacob Tierney, Brendan Brady, Jayme Alter Wilson, Williams, Connor Storrie, Rachel Reid, Ksenia Daniela Kharlamova and Christina Chang appear at the summit on Wednesday. (Jason Lowrie/BFA)

Months of sales in two days

That choice had an immediate impact on Louis's small business.

The brand gained hundreds of new followers throughout the day. The cardigan sold out and other pieces began selling, too.

Louis estimates the shop did two to three months worth of sales in just two days.

While the brand hadn't planned on restocking the cardigan, the huge surge in demand persuaded Louis to open up pre-orders.

"For an independent small business, it helps out so much," he said. "It's just been kind of a whirlwind."

Design based on a dream

Louis says the design came to him in a dream he had while feeling disconnected and homesick and living about 12 hours from the community where he grew up.

Loius says the design for the cardigan came to him in a dream. (Alex Waber)

In the dream, he was back at his father's place, walking across the pasture in winter under the night sky, wondering where his ancestors were.

"The stars in the sky lit up and then they turned into eyeballs and looked right at me," Louis said.

"It was just kind of like this reminder that they're always with you wherever you are, no matter how far from home you are."

Louis says Williams messaged him directly to thank him for the cardigan. They've stayed in touch, and the designer says he'd love to work with Williams again.

But for now, he's focused on continuing to design and build his labels.

Here's his advice to other designers and small businesses: stay intentional and true to your values and culture.

"That makes us who we are," he said. "Showcasing the beauty that exists within our communities. I think there's so much talent and the storytelling that comes from our people and our stories. It's what sets us apart. And I think staying true to that is so important."

World.title: Jesse Kline: CBC shows anti-Jewish bias with suspension of Neil Herland
World.content:
It has long been apparent that the CBC’s coverage of the Middle East has had a clear anti-Israel bias. But recent events hint at something much darker: an institutional willingness to downplay or minimize harms caused to Jews, including those living right here in Canada.

In the lead-up to last month’s 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, the public broadcaster came under fire for an internal memo sent by its senior director of journalistic standards and public trust, Basem Boshra, cautioning journalists not to refer to the events as “terrorist attacks,” unless quoting someone else.

The backlash was so severe that Boshra ended up capitulating the following day, saying, “After reviewing our current language guidance, we have decided to adjust it to clarify that direct attribution is not required for describing the historic events of 9/11 as terrorism.”

But that policy change did not extend to the broadcaster’s coverage of Hamas’s October 7 massacre, in which 1,200 people, mostly civilians, were brutally murdered — many having been raped, tortured and dismembered — and more than 250 were abducted into captivity by a group classified as a terrorist organization in Canada.

Whether that was a terrorist attack is apparently still up for debate, according to our taxpayer-funded public broadcaster.

The effects of the CBC’s refusal to call a spade a spade when it comes terrorism was on full display on Wednesday morning, after the co-pilot on a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying around 180 passengers, mostly Israeli, allegedly stabbed the pilot, causing the plane to plummet over 5,000 metres in less than a minute.

The only thing that prevented another 9/11-style event was a group of heroic Israeli passengers who reportedly stormed the cockpit, restrained the would-be terrorist and managed to stabilize the plane, along with two off-duty pilots who successfully performed an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia an hour later.

Yet when the CBC published a Reuters wire story on the incident at 6:15 a.m. ET on Wednesday, its initial headline read: FlyDubai Flight En Route To Israel Descends Rapidly, After Reported Disturbance In Cockpit.

This was a clear attempt to minimize the incident by calling what appears to be an attempted hijacking a “disturbance in the cockpit,” and characterizing a narrowly averted plane crash as a rapid descent.

It is the opposite of clickbait: a headline crafted to ensure as few people as possible actually bother to read the story, which clearly stated that Israeli officials had characterized it as a “terror attack.”

Given the CBC’s history of bias against Israel, one has to wonder if the story would have been treated differently if the vast majority of the passengers weren’t Israeli.

Or perhaps I should say if the passengers weren’t Jewish, because while the broadcaster’s post-October 7 coverage has both denigrated Israel and highlighted the plight of the Canadian victims of antisemitism, the CBC showed its true colours in its handling of radio host Neil Herland.

Herland made headlines last week when he tweeted about his experience being accosted by protesters on his way to a Yom Kippur service held at the Meridian Arts Centre in northern Toronto. Video shared by Herland shows a group of agitators standing outside the front entrance of the building waving Palestinian flags.

A man with a megaphone can be heard shouting “Zionist alert,” as a woman beside him holds a sign reading, “Where’s Your Humanity.” Another man puts a megaphone next to Herland’s ear and repeatedly screams, “You’re going to hell!”

Others were also reportedly berated by the demonstrators, including a woman who was called an “ugly Jewish b–ch,” and a cantor (who’s responsible for the musical part of the service), who heard someone shout, “The Jew smiles while he murders babies in Gaza!”

Given what took place, I’d forgive Herland if he had some choice words for the people who had gathered to harass Canadian Jews attending a religious service on the holiest day of the year, but that’s not what he did.

Describing himself as a journalist who happens to be Jewish, he instead recounted his experience being “met by protesters trying to taunt and intimidate me from entering the building.”

In a series of follow-up tweets, he talked about how his father was an Austrian Jew who survived the Holocaust, and how he recently got an Austrian passport in case he needs to flee Canada due to rampant antisemitism.

He discussed how congregants at the synagogue were already on edge, given that the cantor’s nephew had recently been murdered in a suspected hate crime in Ukraine and a gunman tried to slaughter a shul full of people in Belleville, Ont., the night before.

He spoke out against this country’s antisemitism problem and the lack of awareness many Canadians seem to have about it. And he noted that the guest speaker that evening gave a speech about “making peace in the Middle East” — hardly something anyone should be protesting against.

It was, in other words, the sharing of a “lived experience” that one would think would warm the cockles of the hearts of the CBC’s lefty executives. Yet instead of praising, or offering sympathy for, Herland, they suspended him.

When the CBC received a complaint in 2022 that a Muslim journalist gave her personal opinions in an interview during the coverage of a vigil for the four Muslim victims of a truck-ramming attack in London, Ont., the previous year, then-CBC ombudsman Jack Nagler stated that her observations “should be seen as reporting based on ‘lived experience’ that gives non-Muslim Canadians insight into the lives and perspectives of Muslims in our community.”

Which is exactly what Herland did, only he was sharing insights into the lives of Jewish-Canadians.

Perhaps Herland is being treated differently because he’s a host, rather than a reporter or a pundit, or because his report was delivered via Twitter, outside the CBC’s editorial control.

It’s also possible that the CBC succumbed to a campaign launched by Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East, a group that commonly files complaints against anyone in the media who dares express pro-Israel sentiments and has lodged a complaint with the CBC ombudsman accusing Herland of spreading “disinformation that defames pro-Palestinian activists.”

Or maybe the broadcaster really does have a systemic bias against Jews and is trying to minimize Jewish suffering by writing misleading headlines and silencing Jewish journalists.

We don’t know because CBC execs apparently don’t think they’re accountable to the taxpayers who pay their salaries, and are refusing to comment on the situation due to “privacy” concerns.

Unlike the backlash against the broadcaster’s 9/11 policy, which affected people from a wide range of ethnic backgrounds in Canada and internationally, it would appear as though when Jews are the sole victims, it is largely left to the Jewish community to fight for what is right.
