World.title: I moved to Mexico City in my 20s. Here’s what I learned
World.content:
If you move to Mexico City in your 20s, I hope it becomes a home and not just a destination.

I came to Mexico at 25 thinking I was moving abroad one more time. I had already lived outside Spain, so I knew what it meant to arrive somewhere new, figure out a city, make friends and eventually find my way around. I thought Mexico City would be another chapter in that story.

A year later, I realized something else happened. I didn’t just move to Mexico; I started building a life here.

When you’re in your 20s, it’s easy to romanticize starting over somewhere else. How many of us, after a mental breakdown, have thought about leaving everything behind? Maybe moving to Paris like Blair, or finding the messy, exciting life Carrie Bradshaw had in New York City in her 30s.

I’m not saying New York or Paris won’t give you what you need to find. They might. But I found something in Mexico City that I wasn’t necessarily looking for: a place where I could become a slightly different version of myself.

Asking better questions in a new city

For me, my 20s have become less about figuring everything out and more about asking better questions. Do I want to become a mother? Will I get married? What do I want my career to look like? What kind of woman do I want to become? What do I want my future family to look like? I don’t have the answers yet. But living abroad has made me more conscious of the questions.

When I told my friends in Europe that I was moving to Mexico, some of them were worried. I wasn’t particularly afraid. My biggest concern was more mundane: I love walking, and I simply wondered whether I would be able to walk as much as I did back home. I quickly found out I could. I walk from our apartment in San Miguel de Chapultepec to Condesa to see friends, or go to a class. I walk through Chapultepec Park almost every day, and sometimes all the way to Polanco, which can take close to an hour.

One of the first things Mexico City taught me was how easily we can misunderstand places we’ve never experienced ourselves.

Before coming to Mexico, I only knew two Mexicans. They had been exchange students in Finland when I was studying there in 2020 and 2021. We weren’t friends. I just remember them being very good at beer pong and drinking rum or gin with water.

Then I arrived. And I started meeting people.

Finding kindness in the unlikeliest moments

Before Mexico, the country that completely changed my understanding of human connection was Cuba. I would need to write another article about everything that island gave me, but I truly thought nothing could surprise me in the same way again. Until Mexico did.

On my third day living in Mexico City, I was waiting in line to pay for a haircut. The woman behind me noticed what I was doing and immediately told me there was a cheaper hairdresser in the shop across the street. This act of kindness was the first one that people have shown me here. They aren’t normally dramatic moments, but they happen very often. Sometimes it is smiling in the street, starting a conversation or simply making an effort when they have no reason to.

At home, you move through your busy day surrounded by people and routines that are familiar. Abroad, you become more aware of your interactions, and they end up becoming part of what makes a place feel like yours.

There was another adjustment I was not expecting. As a European — very active and not particularly patient — I was struck by how slowly life seemed to move here. I learned that “ahorita” doesn’t necessarily mean right now. It can mean soon. It can mean later. Most of the time it’s just a polite way of saying something will happen when it happens. And you’ll get your coffee when you’re meant to get it. If you’re in a hurry, I recommend you insist a couple of times.

How different neighborhoods shape who you are

One of the things that continues to amaze me about Mexico City is how different each neighborhood feels. Polanco and Santa Fe have their own rhythm: business, luxury, restaurants, offices, polished cars and people dressed for work.

Then you go to Condesa or Roma, and suddenly you’re surrounded by leafy streets, cafes, parks and lots of dogs. I spend a lot of time in Parque México with a good friend of mine who has lived here since 2024, and we still find ourselves surprised by what we see: people dancing, doing karate, playing pickleball, learning to skate, practicing hula-hoop, someone selling poems, couples sitting on benches, foreigners taking photographs of a scene that locals barely notice because, to them, it’s simply Tuesday. That is Mexico City.

The Historic Center still leaves me speechless: the old buildings, the ruins, the Zócalo, Alameda Central, Palacio de Bellas Artes, Museo Nacional de Arte (MUNAL), the markets and the streets where centuries of history exist on top of each other.

And then there is Coyoacán, Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera, colorful markets, museums, and streets that feel completely different from the rest of the city.

The most interesting part is not just that these neighborhoods look different. They also make you feel different. You become a different version of yourself depending on where you are in the city. And in your 20s, that gives you something I have learned to appreciate: perspective.

Experiencing Mexican art and architecture

I’ve visited many museums since arriving — some of the famous ones and others that are less known. I don’t want to pretend I can explain Mexican art after a year here. But I can say that I have never experienced history through public art in quite the same way. The murals of Diego Rivera are not simply beautiful paintings. They tell stories about Mexico, its people and its history. Artists like Frida Kahlo transformed personal pain into art and became part of a cultural identity recognized around the world. I was also so impressed by Luis Barragán. Have you seen his house in San Miguel de Chapultepec? It was designed in the late 1940s, and I swear if you discover it today, you’ll want to move in there. Mexico City reminds me that contemporary doesn’t always mean new.

The joys of Mexican food

The same happened with food. Unpopular opinion: I’m not a foodie. I enjoy a latte and a cookie as much as avocado toast or a good meal at a cool restaurant every once in a while. Just give me some food when I’m hungry, and I’ll be happy. But even I have been fascinated by Mexican food. Mexican cuisine was recognized as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2010, and one of the things I’ve learned is that there is no single thing called “Mexican food.” Ingredients, dishes and traditions change so much from state to state.

Even as a vegetarian, I have found myself trying things I never expected to eat: nopal, huitlacoche and many other ingredients I did not know of before arriving.

And Mexico City is not only Mexican food. You can eat Thai, Italian, Spanish, Chinese … you name it, you’ll find it. I even discovered one of my favorite Lebanese places here in the Historic Center.

Lessons in community through Día de los Muertos

I moved to Mexico City about a year ago, just as the rainy season was ending and Independence Day celebrations were beginning. I was warned before arriving that people knew how to celebrate. “But isn’t that true everywhere?” I thought. Especially coming from Spain, where we’re always down to party. But I understood quickly that celebration here can mean something bigger than drinking late into the night. There is a sense of community, belonging and gathering together.

To this day, experiencing Día de los Muertos in Mexico has been one of the best experiences of my life. We went to the village of Malinalco, less than two hours from Mexico City, to visit family altars. We entered house after house, each one belonging to families that had lost someone that year. Every house was different. Some had large patios and modern buildings; others were old. In all of them, they replicated the profession of the person who had died through objects, decorations and food: a baker, a secretary, a police officer, a chef. The altars were filled with bright orange cempasúchil flowers and candles.

In some of them, we lit our own candles as a sign of respect. Every family gave us something to eat and drink — from tamales and tacos to mezcal, tequila or warm spiced wine. In some of them, you could really feel the presence of the person being remembered. How generous of those families, after losing their loved ones, to celebrate their lives with us, strangers to them. It was so magical. I left with tears in my eyes from the lesson in humanity I had just experienced.

Building a life together while making it your own

I’m not single, and my boyfriend and I moved here together. Some people might think moving with your partner in your 20s means you miss out on the experience. That hasn’t been our case. If anything, moving here has made us more intentional about building a life, both individually and as a couple.

Marta Delgado is a Spanish writer and marketing professional from Galicia, Spain, currently based in Mexico City. She writes about culture, lifestyle, and what it means to build a life abroad, drawing from her own time living in different countries.

World.title: 2 Mexico City chefs launched an international ‘Pay What You Can’ model. How did it go?
World.content:
Food is, in many ways, the greatest of social equalizers. Everyone, after all, must sit down to eat at various points in the day, and there’s no escaping the fact that we must all break bread together.

But too often, there’s an exclusivity around who gets to actually sit at the proverbial table. In a bustling metropolis like Mexico City, in particular, many residents are gatekept and unable to enjoy the city’s most sought-after offerings, largely due to massive socioeconomic barriers.

Wealth disparities shape capital dining

The gap between those who can, or can’t, access Mexico City’s jeweled offerings is wider than ever. A 2026 report from Oxfam Mexico revealed just how disparate Mexico has become as a nation, with 1% of the population hoarding 40% of the country’s wealth.

The divide is glaringly obvious in high-end neighborhoods like Mexico City’s Santa Fe. Oscar Lopez of The Guardian wrote about how “unbelievably unequal” certain areas of Mexico City actually are: “The stark contrast in this little enclave of the capital is a microcosm of a problem that has plagued Mexico for decades: rampant income inequality, with a small slice of the population living in opulence while millions of families languish in poverty.”

The irony, of course, is that the essential workers who sustain the infrastructure for opulent lifestyles in Mexico rarely — if ever — get invited to partake in it. That trickles down to something like booking a table at a popular restaurant in CDMX, which only a select few get to enjoy.

Taking that reality into account, Norma Listman and Saqib Keval — the married chef-owners of Masala y Maíz, a prominent Michelin-starred eatery in Mexico City’s historic center that serves a blend of Mexican, Indian and East African dishes — have made efforts to raise awareness around such issues in the food industry, including workers’ rights and dining accessibility for all.

A global movement for humane hospitality

This summer, they initiated a “Paga Lo Que Puedas” or “Pay What You Can” (PWYC) day, effectively opening their doors to every diner, regardless of their tax bracket or bank account. A powerful and unprecedented gesture, it triggered a wave of support among participating restaurants who joined the cause throughout Mexico, and beyond, to galvanize a movement centered on humane hospitality.

“As the city becomes more expensive and more oriented toward tourism and higher-income visitors, there are people who have lived here and built these communities who are increasingly unable to participate in the spaces around them. For us, that contradiction is important,” Listman and Keval told Mexico News Daily. “Restaurants are part of neighborhoods and communities, but they can also become spaces that feel increasingly inaccessible to the people who live there.”

The couple went on to say, “Dining out has become a privilege for many people, and as it becomes more expensive, it can become more segregated by class. That goes against how we understand hospitality and why we entered this industry in the first place. ‘Paga Lo Que Puedas’ was one small way of responding to that reality.”

In Mexico City, more than 20 restaurants — including MUX, Sin Nombre, Baldío, Cicatriz and Fideo Gordo — declared their commitment to “Paga Lo Que Puedas,” which took place Aug. 26. More than 100 dining institutions across 14 countries also joined in.

So how did it fare? Masala y Maíz, along with 12 participating restaurants, shared their experiences with us.

The origins, challenges and joys of a novel model

The concept originally emerged years ago, during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, when Listman and Keval — who initially opened their restaurant as a small brick-and-mortar in San Miguel Chapultepec back in 2017 — were experimenting with ways to attract customers during a challenging time for food businesses to keep their staff employed and to provide the luxury of dining out in their community.

That evolved into a regular practice, in which diners would enjoy a meal and leave whatever they could afford inside an envelope. What began as an in-house tradition ballooned into a bigger idea that would, years later, result in a global effort.

“From the beginning, we were thinking about how we could make the restaurant more accessible while also creating a tangible way to support the people around us and keep our staff working,” they noted. “It started as a small gesture, but it was also an experiment in trust: What happens when we remove the fixed price from the menu and ask people to honestly decide what they are able to pay for their meal? In Mexico City, that question felt particularly relevant because we were already seeing how quickly the cost of living was changing around us.”

Social media deepens urban segregation

In the fall of 2026, those factors had only become more urgent. In analyzing the stratification of diners in Mexico City through the increased use of social media, Guillermo Echauri of the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) found that the role and perception of food influencers in Mexico City have only exacerbated the problem of inaccessibility.

He writes that “the attributes, perspectives, and personal experiences of the foodies themselves are integrated into an environment of significant socioeconomic disparities, urban segregation, and ethnic discrimination. This shapes their representation of the culinary landscape in the Mexican capital, as digital dynamics intensify existing inequality.”

In other words, the systemic issues around dining accessibility that Listman and Keval were attuned to nearly a decade ago haven’t disappeared — they’ve arguably worsened with the rise of food influencers and rampant social media usage, among other shifts in the community and global economy at large.

By reviving the PWYC initiative in Mexico City, the founders of Masala y Maíz — and the many restaurateurs who chose to join them — are emphasizing the ongoing need for inclusivity and egalitarianism through local and international gastronomy.

Measuring turnout and financial realities

Despite logistical complications that arose through staffing and clarity around how to accept payments in a PWYC framework (in which some diners paid with non-monetary goods, such as original artwork), a survey of 12 participating restaurants unanimously confirmed a “very positive” experience and that the day “opened doors to new audiences,” with 83% of the restaurants declaring they would “definitely” participate again.

“The response we experienced was largely one of curiosity and solidarity,” Listman and Keval affirmed. “Other chefs and restaurant owners were also thinking about accessibility, rising costs, and what it means to be a restaurant within a community. We did not approach this as a model that every restaurant should adopt. Restaurants have different circumstances and different economic realities, and sustainability for the restaurant and for its workers is important. What we wanted to do was create an invitation to think differently about what hospitality can look like.”

In terms of profitable sales, the results were mixed — although that’s to be expected when the public is invited to pay whatever they wish.

Forty-two percent of the surveyed restaurants reported a “better” day of sales; a combined 33% reported either “much worse” or “about the same.” Conversely, 75% of the food businesses shared that they saw a “much higher” or “higher” turnout than an average day, while 25% believe they saw “about the same” number of diners that they would have during normal hours. In all, it seems that the restaurants saw a boom in diners, but not necessarily in income (in an act of reciprocal care, tips reportedly went up by 42%).

Building connection beyond the dining table

Importantly, 58% of the diners self-identified as first-timers at the surveyed restaurants, indicating demand and engagement from a wider range of customers than usual, and affirming the PWYC blueprint as socially equitable.

“What has stayed with us most is the sense of connection that the initiative created. For us, the success of Paga Lo Que Puedas is not simply measured by how many meals were served or how much money was collected. It is also about what happens when people feel that a restaurant is making room for them,” Listman and Keval said. “We hope that diners experience a sense of belonging and joy, and that they are able to enjoy a meal without the usual anxiety around whether they can afford to be in that space. We also hope the experience encourages people to think about the labor, care and knowledge that goes into a meal, and to recognize the workers who make that experience possible.”

Nourishing a better city

In a city as increasingly divided as Mexico City has become in the past half-decade alone — due to gentrification, mass tourism and other sociopolitical factors — PWYC is a bold, if not necessary, kind of reclamation for the people. However, that responsibility shouldn’t fall solely on small-business owners and their staff to level the playing field (or dining tables, in this case); that work should ultimately be the focus of elected officials and local governments, who should be looking for ways to support not only diners, but those who provide the city’s best dining experiences.

Without them, what would be left to nourish and feed us when we want a transcendent meal or simply a night out? Keeping local culinary arts scenes alive — and attainable for diverse residents — should be every world-class city’s priority. No matter the price.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Does civility in politics still exist? A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
I am currently spending a few days visiting family and friends in the U.S. and, being a month away from the midterms, have had the opportunity to experience firsthand the run-up to the elections in multiple states. As is always the case now, the TV ads and political speeches of the candidates are increasingly over the top.

Do I choose the candidate who wants to turn the U.S. into a communist country? Or the one who wants to further enable a dictatorship? Do I prefer the candidate who wants to put a data center in my backyard? Or the one who wants to increase my energy costs and threaten my water supply with a data center that’s not in my backyard? It’s all so silly, so anxiety-producing, so insulting to our intelligence. In Mexico, where paid political ads on radio and TV are prohibited, it’s refreshing to not be subjected to this every two years.

Mexican politics, of course, are far from perfect, but there have been some examples of real civility demonstrated lately that give many of us some hope and inspiration. And that civility comes from the tone being set from the top by President Sheinbaum. Let me explain.

The word I most often hear to describe President Sheinbaum is “classy.” The way she dresses, the way she smiles, the way she carries herself, and the way she interacts with people are all frequently mentioned. Even those who don’t agree with all of her policies are impressed by that aspect of her.

Being an American, I have found the contrast to my native country and the increasing lack of class in politics in the United States to be maddening. I can understand genuine differences of opinion on important issues and on the general direction of the country, but I cannot get past the lack of class being exhibited by politicians that we see on a daily basis. The name-calling, the put-downs and the unwillingness to acknowledge anything positive from the other side is really depressing to watch. And it’s on both sides of the political aisle. I know I am not alone in often thinking, “We pay these people to represent us, find compromise, and make decisions — why can’t they seem to actually do it anymore?”

Which brings me back to Sheinbaum. There have been three incidents in just these past few weeks that were impressive examples of civility.

1. The U.S. administration has been back at it again, attacking Mexico for supposedly not doing enough to combat the cartels. This is despite nearly daily progress on high-profile arrests, drug and weapons seizures, and a significant reduction in homicides throughout the country. Marco Rubio, the U.S. Secretary of State, again hinted that the U.S. could act unilaterally against criminal organizations in Mexico. President Trump, acknowledging progress but not wanting to be outdone, added: “However, Mexico must take additional action against the narco terrorist organizations that dominate vast areas of its territory and continue to threaten the American people,” and arrest “the many corrupt public officials” who have colluded with them.

Sheinbaum responded calmly, saying that Mexico doesn’t need to be judged “from the outside.” She went on to say that she would like to see “a report about what the U.S. government is doing in the United States” to reduce drug use and combat drug trafficking. She asked, “Where is the effort being made to stop drug cartels and distributors in the United States? What’s going on with money laundering in the United States?” Fair questions of a government that has no problem frequently questioning her and her administration.

2. Sheinbaum recently completed her second year in office and as a result, just gave her second annual “state of the union” address. She then did something similar to last year, traveling to each of Mexico’s 32 states over a period of several weeks to personally give a “state of the state” address in which she presented, in detail, what the government has accomplished for the people of the state in the past year and what is planned for the following years.

Regardless of which political party is leading the state she visited, or which candidate they voted for, she showed up and presented a business-like progress report for the state. There was no avoiding the states that didn’t vote for her. There was no minimizing the progress in states that don’t support her. But rather a consistent, fact-based, optimistic outlook on what the government is doing to improve things in the state. It’s inspiring to watch, and impressive to see her making the effort to visit every state and make the individual presentations.

3. Sheinbaum’s visits to two states in particular, Jalisco and Nuevo León, most caught my attention. These states have the second and third largest cities in the country after Mexico City, and neither state has a governor of the Morena political party that Sheinbaum is part of. It didn’t matter; Sheinbaum showed up in both states, was warmly greeted by the governors, and spoke about the progress that the federal and state governments have made working together. This was not a post-natural disaster photo op. This was a real effort to present a progress report to the people of these states and present a united front of government.

The governor of Jalisco greeted Sheinbaum along with famous singer Vicente Fernández’s wife (Doña Cuquita). In Nuevo León, she was greeted by Governor Samuel García, his wife and their two daughters. The images of Sheinbaum kissing their youngest daughter with a beaming Governor García looking on would touch even the biggest cynic of politicians.

What we are seeing lately in Mexico is a welcome reminder that politics doesn’t have to be so classless, so off-putting, so negative, so nasty. It hasn’t always been this way in the U.S. — I’m not sure how it got this bad.

I’m not saying things are perfect in Mexico. They are far from it. But seeing politicians of different political parties together, seemingly genuinely acting like polite, kind, classy people is quite inspiring and uplifting. Perhaps that is why a recent poll just put the level of national pride of Mexicans at 90%, a record high.

Let’s hope it continues for the good of the country!

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Mexico’s fastest-growing states aren’t the ones having the most children
World.content:
The 2025 Intercensal Survey by the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) has revealed a paradox in Mexico’s new demographic map: The states that have seen the greatest population growth are not those with the highest fertility rates.

Mexico reached a population of 130.9 million in 2025 – the country’s highest population in history. However, the population grew at an average annual rate of just 0.7%, its slowest pace in recent decades, with growth concentrated in states in the north and southeast of the country.

Which states lead population growth?

According to INEGI, Baja California Sur led in population growth with an average annual rate of 3.4%, followed by Quintana Roo at 2.2%. Querétaro recorded 1.7%, while Nuevo León and Coahuila grew by 1.5% annually.

Population growth in Quintana Roo is a result of its population dynamics: For years, the state has recorded growth linked to an influx of people from other states and the expansion of its urban and tourist areas, among other factors.

The same pattern is observed in Baja California Sur. Meanwhile Baja California, Querétaro and Nuevo León are attracting new residents thanks to urbanization, employment and internal migration.

In contrast, Guerrero and Veracruz lost population, shrinking by -0.6% and -0.3%, respectively.

Which states have the highest and lowest fertility rate?

The states topping the growth rankings are not the same ones showing the highest fertility rates. The Intercensal Survey revealed that Chiapas had the highest fertility rate at 1.8 children per woman, followed by Guerrero (1.6) and Durango (1.5).

The contrast is particularly striking in Baja California Sur and Quintana Roo. Despite ranking at the top for population growth between 2020 and 2025, their fertility rates were among the lowest in the country — 1.2 and 1.1 children per woman, respectively.

Mexico City has the second largest population of any entity or state, despite having the lowest fertility rate (0.8). According to the survey, its population stands at 9.1 million, just behind México state, which with 17.5 million inhabitants is the most populous state in the country.

With reports from Uno TV

World.title: Mexico’s City’s chinampa restoration project Arca Tierra wins 2026 Champions of Change Award
World.content:
Arca Tierra, a Mexican sustainable agriculture initiative founded by brothers Lucio and Pablo Usobiaga, has won the Champions of Change Award 2026 by The World’s 50 Best Restaurants in Latin America.

The award honors their work to restore the chinampas of Xochimilco — an agricultural system set on man-made islands, used by the Mexica people in pre-Hispanic times. They are raised plots anchored to the lakebed, created from mud, organic matter and vegetation.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The 50 Best Restaurants (@theworlds50best)

Today they are known as a Mexico City tourist attraction due to the boat rides aboard traditional trajineras. But the Xochimilco chinampas remain part of the capital’s productive and cultural landscape

They face, however, challenges, such as environmental degradation, urban expansion, and declining profitability for those who work the land.

Arca Tierra seeks to improve their condition to create a food supply chain that is fairer, local and regenerative. Their project seeks to produce high-quality food with a lower environmental impact, preserve traditional farming knowledge, and expand access to local products for restaurants, consumers and communities in Mexico City.

“This recognition confirms that we are on the right track and inspires us to continue working hard with the farmers and producers that collaborate with us,” Lucio said in a statement.

In the capital, Arca Tierra produces around five tonnes of food per hectare per month. Its harvests supply 47 restaurants in Mexico City and reach more than 300 families through weekly baskets.

The initiative has also developed culinary and rural tourism offerings designed to connect chefs, diners, and visitors with the origins of their food. Its projects include Baldío — a Mexico City restaurant created in collaboration with British chef Douglas McMaster — which focuses on comprehensive use of ingredients and on waste reduction. For example, vegetable peels are fermented to make a traditional beverage called tepache, or repurposed into a syrup that is then diluted and fermented before being incorporated into other dishes.

Ultimately, Arca Tierra seeks to turn the spotlight to a process often overlooked by diners — the production and sourcing of local ingredients.

“In the value chain, the person who produces the food earns the least money — it’s a total contradiction because they’re the most important of all,” Pablo said.

With the mission to bring quality produce to more people, Arca Tierra has expanded its vision beyond Xochimilco and it now operates in Huasca de Ocampo, Hidalgo, and Amanalco de Becerra and Polvillos, in México state.

With reports from El Estímulo and Cool Hunter Mx

World.title: St Vincent Fuel Surcharge Up 45% Since March as Debate Grows Over a Flat Fee
World.content:
Kingstown, capital of St Vincent and the Grenadines, where power bills now carry a fuel surcharge higher than the base rate. (Photo: Luisrpaz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

ENERGY · ST VINCENT AND THE GRENADINES

Key Facts — The country St Vincent and the Grenadines, an eastern Caribbean island state. Its state-owned utility, VINLEC, generates most of its power from imported diesel.

— What happened VINLEC’s fuel surcharge on September 2026 bills was 79.67 EC cents per kWh (about US$0.30), up 45% from 54.90 cents in March, its published notices show.

— The numbers The surcharge peaked at 83.20 cents on July bills. The base rate is 50 cents a unit. Fuel burnt in August cost EC$12.3m (about US$4.6m), per VINLEC.

— What it means for you On 250 units, the September surcharge alone adds about EC$199 (about US$74) to a household bill, before the base charge. EC$2.70 = US$1 (2 October).

— Still open The October rate, based on September fuel costs, and whether May’s matching discounts still apply. VAT changes on domestic electricity are expected this month, an iWitness News column says.

The St Vincent fuel surcharge has become the largest line on many household power bills. On September bills it stood at 79.67 Eastern Caribbean cents per kilowatt hour (kWh), about US$0.30, the state utility’s notice shows.

That is 45% above March and well above the 50-cent (about US$0.19) base rate for the electricity itself. A column published by iWitness News on Saturday 3 October argues that replacing the surcharge with a flat fee would not help.

How the St Vincent fuel surcharge is calculated

VINLEC, St Vincent Electricity Services Limited, is state-owned and passes fuel costs to customers monthly. The rate is the fuel cost above a fixed base price, divided by the units sold.

For September bills, fuel burnt in August cost EC$12.29m (about US$4.55m), VINLEC’s notice shows. The base price covered only EC$421,235 (about US$156,000), leaving EC$11.86m (about US$4.39m) for the surcharge.

VINLEC says it makes no profit on the charge. Its notices show the rate rising from 54.90 cents in March to a peak of 83.20 cents in July.

VINLEC fuel surcharge on monthly power bills, January to September 2026, in Eastern Caribbean cents per kWh; the base rate is 50 cents. Source: VINLEC monthly fuel surcharge notices, 2026.

The July rate came after VINLEC applied a subsidy of EC$734,959 (about US$272,000), iWitness News reported on 23 July. The rate eased to 76.70 cents in August, then rose again to 79.67 cents.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Relief measures and their limits

On 27 May Prime Minister Godwin Friday waived customs and excise charges on diesel for power generation for three months. He put the revenue forgone at about EC$1.65m (about US$611,000).

He also told VINLEC to share the cost once the surcharge passed set thresholds, iWitness News reported. Above 71 cents the utility was to match 50%, and above 77 cents it was to match 100% for households.

On 4 August Friday told NBC Radio the surcharge was “too high” but lower than it would have been. Without the measures, he said, it would be over 90 cents.

Opposition leader Ralph Gonsalves said in July there was no cap, citing VINLEC’s chief executive, St Vincent Times reported. He called the government’s account “smoke and mirrors”.

The flat-fee debate

Calls to swap the St Vincent fuel surcharge for a standing charge recur on call-in radio and social media, the column says. It is written by Guevara Leacock under the title A View from the Outside.

A standing charge is a fixed fee per customer, whatever the usage. The column argues it would shift fuel costs from large users onto small households.

A fixed unit price set for a year would not lower costs either, it says. When diesel rose above that price, taxpayers would cover the gap through the state-owned utility.

The frustration is real. A St Vincent Times commentary on 27 September described an EC$318.68 surcharge against an EC$200 energy charge (about US$118 and US$74).

Solar, rivers and an old law

Only about one sixth of the country’s electricity comes from rivers and the sun, the column says. It points to a battery system at Cane Hall and an upgraded Lowman’s Bay solar farm due in November.

It also calls for updating the 1973 Electricity Supply Act to pay a fair price for rooftop solar power. VINLEC chief executive Vaughn Lewis has called for the law to be modernised, the column says.

Background on the economy is in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines Explained 2026. Oil supply decisions abroad, as in G7 Frees 100 Million Barrels as Mexico Needs US Diesel, feed into the price VINLEC pays.

What Is Not Yet Known

VINLEC has not yet published the rate for October bills, which reflects fuel burnt in September. The column expects higher world oil prices to show up on October and November bills.

It is unclear whether the 50% and 100% matching rules announced in May still apply, since rates topped 77 cents in July and September. The column’s figure of EC$100m (about US$37m) in fuel spending this year is not independently confirmed.

The column also expects VAT changes on domestic electricity this month. Their scope has not been set out.

Sources: VINLEC, monthly fuel surcharge rate notices, January to September 2026 bills; iWitness News, “The fuel surcharge: A real problem for Vincentians” (column by Guevara Leacock), 3 October 2026; iWitness News reports of 27 May, 23 July and 4 August 2026; St Vincent Times, 28 July and 27 September 2026.

World.content:

BUSINESS · ST KITTS AND NEVIS

Key Facts — The country St Kitts and Nevis is a two-island federation in the eastern Caribbean. Nevis has its own island government and its own branch of the financial regulator.

— What happened Phil Jones became dedicated Regulator, Online Gaming, after handing international banking to Marie-Grace Michel on 1 October 2026, the Nevis Island Administration said on 2 October.

— Who is involved The Nevis branch of the Financial Services Regulatory Commission (FSRC) and the island’s Online Gaming Authority, created under an ordinance in force since 1 May 2025.

— What it means for you Licensed and applicant gaming operators face one official focused mainly on their compliance. The announcement does not change the rules themselves.

— Still open How many operators hold Nevis licences, and when the next international anti-money-laundering evaluation of the federation will take place.

Nevis online gaming now has a dedicated regulator. The island’s financial watchdog designated Phil Jones as Regulator, Online Gaming, the Nevis Island Administration (NIA) announced on 2 October.

Jones previously covered both international banking and gaming. He handed banking to Marie-Grace Michel on 1 October, so the young gaming sector becomes his primary portfolio.

What changed at the regulator

The change sits inside the Nevis branch of the Financial Services Regulatory Commission (FSRC), the body that supervises offshore banks, trusts and companies. The NIA release says the designation reflects the gaming sector’s “growing importance and continued expansion”.

Jones will oversee the supervisory framework set up under the island’s Online Gaming Ordinance. He will also work with the Online Gaming Authority, the separate body that handles licensing.

Michel, his successor in banking, brings experience in auditing, financial crime risk and anti-money-laundering compliance. She also holds an accounting qualification and an MBA, according to a second NIA release.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A young industry built for diversification

The Nevis Island Assembly passed the online gaming bill on 29 April 2025. The NIA says the ordinance took effect on 1 May 2025.

Premier Mark Brantley sold the law as a hedge against the island’s heavy reliance on tourism. The NIA said revenue would come from application fees, annual licence fees and penalties.

The law requires operators to incorporate on Nevis, run responsible gaming tools and offer dispute resolution. Brantley told AGB, a gaming trade outlet, in January that “only reputable entities need apply”.

The Curaçao Chronicle reported in July a flat annual licence fee of €28,000 (about US$31,500 at 0.889 euros per dollar, 2 October). That figure has not been independently confirmed.

The same paper described Nevis as new competition for Curaçao’s licensing business. For the wider regional picture, see Latin America’s Online Gaming Market: Brazil’s Regulated Market and What Comes Next.

The money-laundering review ahead

The NIA links the move to the federation’s coming fifth-round Mutual Evaluation. That is a peer review of anti-money-laundering controls by the Caribbean Financial Action Task Force (CFATF), part of the global FATF network.

The last full review had its on-site visit in March 2021, with the report published in February 2022. A 2025 follow-up report found 35 of the 40 FATF standards rated compliant or largely compliant.

Online gambling can move money quickly and across borders, so evaluators tend to ask how it is supervised. A dedicated regulator gives Nevis a clearer answer to that question.

What it means for the island

For Nevis online gaming operators, the practical effect is closer supervision and a single point of contact. For Nevis, it is a bet that tighter oversight attracts better licensees rather than scaring them away.

The open question is capacity, since the NIA has not said whether the gaming desk gains staff. Meanwhile the federation is also courting new industries, as in St Kitts and Nevis Geothermal Plant Gets EU Offer.

What Is Not Yet Known

The NIA has not said how many gaming licences Nevis has issued, nor how much revenue they have raised. Neither release gives a date for the CFATF on-site visit.

It is also unclear whether the regulator’s office will hire extra staff for gaming. Trade press has reported a different in-force date for the ordinance than the NIA.

More: Saint Kitts and Nevis Explained 2026, a country guide from The Rio Times.

Who regulates Nevis online gaming?

The island’s Online Gaming Authority handles licensing. Phil Jones, at the Nevis branch of the Financial Services Regulatory Commission, now serves as dedicated Regulator, Online Gaming.

Have the gaming rules changed?

No. The announcement leaves the Online Gaming Ordinance passed in 2025 as it is. What changed on 1 October 2026 is that its supervisor no longer also covers international banking.

What is the Mutual Evaluation?

A peer review of a country’s anti-money-laundering system by the Caribbean Financial Action Task Force. Poor results can lead to closer international monitoring and higher costs for local banks.

Sources: Nevis Island Administration, gaming regulator release and banking regulator release, 2 October 2026; NIA, gaming bill passed, 30 April 2025, and ordinance in force, 25 July 2025; Nevis Pages, 3 October 2026; FATF, St Kitts and Nevis follow-up report, 2025; Curaçao Chronicle, 8 July 2026; AGB, 25 January 2026; SiGMA, 31 August 2025.

COURTS · BARBADOS

Key Facts — The country Barbados, an eastern Caribbean republic since 2021. Its High Court hears constitutional claims, and the Caribbean Court of Justice is its final court of appeal.

— What happened Justice Shona Griffith withdrew from a retired judge’s lawsuit against the State and a former chief justice, citing a conflict of interest, Barbados Today reported on 3 October 2026.

— Who is involved Dr Sonia Richards, a High Court judge from 2006 to 2022, is suing the Attorney General and Sir Patterson Cheltenham, chief justice at the time. Sir Patterson has denied the allegations.

— What it means for you The case continues before Justice Patrick H Wells on 29 October. It tests how the courts handle a judge’s claim against the judiciary’s own former leadership.

— Still open Whether the re-amended claim filed on 30 September meets the court’s order, and when the defendants file their defence.

A Barbados judge has stepped aside from retired judge Dr Sonia Richards’ constitutional lawsuit, citing a conflict of interest. Justice Shona Griffith had ruled in July that the case should go to trial, Barbados Today reported on Saturday 3 October.

Dr Richards is suing the State, through the Attorney General, and Sir Patterson Cheltenham, then chief justice and head of the judiciary. She alleges defamation, negligence and breaches of her constitutional rights.

Why the Barbados judge stepped aside

Justice Griffith said the conflict arose because she had sat on the bench at the same time as Dr Richards. Recusal is the standard step when a judge’s impartiality could reasonably be questioned, and it decides nothing about the claim.

First she ordered Dr Richards to re-amend her claim and serve it on Roger Forde KC, senior counsel for both defendants. The revamped claim was filed in the High Court on Wednesday 30 September.

Justice Patrick H Wells will now hear the case on 29 October. Her July order had already said the next hearing would take place before a different judge.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the July ruling left standing

In a 76-page judgment issued on 31 July, Justice Griffith struck out four claims as disclosing no reasonable grounds. They concerned security of the person, protection from inhuman and degrading treatment, and consideration for an extension of tenure.

The fourth alleged removal from office in breach of sections 84(3) and 84(4) of the Constitution. That left the case narrower, but alive.

Dr Richards may still argue that her security of tenure was breached, though not through any alleged removal from office. She may also claim a breach of her right to the protection of the law, once she pleads how it arose.

Three separate defamation claims go forward, along with claims over her terms of employment and the duty of care. Her redrafted claim seeks stigma, exemplary and constitutional or vindicatory damages.

How the dispute began

The retired Barbados judge joined the bench on 1 April 2006 and retired on 17 May 2022, aged 66. She alleges that on 12 April 2022 she found the lock to her office changed and her name removed from the door.

She says she asked to serve two years beyond the retirement age of 65 and was granted one by the then governor-general. She argues that the consultation required by section 84(1A) of the Constitution never took place.

Barbados Today called the suit unprecedented when it reported the filing in April 2026. In May the defendants sought to strike out the whole claim, arguing that judicial immunity covered the former chief justice’s official acts.

The defence position

Sir Patterson told Barbados Today in April that he rejected all of the assertions against him. Attorney General Wilfred Abrahams, the government’s chief legal officer, said then only that he was aware of the matter.

On Friday Mr Forde said his first priority was whether the claimant had complied properly with the judge’s order. “The judge told them to do something in a particular way,” he told the newspaper.

The handover keeps the case on track, since a new judge and a hearing date are already set. Dr Richards is represented by attorney-at-law Lalu Hanuman. For background on the island’s institutions, see Barbados Explained: The Island, the Economy, the Republic and What to Watch.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is not yet known whether the defendants will challenge the re-amended claim for non-compliance. The July order warned that missed deadlines could lead to a party’s case being struck out, or to costs.

The defendants have six weeks from service of the statement of claim to file a defence, so that date is also open. No other outlet had reported the recusal by Saturday afternoon, and the details are not independently confirmed.

Sources: Barbados Today, “Judge recuses herself from constitutional lawsuit”, 3 October 2026; Barbados Today reports on the case of 7 April, 20 May and 31 July 2026; Nation News, “Mixed ruling”, 2 August 2026.

World.title: Paraguay Votes Sunday for 263 Mayors, Asunción in Focus
World.content:
Asunción, the Paraguayan capital (Photo: Stefano Vigorelli, CC0 via Wikimedia Commons)

PREVIEW · PARAGUAY ELECTIONS 2026

Key Facts — The vote Paraguay elects mayors and municipal councils on Sunday 4 October 2026. Polls are open 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. local time: 6 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern Time, 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. in Lisbon.

— What is chosen 263 mayors (intendentes) and municipal councils in 263 districts. 5,043,154 voters are registered (TSJE).

— The count The electoral court’s preliminary system, TREP, is expected to start near 5:30 p.m. local time (4:30 p.m. ET). Officials expect results from all districts by 8 p.m. local (7 p.m. ET) at the latest.

— The contest In the 2021 municipal vote the ruling Colorado Party (ANR) won 163 mayoralties and the Liberal Party (PLRA) 62. The result is read as a test for President Santiago Peña before the 2028 national vote.

— Four cities Asunción: Camilo Pérez (Colorado) leads the polls. Ciudad del Este: Colorado against the opposition mayor’s camp. Encarnación and San Lorenzo: Colorados face a united challenge.

— Why Americans care Paraguay is the only South American country with ties to Taiwan, and it grew 4.0% in the second quarter (BCP). A Colorado sweep would signal continuity for Peña’s pro-Taiwan, pro-investment line.

Paraguay votes on Sunday in municipal elections that double as a test for President Santiago Peña and his Colorado Party. Polls open at 6 a.m. Eastern Time and close at 4 p.m. (7 a.m. to 5 p.m. in Paraguay). The electoral court, TSJE, expects its first preliminary figures from about 4:30 p.m. ET.

The vote picks 263 mayors and municipal councils. It does not change the national government. But the Colorados have ruled Paraguay for most of its modern history, and mayoral wins feed their machine ahead of the 2028 presidential vote.

For US readers, the questions are simple. Does the pro-Taiwan, investor-friendly ruling party keep its grip on local government? And do the opposition’s wins in places like Ciudad del Este signal a real challenge? Here is what to watch, in Eastern Time.

The timetable in Eastern Time

Event Paraguay Eastern Time Lisbon Polls open 7 a.m. 6 a.m. 11 a.m. Polls close 5 p.m. 4 p.m. 9 p.m. First TREP data expected about 5:30 p.m. about 4:30 p.m. about 9:30 p.m. Results from all districts expected by 8 p.m. 7 p.m. Midnight

Publishing exit polls and survey data is banned until one hour after the polls close. TREP is a preliminary, non-binding count. The electoral tribunals in each circuit do the official count and proclaim winners.

The Paraná River at sunset from the Encarnación waterfront. Encarnación is one of the four cities to watch on Sunday. (File photo) Photo: Horacio Cambeiro, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on paraguay elections Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Asunción: the Colorado favourite

The capital is the biggest prize. Camilo Pérez, the Colorado candidate, faces Soledad Núñez, who leads an opposition alliance backed by the Liberals. Two September polls put Pérez well ahead. Ati Snead (11–16 September) gave him about 52.6% to 34.3%. Grau & Asociados (16–17 September) had 50.8% to 27.0%. Outlets that published them lean towards the ruling party, so treat the gaps with care.

Ciudad del Este: the opposition’s test

Ciudad del Este, on the Brazilian border, is a major border trading city. Daniel Mujica of the Yo Creo movement won the November 2025 by-election by 40 points after the removal of Miguel Prieto. Rigoberto Chamorro runs for the Colorados, on the team of Governor César “Landy” Torres. Prieto, removed from office in August 2025, predicted a historic Colorado defeat. No recent public poll was available to us.

Encarnación and San Lorenzo

In Encarnación, on the Argentine border, the Colorado candidate is deputy Sebastián “Cheba” Remesowski, who won his primary with 76%. His main rival is Carlos Pereira of the Alianza Encarnación en Marcha. In San Lorenzo, near Asunción, Felipe Salomón, Colorado mayor in 2021–2026, seeks to return against Luz Bella González, the Liberal chosen as the opposition’s consensus candidate.

What it means for 2028

Peña cannot run again, but his party’s machine wants to keep the presidency. A broad Colorado win would show strength. A loss in Ciudad del Este or other big towns would give the opposition a story about a challenge. Local races follow local logic, so municipal results do not translate directly into national votes.

The US view: Taiwan and the economy

Paraguay is the only South American state that recognises Taiwan, one of 12 governments worldwide that do, and ties date from 12 July 1957. Washington backs Taipei, so a stable pro-Taiwan government in Asunción suits US policy. Debate over opening trade with mainland China continues inside Paraguay.

The economy is growing, but more slowly. Paraguay’s central bank (BCP) reported 4.0% growth year on year in the second quarter, down from 7.3% in the first, and 5.7% for the first half.

What it means for you

Investors: expect continuity. Municipal races rarely move Paraguayan assets, but a surprise opposition run in big cities would shape the 2028 debate. Expats: foreign residents should expect police and crowds near polling places. Travellers: expect quiet streets and some restrictions on Sunday.

What is not known

We found no recent public polls for Ciudad del Este, Encarnación or San Lorenzo. We do not know turnout, how many opposition alliances will hold, or the exact time of the first TREP figures, which depend on how fast results arrive.

When do Paraguay’s polls open and close?

Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. Paraguay time on Sunday 4 October. That is 6 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern Time. Anyone inside a polling place at closing time can still vote.

When will preliminary results be published?

TSJE’s preliminary system, TREP, is expected to start around 5:30 p.m. Paraguay time, or about 4:30 p.m. Eastern. TSJE expects results from all districts by 8 p.m. local (7 p.m. ET) at the latest. TREP is not official.

What is Paraguay voting for?

Voters elect 263 mayors and municipal councils among 5,043,154 registered voters. There is no presidential or congressional vote.

Who leads in Asunción?

Colorado candidate Camilo Pérez led two September polls by 18 to 24 points over opposition candidate Soledad Núñez. The outlets that published the polls lean towards the ruling party.

Why does the vote matter for the US?

The ruling Colorado Party backs Taiwan, and Paraguay is the only South American country with ties to Taipei. Results also show the strength of Peña’s party before the 2028 presidential election.

World.title: Peru Votes Sunday in Regional and Lima Elections
World.content:
ANALYSIS · PERU ELECTIONS 2026

Key Facts — The vote Peru elects regional and local officials on Sunday 4 October 2026. Polls are open 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. in Lima: 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern Time, 1 p.m. to 11 p.m. in Lisbon.

— What is chosen 13,148 posts, including 25 regional governors, 196 provincial mayors and 1,696 district mayors, for terms from 2027 to 2030 (ONPE). Nobody elects a president or Congress.

— Who votes 26,314,648 Peruvian voters, plus 76 foreign residents who may vote only in municipal races (ONPE).

— Lima Former mayor Rafael López Aliaga leads every final poll, with 20% to 30% depending on the pollster. The electoral jury has not said whether he could take office if his list wins.

— The count ONPE says its results site opens at 6 p.m. ET and fills as tally sheets arrive. A governor needs 30% of valid votes to avoid a runoff, set for Sunday 29 November.

— Why Americans care Peru mined about 2.7 million tonnes of copper in 2025 (USGS estimate). Southern Copper, Freeport-McMoRan and Buenaventura trade in New York, and mining regions vote on Sunday.

Peru, a copper powerhouse in the Andes, holds regional and municipal elections on Sunday. Polls open at 8 a.m. Eastern Time and close at 6 p.m. (7 a.m. to 5 p.m. in Lima). The national electoral office, ONPE, says its results website starts showing counted tally sheets from 6 p.m. ET.

The vote does not change who runs the country. President Keiko Fujimori, who took office on 28 July, stays in place. But the races decide who governs 25 regions and the capital, and several of them sit on top of the world’s big copper deposits.

For US readers, the stakes are mining, security and politics. This guide explains the Lima race, the regions to watch, the violence that has marked the campaign and the timetable of the count. Official results can take weeks, so Sunday night will give a first picture, not a final one.





Peru votes · Regional and municipal elections · Sunday, October 4 Peru Election 2026: Live Map of the Regions and Lima Polls are open 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. in Lima (8 a.m. to 6 p.m. ET, 13:00 to 23:00 Lisbon). The electoral office ONPE publishes official results from 6 p.m. ET; this page carries them with the time of each update. 0% of tally sheets counted (ONPE) Count starts at 6 p.m. ET Lima: who becomes mayor Key numbers 26.3 million registered voters (ONPE) 13,148 posts on the ballot 25 regional governors 30% of valid votes a governor needs to avoid a runoff Election night and what comes next Sunday, 8 a.m. ET Polls open (7 a.m. Lima, 13:00 Lisbon).

Sunday, 6 p.m. ET Polls close (5 p.m. Lima, 23:00 Lisbon). ONPE's results site starts showing counted tally sheets.

About two weeks ONPE's acting head says a full count of the regional races takes about two weeks; the JNE resolves disputed sheets.

Sunday, November 29 Runoff for regional governor wherever no candidate reached 30% of valid votes. Mayors have no runoff.

January 1, 2027 New governors and mayors take office. What is on the ballot Regional governors 25, plus 25 vice-governors

Regional councillors 364

Provincial mayors 196

District mayors 1,696 Nobody elects a president or Congress on Sunday. Voting is compulsory for Peruvians; foreign residents may vote in municipal races only. The regions: tap a region 2026 count Macro-regions Voters Mining regions Choose a region Tap any region on the map, or a row below, for its capital, people and voters, its economy, the 2022 result and, from Sunday night, the official count. Region by region Show all 26 Lima Metropolitana elects a mayor and no governor. Region facts were researched twice independently; a value appears only where both agreed. The final Lima polls Publishing polls has been banned since September 28, so these are the last public numbers. Rafael López Aliaga ran Lima from 2023 to 2025 and is on the ballot as first councillor, not as mayoral candidate; the electoral jury (JNE) has not said whether he could take the mayor's credential if his list wins. Sources: ONPE (official results, posts on the ballot, registered voters); JNE (lists, runoff date); INEI (population); Ipsos, Datum, CPI and IEP as published until September 28; region facts from INEI, JNE, ONPE, BCRP and Peruvian media where two independent checks agreed. Map: geoBoundaries (public domain). The Rio Times does not call races; a winner or a runoff is shown once ONPE or the JNE declares it.

What Peruvians are voting for

Peru has three layers of local government. Sunday’s ballot fills all of them at once. ONPE lists 13,148 posts in total.

Post Seats on the ballot How a winner is decided Regional governors 25 (plus 25 vice-governors) At least 30% of valid votes, or a runoff on 29 November Regional councillors 364 Seats allocated by party list Provincial mayors 196 (plus 1,724 councillors) Most votes wins, no runoff District mayors 1,696 (plus 9,118 councillors) Most votes wins, no runoff

Voting is compulsory for Peruvians. Voters can use expired identity cards, the electoral jury says. Foreign residents can vote only for mayors and councillors.

Voters gather outside classrooms used as polling stations at a school in Callao. More than 10,000 schools serve as voting sites on Sunday. (File photo)

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Lima (Peru) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The race for Lima

Lima is the prize. It is Peru’s capital and by far its largest city, and its mayor runs local transport, streets and municipal services. Publishing polls has been banned since 28 September, so the numbers below are the last public ones.

Pollster and dates López Aliaga (Renovación Popular) Carlos Bruce (Somos Perú) Francis Allison (Avanza País) Datum, 23–25 Sept (simulated valid votes) 29.6% 17.2% 13% Ipsos, 24–25 Sept (valid-vote simulation) 30% 15.6% 15.1% CPI, late Sept (valid-vote simulation) 27.2% 15.2% 10.4% IEP, 4–10 Sept (voting intention) 20.1% 17.1% 4.7%

Ipsos’ direct question, a different measure, gave López Aliaga 25%, Bruce 14% and Allison 13%. Daniel Urresti (Podemos Perú) had 8% and Samuel Daza of President Fujimori’s Fuerza Popular 6%. All four polls point the same way, but the gap to the runner-up ranges from 3 to 14 points.

There is one legal catch. López Aliaga ran Lima from 2023 to 2025 and is on the ballot as first councillor, not as mayoral candidate, because of rules on immediate re-election. If his list wins, it is unclear whether the electoral jury (JNE) would give him the mayor’s credential. JNE president Roberto Burneo said on 28 September that the full court will decide, and no date has been announced. See our Lima poll report.

The regions to watch

Regional polling is thin. Ipsos published a scientific survey for Arequipa and Datum one for Callao. For most other regions we found only candidate lists and online straw polls, which are not representative, so we do not rank them.

Region Why it matters Latest public signal Arequipa Peru’s second city; home to the Cerro Verde copper mine and the Tía María project Ipsos, 23–25 Sept (405 interviews, margin ±4.9 points): Elmer Cáceres (APP) 12%, Florentino Zegarra (Fuerza Arequipeña) 12%, Benigno Cornejo 10% Áncash Hosts the Antamina copper and zinc mine; candidate Susy Aponte Polo was shot dead on 19 September Eleven slates remain. No scientific poll found Callao Peru’s main port, next to Lima Datum (6–21 Sept, 1,700 interviews) has Pedro Spadaro ahead in the race for regional governor La Libertad Home to the Pataz gold district; eight slates No scientific poll found Cusco, Puno, Cajamarca, Piura Mining and energy interests across the Andes and the north No scientific poll found; Cajamarca has nine slates Moquegua and Apurímac Core copper regions No scientific poll found

With fragmented fields, a 30% winner is not guaranteed. Runoffs are likely wherever the vote splits many ways.

Mining, informal miners and the vote

Peru mined about 2.7 million tonnes of copper in 2025, the USGS estimates. Mining taxes and royalties flow to regional and local budgets, so governors and mayors in mining regions control real money.

An open-pit mine in the Peruvian Andes. Antamina, in Áncash, is one of the country’s largest copper and zinc mines. (File photo)

Mining licences and environmental approvals are national decisions. Regional and local governments still shape the climate around a project: they spend part of the revenue, mediate protests and decide how hard to push on informal mining.

That last issue is on the ballot. A database compiled by Territorio Tomado and reported by the trade outlet Todominería lists 735 candidates for governor, councillor and mayor registered in REINFO, the formalisation register for small and artisanal miners, whether current or suspended. Of them, 43 run for regional governments in 15 departments. Parties with the most REINFO candidates include Ahora Nación, APP, Perú Primero, Podemos Perú, Progresemos, Somos Perú and Acción Popular.

Security and violence

The campaign has been marked by the killing of Susy Aponte Polo, a journalist and candidate for governor of Áncash. She was shot dead at a market in Caraz on Saturday 19 September. Prosecutors treat it as a contract killing with a possible political motive. Press reports say the 15-day preliminary detention of two suspects runs out around election day. Our Caraz case report follows the investigation.

The state has answered with force. The National Police and the Interior Ministry will deploy 57,738 officers, about 46,000 at polling sites and 11,000 escorting election material. More than 41,000 soldiers also deploy, La República reported. See our security plan report. Prosecutors say they will have more than 6,800 staff on duty.

A dry law bans alcohol sales from 8 a.m. on Saturday 3 October to 8 a.m. on Monday 5 October, and rallies are banned. For travellers, expect closed bars, police at schools and slower transport. Details are in our dry-law explainer.

How the count works, and when to expect results

Event Lima Eastern Time Lisbon Polls open 7 a.m. 8 a.m. 1 p.m. Polls close; ONPE results site opens 5 p.m. 6 p.m. 11 p.m.

Results appear on ONPE’s official site. Exit polls and private quick counts are estimates, not official figures. ONPE’s acting head, Bernardo Pachas, said a full count in regional races takes about two weeks. The JNE resolves disputed tally sheets and proclaims the winners. Close races may stay open for weeks while disputed sheets are reviewed.

What is at stake

Nationally, this is the first test for President Fujimori, who beat Roberto Sánchez in the June runoff by 50.135% to 49.865% on ONPE’s final count. Her party’s Lima candidate polls only 6%, so the vote will show how much local ground Fuerza Popular holds.

For investors, nothing on Sunday’s ballot changes national mining or tax law. The risks are local: protest, informal mining and the safety of candidates. The US-listed names with Peruvian exposure include Southern Copper, Freeport-McMoRan, which holds a stake in Cerro Verde, and Buenaventura. A governor who backs or blocks a project can matter more than a national headline.

The wider picture is in our guide to Peru’s role in Latin America.

The runoff on 29 November

Where no governor reaches 30% of valid votes, the top two meet on Sunday 29 November. The JNE set the date on 30 September and will ask the president to formally call it. New officials take office on 1 January 2027. Mayors have no runoff. Read more in our runoff-date report.

What it means for you

Investors: expect a slow, noisy count. Do not read Sunday’s early numbers as final, and watch mining regions for governors who take a firm line on protests or informal mining. The EODHD calendar lists a central-bank rate decision on 7 October, with the policy rate previously at 4.25%.

Expats and residents: Peruvians must vote. Foreign residents can vote only in municipal races. Carry your documents, and avoid buying alcohol on Saturday and Sunday.

Travellers: bars and shops stop alcohol sales until Monday morning. Police and soldiers will be at schools. Avoid large political gatherings and follow instructions at polling sites.

What is not known

Four things remain open. First, whether López Aliaga could take the mayor’s office if his list wins. Second, how many regions need a runoff. Third, how quickly ONPE can count in close races. Fourth, whether the Caraz suspects’ detention is extended after Sunday. We found no verified regional polls for most regions.

What time does Peru vote on Sunday, and when are results published?

Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. in Lima on Sunday 4 October. That is 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern Time. ONPE says its results site opens at 6 p.m. ET and fills as tally sheets are processed.

What is Peru voting for on 4 October?

Voters choose 25 regional governors, 196 provincial mayors, 1,696 district mayors and councillors, 13,148 posts in all. They do not choose a president or Congress.

Who leads the race for mayor of Lima?

Rafael López Aliaga leads the last public polls, with 20.1% to 30% depending on the pollster and measure. Carlos Bruce is second in all of them. The JNE has not said whether López Aliaga could take office if his list wins.

Will there be a runoff?

Only for regional governors. If no candidate wins 30% of valid votes, the top two meet on Sunday 29 November. Mayoral races have no runoff.

Why does the vote matter for US investors?

Peru mined about 2.7 million tonnes of copper in 2025, and mining regions elect governors on Sunday. Nothing on the ballot changes national mining law, but local governments shape protests, revenue use and informal mining.

How long will the final results take?

ONPE’s acting head says a full count in regional races takes about two weeks, and disputed tally sheets must be reviewed by the JNE. Close races may take longer.

World.content:

POLITICS · TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO

Key Facts — The country Trinidad and Tobago, a twin-island Caribbean republic governed by Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar’s United National Congress (UNC) since 2025.

— What happened A cabinet realignment took effect on 30 September 2026. It was set out in Gazette No. 166, published on Friday 2 October, CNC3 reported.

— Who is involved Eight ministers gain duties; nine office-holders, including the Prime Minister, give some up. Land and Legal Affairs Minister Saddam Hosein gains 11 items, by the Rio Times count of the published list.

— What it means for you Self-help housing schemes, the farm lender and disaster management now answer to different ministers. Applicants and borrowers keep dealing with the same agencies.

— Still open No official reason has been given. It is unclear whether staff and budgets follow the moved programmes.

Trinidad and Tobago’s Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar has carried out a cabinet realignment, moving programmes and state companies between her ministers. The changes took effect on 30 September.

They are set out in Gazette No. 166, published on Friday 2 October, CNC3 and the Trinidad Guardian reported on 3 October. No minister has been reported moved to a new ministry or dropped from the Cabinet.

Housing and sugar-era firms go to Hosein

The largest single shift goes to Land and Legal Affairs Minister Saddam Hosein. He takes over the Government Aided Self-Help Housing Programme (GASHHP) and the Housing and Village Improvement Programme (HVIP).

He also gains Hydrographic Surveys and a cluster of state companies. They include Caroni (1975) Limited, the former state sugar company, plus Rincon Development, Taurus Services and TRINTOC Services.

Items newly assigned per minister in the cabinet realignment effective 30 September 2026; Hosein gains 11 of 22, and the Prime Minister sheds six. Source: Trinidad and Tobago Gazette No. 166, as reported by CNC3, 3 Oct 2026.

Housing Minister David Lee picks up the Home Improvement Policy and the Oropune Project. Social Development Minister Vandana Mohit takes the National Commission for Self-Help Limited.

The Prime Minister herself gives up six items, including both self-help housing schemes and the Oropune Project. Those duties now sit with Hosein, Lee and Mohit.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Trinidad and Tobago Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Disaster management moves to Defence

Defence Minister Wayne Sturge takes national emergency and disaster management, including the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Management (ODPM). He also gains the National Emblems Committee and the National Mentorship Programme.

Homeland Security Minister Roger Alexander gives those up. In exchange he takes over the management of illegal immigrants and deportees, previously with Sturge.

Finance Minister Davendranath Tancoo gains the Agricultural Development Bank, the state farm lender, from Agriculture Minister Ravi Ratiram. Health Minister Lackram Bodoe hands insect vector control to Local Government Minister Khadijah Ameen. Public Utilities Minister Barry Padarath takes On-the-Job Training from Tertiary Education Minister Prakash Persad.

A realignment, not a reshuffle

The cabinet realignment follows weeks of speculation. Guardian Media reported on 17 September that a list naming Hosein as Attorney General had circulated online.

Persad-Bissessar rejected that list. “So there will be no reshuffle at this time,” she told Guardian Media, adding there was “always room for improvement.”

The reported changes move duties rather than ministers, which fits that line. Because they are gazetted, there is a public record of who answers for what.

Mickela Panday, leader of the opposition Patriotic Front, questioned the logic on social media. She asked whether “experience, expertise, performance” decided the moves, CNC3 reported.

The shift comes as Parliament pushes through major bills, including the Trinidad Procurement Bill Curbing Contracts Watchdog Passes by One Vote. Background on the two-island state is in Trinidad and Tobago Explained: Gas, Politics, the Two Islands and What to Watch.

What Is Not Yet Known

The government has not published a reason for the cabinet realignment, and no statement from the Office of the Prime Minister was reported. The Rio Times has not seen the Gazette itself.

It is not yet clear whether staff, offices and budget lines move with the programmes. Nor is it known whether a fuller reshuffle remains on the table.

Sources: CNC3, “PM realigns Cabinet portfolios”, 3 October 2026; CNC3, “Panday questions Cabinet realignment”, 3 October 2026; Trinidad Guardian, “PM realigns Cabinet portfolios”, 3 October 2026; Trinidad Guardian, “PM shuts down Cabinet reshuffle rumours”, 17 September 2026. The 3 October reports cite Trinidad and Tobago Gazette No. 166.

HEALTH · PUERTO RICO

Key Facts — The country Puerto Rico, a US territory in the Caribbean, where the Health Department considers dengue endemic because cases appear all year.

— What happened The Health Department’s weekly report, dated 23 September, counts 922 dengue cases with symptoms starting between 1 January and 16 September 2026.

— The numbers 456 patients (49.5%) were hospitalised, 36 (3.9%) had severe dengue and four deaths were linked to the disease, with two more under investigation (report of 23 September).

— What it means for you Weekly cases sat below the epidemic threshold in mid-September. The department still urges repellent, window screens and emptying anything that holds water.

— Still open Whether the two deaths under review are confirmed as dengue. The report for week 38 had not been published as of 3 October.

Puerto Rico dengue cases reached 922 in 2026, and nearly half of those patients needed a hospital bed. The Health Department’s weekly arboviral report, dated 23 September, puts the hospitalised share at 49.5%.

The figures gained wider attention this week after Iris Cardona, the department’s principal medical officer, presented them in Caguas. Metro Puerto Rico and NotiCel reported her remarks on 2 and 3 October.

What the Puerto Rico dengue report shows

The report covers week 37, with symptom onset up to 16 September. Of the 922 cases, 626 were confirmed by molecular or antigen tests and 296 were probable, based on antibody tests.

Some 36 patients met the World Health Organization definition of severe dengue. Four deaths were linked to the disease this year, and two more remain under investigation.

Cumulative dengue cases by Health Department region, symptom onset 1 January to 16 September 2026 (922 in total). Source: Puerto Rico Department of Health, arboviral report week 37, 23 Sep 2026.

Cases cluster in the east and south. The Caguas health region leads with 313 cases, followed by Ponce with 237 and Bayamón with 171.

By municipality, Caguas has the most cases, at 118. Arroyo and Guayama have the highest rates, with about 241 and 238 cases per 100,000 residents.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who is getting sick

Teenagers and children carry a large share of the burden. People aged 10 to 19 account for 312 cases, about a third of the total.

Almost all typed cases are serotype 3: 561 of 567, or 98.9%. Three were type 1, and the three type 2 cases were linked to travel outside the island.

Why the hospital share needs context

The surveillance system is based on laboratory results. Mild infections that never reach a clinic or a test are therefore not in the count.

The share is also not new. In 2025 the island logged 3,385 cases, of which 51.7% were hospitalised and nine deaths were linked to dengue.

Transmission has eased since the 2024 epidemic. The department declared a dengue public health emergency in March 2024, according to the report.

Health Secretary Víctor Ramos did not extend it beyond 31 December 2025, El Nuevo Día reported. He said cases had stayed below the threshold for almost 20 weeks.

How the island fights the mosquito

Cardona spoke at the sixth annual Puerto Rico Vector Convention, held at the Caguas fine arts centre. The island’s Vector Control Unit is a programme created in 2016 with the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

From 2024 to December 2025, a CDC project in Bayamón put over 54,500 passive emanators in 5,450-plus homes, NotiCel reported. The devices release transfluthrin, which disorients mosquitoes and cuts their ability to bite.

Another programme fits screens on doors and windows in eight San Juan public housing complexes since January 2026. Unit director Julieanne Miranda Bermúdez said continued cases demand effective, sustainable options for towns and communities.

For background on the territory, see Puerto Rico Explained 2026, a U.S. Territory Guide and Moving to Puerto Rico 2026 Step by Step.

What Is Not Yet Known

The data are preliminary and subject to revision, the department says. It is unclear whether the two deaths under investigation will be added to the toll.

It is also unclear how the autumn months will shape the Puerto Rico dengue curve. The week 38 report had not appeared on the department’s data portal by 3 October.

Sources: Puerto Rico Department of Health, arboviral surveillance report, week 37, 23 Sep 2026 · NotiCel, 3 Oct 2026 · Metro Puerto Rico, 2 Oct 2026 · El Nuevo Día, 12 Dec 2025
