World.title: Elmo Nüganen: Burning Dostoevsky won't burn down the Russian world
World.content:
Actor and director Elmo Nüganen, who in recent years has been closely involved with Südalinna Teater (formerly the Russian Theater in Tallinn), says he understands those who do not wish to consume Russian‑language culture — but avoiding Russian‑language culture will not destroy what Russia as a state is.

This autumn is a busy one for Nüganen. A few weeks ago, VAT Theater premiered Merle Karusoo's documentary production "Kui juuri raiutakse…" ("When Roots Are Cut…"), in which Nüganen also appears on stage as an actor. The production brings to the stage the family stories of Estonian theatre makers with Ingrian Finnish roots.

According to Nüganen, being on stage as himself is a different kind of experience. The process of creating the production has also been different, because, he says, the issue is not what is being talked about, but how it is done.

"You have to stay within a certain frame. Merle had quite a hard time with me. She mentioned the metaphor of a trotting race several times: if someone breaks into a gallop during a trotting race, they get disqualified. She hinted to me repeatedly during rehearsals that I should be disqualified here, because there is a certain established form or expectation of how an actor exists on stage in this kind of story," Nüganen said.

How much the actors reveal about themselves to the audience was up to each performer. "Merle has great experience with these kinds of works, and she always asks at a certain stage whether everyone agrees that what has been said so far will remain, or whether someone wants to remove a topic," he explained. In this production, no one removed anything.

Last year, Nüganen staged "Jumalad" ("Gods"), a production about the war in Ukraine, at Südalinna Teater. He said the theatre was a good place for it because he wanted to stage the work in two languages — Estonian and Russian.

"I don't think I've ever had a theatre project where I could think so broadly about which actresses of different generations would fit into the story, regardless of which theatre they come from. Their individuality is such that their combination could be as interesting and unique as possible," he said.

"OP" Autor/allikas: Ken Mürk/ERR

This Friday, Südalinna Teater will premiere Johan Elm's production of Jaan Kruusvall's final play "Kõrberebase elu" ("Life of the Desert Fox"), with Nüganen playing the lead role. As in Kruusvall's other texts, this one also contains many undercurrents, he noted.

"The situation is contemporary in the sense that what runs underneath in this story is very similar to what is running underneath in our society right now," the actor said, lifting the veil slightly.

The production is performed in Russian with simultaneous translation into Estonian. Nüganen says he also understands those who do not wish to attend Russian‑language cultural events.

"My hand doesn't reach for Dostoevsky either — his books stand untouched on my shelf," he said. "If some people think that way and stay away, then in the big picture it doesn't matter — they can burn the books, but burning Dostoevsky won't burn down the Russian world. These are separate things. I understand the person who doesn't want to hear Russian, doesn't want to pick up a Dostoevsky book, but unfortunately that doesn't annul anything."

In addition to his theater work, Nüganen is once again active at the drama school, where he has taken on a new class this year. He says his feelings toward the group are good: "There's no confusion in me, no excessive anxiety — just a calm, steady start."

World.title: Raul Rebane: In praise of the provinces
World.content:
Estonia shows a pattern in which many county centers are, relative to their population, almost oversupplied with sports, education, culture and public services, Raul Rebane writes.

I titled my piece "In praise of the provinces," and I recommend not trying to squeeze this into metropolitan Tallinn. I will prove my point by asking where the most suitable environment for raising children is.

This topic once came up in a conversation with Gerd Kanter's coach, the Icelander Vesteinn Hafsteinsson. He claimed firmly that in the Nordic countries, the best places for children are medium‑sized towns with about 10,000–20,000 inhabitants. He has lived and worked in such towns in several countries, so he knows what he is talking about.

His claim is supported by several arguments. In the Nordic countries — and also here — such towns generally have good schools and solid opportunities for development in both sports and music. The biggest advantages, however, are the significant time savings due to the proximity of important places and, certainly, safety.

Nordic studies use the term "children's independent mobility." This means that a 10–14‑year‑old child saves a great deal of time each day on the route school‑practice‑music school‑friend‑home compared with a big city — perhaps even a whole hour. In Moscow, travel time by bus or metro can easily be two hours; in a normal town, it is 20–40 minutes. That is a major difference in quality of life.

In addition, in a small town it is possible to get around on foot or by bicycle, which is certainly more sensible than bouncing around on a bus. From a child's perspective, the ideal town is not necessarily the one with the most opportunities, but the one where the child can access those opportunities independently.

There is a little‑known term for this: the Goldilocks zone. It comes from the fairy tale where Goldilocks tries three bowls of porridge — one too hot, one too cold, and one just right. "Just right" is the concept that describes optimal size. It is a town large enough to offer choices but small enough for a child to reach them on their own.

We are used to this. Unfortunately, in many countries' big cities, one parent inevitably becomes the child's chauffeur. Children are not allowed to move around alone. According to studies, countries with restricted independent mobility for children include France, Israel, Brazil, Ireland, Australia, Portugal, Italy, and Canada.

"For example, Viljandi and Rakvere have everything — schools, lots of sports, lots of music, good facilities, plenty of extracurricular activities."

Several families who have returned to Estonia say it is a great blessing when a child can move independently and safely, not by car under the supervision of security guards.

Our "just right" towns are slightly smaller than Nordic examples like Porvoo, Rauma, Lillehammer, or Visby, but most of our county centers fit the "just right" concept very well. Viljandi, Võru, Rakvere, Kuressaare, Haapsalu, and many others have the same logic: a strong balance of services, safety, and short distances.

For example, Viljandi and Rakvere have everything — schools, lots of sports, lots of music, good facilities, plenty of extracurricular activities. At the same time, most of the town can be crossed by bicycle in about 10–15 minutes, meaning an 11–12‑year‑old can organize much of their day independently.

In Estonia, one can even say that many county centers are, relative to their population, almost oversupplied with sports, education, culture, and public services.

What does this mean in practice? One aspect is certainly competitiveness — the ability to spend more time on hobbies.

Those who doubt this should consider the fact that the last individual Olympic champion from Tallinn was speed skater Ants Antson in 1964. Yet the capital has roughly as many people, money, facilities, and opportunities as the rest of Estonia combined.

With this story, I tried to turn the word "province," which some see as derogatory, into something else — an environment to be desired.

We are in the right place. The Anglo‑Saxon and parts of Southern Europe's car‑centered child‑rearing model — "an adult escorts the child" — does not suit us. We follow and develop the Nordic and German model, where the child moves independently.

A simple conclusion follows. If we move to Tallinn to increase children's opportunities, we may actually be moving farther away from those opportunities.

World.title: Marica Lillemets: It's time to create a cross‑sector life‑course policy
World.content:
The lack of meaningful integration between the social welfare and healthcare systems forces people in need to navigate a bureaucratic maze that many older adults cannot manage, writes Marica Lillemets.

Estonia has reached a demographic turning point. Population aging is an everyday reality that requires substantive action. We need a new approach that ensures older people have dignified living conditions, access to healthcare services, and social inclusion. The goal should be to shift from providing social assistance to developing a preventive and empowering life‑course policy.

Despite positive steps in recent years — such as the 2023 care reform and the income‑tax exemption for the average pension — significant shortcomings remain that demand full attention and action.

Older people in Estonia face one of the highest poverty risks in the European Union, as pension growth does not keep pace with rising living costs and healthcare prices. We have special‑pension recipients earning around €4,000 per month and others receiving €400. Unfortunately, healthcare pricing does not sufficiently consider older people's financial capacity, and subsistence support does not cover real‑life needs.

We have also failed to ensure that healthcare services are available everywhere in Estonia. The main reason for service inequality is the drastically different capacities of local governments, which leads to unequal treatment depending on where people live. This particularly affects home‑care services and specialist medical care.

Another striking problem in organizing policy for older adults is institutional fragmentation. There is no substantive integration between social welfare and healthcare. This forces people in need to navigate bureaucratic complexity that many older adults cannot manage.

For example, the modern digital system for accessing family‑doctor services is a barrier for many older people living alone. To overcome it, they must rely on younger relatives or acquaintances — or sit at the doctor's door hoping to be seen.

A unified, person‑centered care fund

As a legislative measure, amendments could be initiated to the Social Welfare Act and the Health Insurance Act to create a unified, person‑centered care fund. This would allow different services — such as home nursing and social transport — to be financed from a single platform. This would reduce pressure on emergency departments and the hospital network. The step would help build an integrated care model, add a preventive component, and increase people's motivation to stay healthy and active for as long as possible.

In addition to physical health, we must focus more on mental and social well‑being. Together, these three components give a person a sufficient sense of being healthy. When one is missing, problems arise.

"The digital transition has left some older adults in an information void, deepening loneliness and mental health concerns."

For example, the digital transition has left some older adults in an information void, deepening loneliness and mental‑health concerns. A more serious consequence is social isolation, which increases the feeling of being excluded from life. I am not calling for resistance to technological development, but for early and age‑appropriate digital‑skills training for older adults. Lifelong learning through "senior universities" would be suitable if conducted in small groups led by trained instructors.

The current widespread practice — where a local librarian or shopkeeper performs necessary digital tasks for an older person when dealing with the state — does not teach independent digital skills. But thanks to these helpers, someone still receives assistance.

The Public Information Act could be supplemented with a provision requiring state institutions and municipalities to maintain accessible physical counseling points for older adults who have missed the digital train entirely. Building digital competence should be the responsibility of individuals, the state, and employers to prevent exclusion in our already small society.

Promoting the "silver economy"

Although our physical capacity decreases with age, our knowledge and dedication often peak later in life. Therefore, employing older adults is a tremendous resource, not a burden. Part‑time or flexible work, age‑appropriate retraining, and valuing life experience make older workers highly valuable.

Unfortunately, not all employers recognize this, and the state's tax laws do not support keeping pension‑age people in the labor market. Yet personal dignity and financial stability are closely linked — not to mention the need to feel socially relevant and contributing to one's own and the country's well‑being.

Tax incentives in the Income Tax Act and Social Tax Act could "nudge" employers toward the silver economy. For example, a lower social‑tax rate could be introduced for employers who hire workers aged 55+ (or 65+) with flexible workloads. This would ease labor shortages and keep older adults socially active.

Estonia's success cannot be measured only by GDP growth. It is also reflected in how we treat our older population. The current reactive and fragmented policy must be replaced with a vision in which aging is a safe and dignified process.

I have not addressed all issues related to older adults or all possible solutions, but the proposals presented here could already justify forming an inter‑ministerial working group and preparing legislative amendments. More proposals will come from stakeholder groups. A cross‑sector life‑course policy is unavoidable.

World.title: Universities warn extra funding won't cover surge in applicants
World.content:
The government will provide extra funding to expand study places as record‑large cohorts reach university age, but universities say the money covers only about two‑thirds of what's needed, leaving many applicants without a place.

To ensure that the large cohorts graduating from high school in the coming years can enter university, the government will allocate about €13 million annually to higher education over the next four years. At the same time, the previously promised increase in operating support for universities will be reduced by roughly €9 million.

"This €13 million is essentially sleight of hand, because the real additional funding is just over €3 million. The problem is not solved. Over the next three years, we will indeed have sharply larger cohorts of high‑school graduates. And you cannot tell high‑school graduates to take a break for five years and come to university later," said University of Tartu vice‑rector for academic affairs Aune Valk.

Aune Valk Autor/allikas: Andres Tennus

Valk added that the University of Tartu can increase student numbers in 2027 with the extra funding, but after that the situation becomes difficult.

"The concern is also that students do not study for just one year — they study for three, five, or six years depending on the field," Valk said.

The Ministry of Education, however, believes the amount should be sufficient to cover all university needs.

"This sum already accounts for the fact that students study at least three years in bachelor's or applied higher education programs. Medical students, for example, study six years. This has been factored in," said Margus Haidak, senior adviser for higher education at the ministry.

The reduction in operating support is, in the ministry's view, unavoidable.

"Throughout the period when the state made significant cuts over the last four years, we still managed to increase operating support for higher education. Now we simply have to accept this cut to remain in solidarity with the rest of society," Haidak said.

Tiit Land. Source: Henri-Kristian Kirsip

The state aims for nearly half of adults aged 25–34 to have higher education by 2035. According to Tallinn University of Technology rector Tiit Land, the goal is not achievable.

"With the current level of state funding, definitely not. Today the figure is 41 percent. It is not realistic under the current funding model, which means we need to reconsider the model. From the perspective of TalTech, master's programs could be subject to tuition fees," Land said.

How the money will be distributed among universities and which fields will receive support will be decided in November.

"The main priority is fields with the greatest labor demand, meaning we favor areas where studies show the biggest shortages. But since young people are also interested in studying outside high‑demand fields, part of the additional funding will go there as well," Haidak said.

World.title: Journalist: A 'To Catch a Predator'‑style show could not be made in Estonia
World.content:
A program modeled on the U.S. television show "To Catch a Predator" could not be produced in Estonia, investigative journalist Mihkel Kärmas says, because it would not fit the country's legal or ethical environment.

Last week, Lance Oppenheim's new feature film "Primetime", starring Robert Pattinson, premiered in cinemas. The film tells the story of TV journalist Chris Hansen, who in the mid‑2000s confronted suspected child predators on camera. Estonian TV host and journalist Mihkel Kärmas, who went to see the film, is not impressed.

"I understand why it's a scandalous film that has caused a stir, but I doubt it will become a major hit in Estonia," Kärmas said.

"Primetime" is based on real events but is a dramatization. At its center is the highly controversial NBC program "To Catch a Predator," which aired from 2004 to 2007.

The show's format involved activists posing online as minors and luring men suspected of seeking sexual contact with underage children to a meeting. The encounters were filmed with hidden cameras, and once the man arrived, host Chris Hansen appeared.

"It's psychologically very gripping. He starts off one‑on‑one, so at first the offenders don't realize they're on television," Kärmas explained.

Hansen read sexually explicit messages from chat logs aloud to the suspects and then revealed that they were on a TV show. According to Kärmas, this structure made the program both innovative and extremely controversial.

"At the time it was groundbreaking, very controversial — and it still is. It became a TV sensation in the United States, but also a deeply polarizing phenomenon. It remains very polarizing today."

Kärmas said the problem was not only hidden cameras or setting a trap. Similar methods have been used in Estonian journalism as well. What made the show controversial was its entertainment‑driven and punitive nature.

One of the film's central events is based on a 2006 incident in Texas. During an operation arranged for the show, producers attempted to catch a high‑ranking official who had allegedly communicated with someone posing as a minor. The incident ended with the man's suicide.

Mihkel Kärmas is one of Estonia's best‑known investigative television journalists. Source: ERR

"The trailer mentions 'I want a whale'. What they mean is that in Hollywood storytelling, the pursuit of a new sensation and higher ratings pushes things further and further — ordinary, excuse me, pedophile offenders aren't enough anymore; they want to catch a prominent figure," Kärmas noted.

After the fatal incident in Texas, the show did not end immediately, but NBC eventually cut ties with Hansen. A court case followed, ending in a settlement.

Kärmas said Hansen's work raises the question of where journalism's ethical boundaries lie. He calls it a highly risky method. "We see that he continues. He's had other scandals too, but in that sense he's still on the air."

Kärmas does not see any possibility that such a show could air in Estonia, largely because Estonia's legal and ethical framework differs from that of the United States.

"Just consider the symbiotic relationship they had with the police. They lure the predator to the location, film for a long time, and only then do the police intervene. In Estonia, such cooperation — where journalists participate in a live operation and the police hold back until you finish filming — I cannot imagine," Kärmas said.

World.title: Gallery: Estonia's first industrial foundry opens in Kohila
World.content:
Estonia's first industrial foundry has opened in Kohila, Rapla County, with BLRT Group's subsidiary BLRT Valukoda investing €14 million in the facility. The new plant also has the potential to fulfill orders for the defense industry.

BLRT Group built the most modern cast‑iron foundry in the Nordic region in Kohila after demand increased for heavier cast components. The new plant will help open doors to new clients in the Nordic countries.

"It is possible here to produce large‑scale and significantly heavier cast parts or structures than we used to make. There is particularly strong demand for these, especially among our clients and partners in Scandinavia," said Algerd Andruškevitšus, member of the BLRT Group management board.

The Kohila foundry will allow production volumes to grow to up to 3,000 tons per year.

"This is important for industry and likely for the defense sector in the future as well. So this is a significant investment," Prime Minister Kristen Michal said.

In Kohila, cast‑iron machine‑building blanks will be produced for electric motors, forestry machinery, and boilers.

"We received the usage permit yesterday. That means we will start operations on Monday, but until now we have been setting up equipment, and the first molds have already come off the lines," said BLRT Valukoda managing director Paul Gross, adding that the foundry is currently short ten employees.

The Kohila foundry will eventually employ up to 70 people.

World.title: Publishers say using AI to translate classics is ethically wrong
World.content:
Publishers Krista Kaer and Piret Lemetti warn that AI-assisted re-translations of literary classics appearing on the market are unethical, unfair to readers, and devalue the work of human translators.

Varrak Editor-in-Chief Kaer said that the overall situation for translated literature in Estonia has not improved from the viewpoint of publishers.

"Print runs of books have dropped sharply, and translated literature is expensive to publish. In addition to purchasing rights, there is the translation cost, which is very significant for larger books. Overall, the amount of valuable translated literature has decreased. With the classics, everything is fine — the Hieronymus series publishes books very nicely, and what should have appeared long ago is well covered. However, the situation is bad with contemporary quality literature," Kaer admitted.

"Books are published that are more or less a sure bet. There is nothing to be done; a large part of the world is still uncovered for Estonians, and this situation will not change in the near future either. The Cultural Endowment helps, thank God," Kaer laughed.

"I look with great envy at the French and Germans, where very important works published all over the world appear very quickly and continuously. In Estonia, books that appear quickly tend to belong to the field of entertainment and crime fiction," she noted.

Eesti Raamat Editor-in-Chief Piret Lemetti agreed.

"Often you look at a book that you would very much like to publish, but you know that publishing it would be a very big risk. Especially if it is English-language literature, because people read a lot in English. If you cannot publish the book at the same time it appears in English, then you have already missed the train," Lemetti admitted.

"The share of translations from English is decreasing in other European countries as well because many people read in English. For Estonia, translating literature published in the Nordic countries is becoming more important, as is Central Europe. Of course, Asia is still half-undiscovered for us. South Korean literature is currently making a huge breakthrough, but we simply do not have enough translators," Kaer added.

"It is also very difficult to introduce unfamiliar foreign names to Estonian readers because there is a deep distrust — people prefer to take a book by a well-known author or at least someone who can be associated with something," Kaer noted.

Lemetti added that a point of comparison is crucial for readers. "If readers cannot associate authors with someone or something, they are not very inclined to buy the book," she said.

"If print runs drop by another couple hundred, there will actually be no point in publishing these books anymore," Kaer said, expressing hope that books people hesitate to buy will still be borrowed from libraries, provided libraries have enough money to purchase them.

"At the same time, all agents are gradually raising author fees and translation-rights fees. One can fight this and negotiate down, but these costs are becoming higher and higher. For some reason, there is an opinion that books are being bought more and more and publishers are doing better and better, which of course is not true," Kaer laughed.

The publishers added that exciting niche works remain untranslated because, in Estonia, their target audience would only be 300 to 400 people.

At the same time, older translations are also being updated. Varrak has published Dostoevsky texts, and Kaer herself has retranslated Yeats.

"These are probably needed, but new mystical translations have appeared — for example, of Conan Doyle — that are clearly made with artificial assistance and are completely terrible. Such things are very bad: taking classics to which copyright no longer applies and for which one does not have to pay, and then simply throwing them onto the market in a way that they cannot even be called translations or books," Kaer warned.

Lemetti added that she has encountered such books herself. "It is actually written on the title page that artificial intelligence assistance has been used in translation. I do not understand why this has been done," she noted.

Kaer believes the driver is a quick cash grab.

"This is unfair toward the author, and it is unfair toward buyers and readers. Doing such things is simply ethically wrong," Kaer said.

"This is also the devaluation of the translator's work. Essentially, the translator is reduced to a glorified editor. I do not understand what the point of this is," Lemetti added.

World.title: Construction begins on first phase of Iraq’s Madinat Al Ward
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – ORA Iraq awarded CRC Dorra the building contract for the first phase of Madinat Al Ward, paving the way for large-scale development in Iraq.

The deal was signed in the presence of Naguib Sawiris, Chairman of ORA, and Mohamed Dorra, Vice Chairman of Dorra Group, as the project progressed from ground preparation to primary construction.

CRC Dorra will begin construction after POWERCHINA has completed the earthworks and ground preparation for Phase One, according to ORA Iraq.

The deal adds another important regional contractor to the development.

CRC Dorra is the contracting arm of Dorra Group, an engineering and construction business founded in 1943 that operates in Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Iraq.

Its work includes residential, commercial, office, and hotel developments, as well as design-build projects.

ORA said that the selection was based on CRC Dorra’s construction expertise and capacity to perform large-scale projects.

The commencement of construction marks a key milestone for Madinat Al Ward as ORA expands its investment and development efforts in the Iraqi market.

The company said that it continues to be dedicated to building the project as an integrated community, with the new contract advancing Phase One from site preparation to physical construction.

World.title: US Treasury approves waiver for Iranian flights to Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Minister of Foreign Affairs Fuad Hussein announced on Friday, October 2, 2026, that U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent has agreed to exempt religious pilgrimage flights to holy sites in Iraq from secondary sanctions imposed on Iranian aviation, following intensive bilateral talks held in Washington.

The decision resolves mounting diplomatic friction surrounding the status of Najaf International Airport, granting legal clarity for passenger arrivals while shielding Iraqi aviation infrastructure from punitive measures.

In a statement shared on X (formerly Twitter) and reported by the 964 Network, Hussein outlined that discussions with Bessent encompassed the overarching trajectory of U.S.-Iraqi economic and security ties, regional fiscal stability, and the spillover impacts of American sanctions enforcement on the domestic Iraqi economy.

Hussein specifically raised the operational paralysis facing Najaf International Airport—a vital national transport hub serving millions of international religious pilgrims annually—emphasizing that economic restrictions should not impede lawful civilian travel or religious observances. Secretary Bessent acknowledged Iraq’s sovereign concerns, formally approving a targeted waiver for flights directed toward the holy shrines.

During the diplomatic session, Hussein reaffirmed Baghdad’s appreciation for past U.S. and International Coalition support in the campaign to defeat Daesh (ISIS), while reiterating the federal government’s constitutional roadmap under Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi to monopolize arms under the state and maintain sole authority over war and peace.

Commending Washington’s accommodation, Hussein noted that recognizing the importance of religious freedom and facilitating pilgrim transit reflects shared values of mutual respect and tolerance, reinforcing a stable, long-term bilateral partnership between Iraq and the United States.

World.title: ITEX 2026: Iraqi AI and tech startups expand
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi, regional, and international technology enterprises showcased cutting-edge solutions in artificial intelligence, network synchronization, and enterprise digital transformation during their participation in the Iraq International Information and Communications Technology Exhibition in Baghdad.

The participating companies expressed strong ambition to expand operations and capture growing commercial opportunities in Iraq’s rapidly developing technological sector.

Hassan Abdul-Baqi Khalaf, founder of domestic startup Al-Burhan for AI Image and Video Recognition, told the Iraqi News Agency (INA) that the venture originated from registered patents specializing in automated media verification and tamper protection against digital forgery and deepfakes.

Khalaf—a computer science student at the American University of Iraq – Baghdad (AUIB) collaborating with a doctoral partner in mathematics and physics—highlighted that their platform processes requests for more than 3,000 daily active users across private corporate clients and the public.

Delivering up to 95 percent accuracy in identifying manipulated content, the company is leveraging its inaugural exhibition presence to pursue operational partnerships with federal entities, specifically the Ministry of Interior, to detect fabricated media and enhance sovereign cyber verification tools.

International infrastructure providers also underscored their entry into the domestic market. Engineer Ahmed Mustafa of Canada’s Al-Mamas, an IT and network engineering specialist, revealed that the firm is seeking to establish an operational foothold in Iraq following successful deployments in the UAE, Qatar, and Egypt.

Al-Mamas holds exclusive distribution rights across the Middle East and North Africa for precision German-manufactured timing and synchronization hardware, which is critical for maintaining ultra-low-latency architectures across telecommunications networks, industrial automation, data center facilities, and distributed artificial intelligence systems.

Highlighting regional corporate expansion, Samer Al-Yasin, sales director for Qatar-headquartered conglomerate Mannai Corporation, affirmed that Iraq represents a fertile and attractive destination for long-term tech investment.

Marking its second exhibition appearance in Baghdad, Mannai—which employs over 15,000 personnel across the Gulf—formally established its Baghdad branch three months ago and is actively preparing to launch regional offices in Erbil and Basra.

Al-Yasin emphasized that the group is deploying enterprise digital transformation, cloud integration, and systems architecture tailored for federal ministries, banking institutions, and healthcare providers, aiming to transfer its regional technical expertise to drive national modernization and support sovereign institutional revenues.

World.title: Baghdad hosts major motorsports festival to celebrate Iraqi sovereignty day
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Baghdad hosted a mass motorsports festival on Friday, October 2, 2026, to celebrate Iraqi Sovereignty Day and National Day, organized under the auspices of Iraqi National Olympic Committee President Aqeel Muften and drawing substantial public crowds alongside national sports figures.

The festival, co-organized by the Iraqi Automobile and Motorcycle Federation and secured by the Baghdad Operations Command, showcased competitive and exhibition motorsport performances to highlight domestic stability and nationwide celebrations marking the complete withdrawal of foreign forces.

Farooq Al-Rubaie, President of the Iraqi Automobile and Motorcycle Federation, told the Iraqi News Agency (INA) that celebrating Sovereignty Day honors the resilience and immense sacrifices made by the armed forces and citizens over challenging decades.

Noting the passionate grassroots fanbase for motorsports across Iraq, Al-Rubaie emphasized that staging the festival serves both an athletic and patriotic duty, projecting the reality of a secure and revitalized capital. He urged local and regional media outlets along with content creators to spotlight Iraq’s stability, community engagements, and peaceful public life during major national milestones.

Baghdad Operations Command Media Director, Major General Abbas Hamid, stated to INA that Sovereignty Day—coinciding with Iraq’s National Day—reflects the sovereign resolve of the Iraqi people.

Hamid confirmed that joint security formations under the Ministries of Defense and Interior, alongside military intelligence branches, established comprehensive security perimeters around the capital to safeguard wide-ranging cultural, artistic, and athletic gatherings.

Reaffirming that Baghdad is entering an era defined by urban reconstruction and civic stability, Hamid reiterated the full readiness of security apparatuses to protect public safety and preserve social cohesion across all urban centers.

World.title: Iraq inks data center MoU with Huawei as tech giant employs 10,000 across country
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Ministry of Communications formalized a strategic partnership with global telecommunications giant Huawei on Friday, October 2, 2026, signing a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to construct modern enterprise data centers across the country.

Finalized during the 5th Iraq International Information and Communications Technology Exhibition and Conference (ITEX 2026) in Baghdad, the agreement was concluded under the sponsorship and in the presence of Minister of Communications Mustafa Sanad between the state-owned General Company for Communications and Informatics and Huawei’s executive leadership.

The initiative is aimed at bolstering Iraq’s sovereign cloud hosting, elevating service quality, and broadening international technical cooperation.

On the sidelines of the expo, Huawei confirmed the extensive scope of its commercial footprint in Iraq, revealing that it actively partners with more than 240 domestic Iraqi enterprises across diverse sectors.

Rafid Abbas Al-Khafaji, Vice President and Board Member of Huawei Iraq, told the Iraqi News Agency (INA) that this marked the company’s inaugural participation as an exhibitor at ITEX, expressing admiration for the high caliber of domestic and multinational engagement.

Al-Khafaji noted that Huawei presented specialized end-to-end solutions spanning oil and gas digitalization, telecommunications, smart transportation, healthcare systems, artificial intelligence, and modular data center architecture.

Reviewing the company’s continuous commercial presence in Iraq since 2003, Al-Khafaji emphasized that Huawei remained fully operational through all domestic security and economic challenges, including uninterrupted on-site work by its Chinese engineering teams during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Today, the corporation operates four major regional branches in Baghdad, Basra, Erbil, and Sulaymaniyah, supporting a wider ecosystem of over 10,000 employees.

Addressing public misconceptions, Al-Khafaji clarified that while Huawei is widely recognized among consumers for consumer smartphones, handset sales represent the smallest segment of its business portfolio by volume.

The firm’s enterprise and carrier operations form the backbone of its Iraqi footprint, servicing major mobile network operators alongside key sovereign institutions, including the Ministries of Oil, Transport, Interior, and Defense, as well as the General Secretariat of the Council of Ministers.

Beyond central government networks, Huawei is driving provincial smart security solutions—such as Babylon Governorate’s integrated municipal surveillance network—while advancing intelligent electric vehicle systems and cloud infrastructures designed to anchor Iraq’s next-generation digital economy.

World.title: Russia ‘tearing Kyiv apart’, mayor says, as strikes paralyse traffic
World.content:
Kyiv – Russian attacks on key infrastructure were “tearing Kyiv apart”, the city’s mayor said Friday, as strikes on a bridge linking the capital’s east and west brought traffic to a standstill.

President Volodymyr Zelensky accused his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, of ripping up the rulebook of armed conflict by sanctioning massive attacks on civilian areas, an accusation the Kremlin has rejected.

The grinding conflict, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, has largely focused on ground fighting in the east, with Kyiv largely spared from the devastation wrought near the frontline.

But Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city should now be on a war footing.

“The capital is in a very dramatic situation,” he posted on Telegram. “It’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we lived in peacetime.

“The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”

His message came as the authorities shut one of Kyiv’s main bridges and restricted movement on a second after another wave of deadly strikes by fast-moving, jet-powered drones.

Long lines of stationary cars and buses were gridlocked on main roads as commuters sought alternative routes — or even made their way on foot.

“I’ve been travelling for three hours… to get to work,” said Tetiana Osypenko, a 49-year-old seamstress whose bus was stuck in a traffic jam.

“There’s just no way to get there. Nothing. It’s impossible to cross the bridges today,” she told AFP.

Traffic built up due to the complete closure to all vehicles going in both directions on the Southern Bridge, one of eight bridges connecting the east and west of Kyiv over the Dnipro river.

It was hit several times on Thursday and Friday morning.

The Paton Bridge, further north, was open in one direction only, though there were no reports that it had been struck.

In a post on X, Zelensky accused Putin of last month declaring there were “no rules now”, citing unnamed intelligence and people around Putin.

“The Russians couldn’t occupy us. So now they are doing massive attacks and massive killings,” Zelensky said.

The Kremlin made no immediate public response to the claim, which Zelensky first made in an interview with the Financial Times.

– Daily disruption –

Kyiv has been increasingly under aerial bombardment in recent months, putting the city on near-constant alert and disrupting daily life.

Air raid sirens warning of approaching threats in the skies sound almost round the clock, urging the city’s estimated three million people to seek shelter.

Repeated strikes on trains and petrol stations have already hit the rail and road networks while attacks on energy facilities threaten power and heating as winter approaches.

Osypenko, the seamstress, said she would not get home because of the traffic jams. Previous disruption to subway services during air raids forced her to spend the night in a metro station near the Southern Bridge.

Not being able to work costs her money, compounding the financial pressures caused by the war, she added. “You just spend the whole day feeling completely beaten down.”

The latest Russian attacks killed one person and wounded at least two other people when a 25-storey residential building was hit in southeast Kyiv.

– ‘Political will’ –

Zelensky urged tougher sanctions to prevent Russia from manufacturing its new jet-powered drones, which are faster and harder to intercept.

Russia’s production of the weapons was “critically dependent” on foreign components, he wrote on social media on Friday.

“Every Russian drone can actually be stopped right at the production line. What is needed is the political will of these countries,” he added.

Zelensky has repeatedly called on Ukraine’s Western allies for more military support, particularly for US-made Patriot missile interceptors.

On Thursday, he said Ukraine had used its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, without disclosing where or what it had been used against.

He also said Ukraine was testing five of its own interceptors against drones.

Ukraine’s military on Friday said it struck an oil refinery in Volgograd and another facility in Samara, both in southwest Russia, for allegedly supplying fuel to Russian forces.

Kyiv also dismissed reports that its F-16 fighter jets — another key tool used against jet-powered drones — could be grounded due to delays in maintenance inspection and the supply of parts.

But Zelensky told the Financial Times that around half of Ukraine’s fleet was spending lengthy maintenance periods in Europe.

World.title: Man City verdict a ‘big topic’ for England players, says Tuchel
World.content:
London – Thomas Tuchel said that Manchester City were the talk of the England camp after the club were found guilty of multiple breaches of Premier League financial rules, but insisted that the case would not affect his selection for Saturday’s match in Croatia.

The findings by an independent commission, announced earlier this week, have sent shockwaves through English football.

City, the dominant Premier League force over the past 15 years, face severe sanctions, which could include expulsion from the top division.

Marc Guehi and Elliott Anderson are the only two City players remaining in Tuchel’s squad for the Nations League match in Rijeka after Nico O’Reilly was forced to withdraw due to injury.

“We had some time off and some time between the matches, and it’s a big subject,” Tuchel told his pre-match press conference on Friday.

“Of course the players talk about it, and City players talk about it, and we talk to them, but only briefly.

“They’re ready to go for tomorrow, that’s what they show on the pitch and that’s what they show in camp, but of course it’s a big topic.”

City deny wrongdoing and on Friday lodged an appeal against the ruling.

But unless they can overturn the decision of the commission, they are likely to face at least a points deduction, which would threaten their place in the Premier League.

Tuchel was asked if the club’s players would still be in his mind for selection should they be playing regularly in the lower divisions.

“There’s always a possibility,” he said. “I think I would always try to pick the best team for the camp, for the occasion, for the tournament, and I will never rule out that they don’t play in the top flight in their country.

“So we need to look at this from case by case.”

England’s clash with Croatia, which will take place behind closed doors, is their third of four Nations League games in the current international window.

The Three Lions were beaten 3-2 by world champions Spain on home soil last weekend, but bounced back to beat the Czech Republic 2-0 on Tuesday.

World.title: US posts weak job growth data in September
World.content:
Washington – Employment in the United States grew by 29,000 jobs in September, missing analysts’ expectations significantly, with the unemployment rate rising slightly to 4.2 percent, government data showed on Friday.

Adding to the weak data, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) also revised down job figures for July and August by a combined 60,000 jobs, the department said in a statement.

The revision to July’s data showed that the world’s largest economy lost jobs that month, as opposed to posting a gain of 21,000 as previously reported.

The data comes ahead of key midterm elections in November where President Donald Trump’s Republican Party is facing a stern test over his handling of the economy.

Analysts polled by Dow Jones Newswires and the Wall Street Journal had expected the US economy to add 84,000 jobs in September.

– Health care leads –

Employment in most major sectors was largely unchanged, the BLS reported, with health care posting notable gains of 17,000.

The sector has propped up the labor market in the United States in the last year, as an aging population requires more care both in hospitals and at home.

Still, September’s gains in the sector were slower than its average monthly gain of 33,000 over the last year.

The financial sector continued its downward slide, losing 7,000 jobs in September and bringing its overall slump from a recent peak in May 2025 to 129,000.

Most of the losses in that sector have been among insurance companies.

– Fed implications –

Average hourly earnings for all employees were up 3.0 percent, the BLS said, with wages continuing to lag behind stubbornly high inflation — meaning most workers are seeing real wage losses.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren seized on the data to criticize Trump’s performance since taking office last year.

“Paychecks are growing at their slowest rate in nearly seven years, outside of the Covid-19 pandemic,” she said in a statement.

“Since the start of Trump’s war, real wages have fallen 0.7 percent as his failed agenda keeps pushing prices up,” she said, referring to the US war against Iran launched in late February.

The conflict has plunged the Middle East into violence and sent global energy prices skyrocketing, as Tehran’s retaliatory action has targeted Washington’s regional allies and choked a key trading route.

The data comes after the US Federal Reserve — which has a dual mandate to maintain inflation at a long-term two-percent target while ensuring maximum employment — raised interest rates last month to address high prices.

The US labor market has been largely in balance this year, with modest job gains and a relatively steady unemployment rate.

That steadiness has allowed the Fed to focus on the inflation side of its mandate, but any weakness in the labor market may give policy makers pause.

Raising interest rates tends to cool inflation but can also limit economic activity, which can affect the job market.

This week, two key Fed policymakers indicated that the central bank may not raise rates again at its October meeting, although markets continue to expect a further hike before the end of the year.

Friday’s jobs data “lends support to the less hawkish Fed officials that indicate no need to rush and deliver the next rate hike at the end of this month,” said Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide, in a note.

She added that this could release some pressure on bond yields — which have been spiralling in part due to expectations of interest rate hikes.

Nancy Vanden Houten at Oxford Economics, however, disagreed, expecting upside risks to inflation to continue to dominate Fed policymakers’ thinking.

“We think the upside risks to inflation are still a bigger concern for the Federal Reserve and expect they will raise rates at the end of the month,” she said.

World.title: Drug addicts turn to painkillers amid Nasha Mukt crackdown in J&K
World.content:
SRINAGAR: Drug users and peddlers in Jammu & Kashmir are increasingly turning to pharmaceutical opioids, primarily painkillers, amid an intensified crackdown under Nasha Mukt Abhiyaan to make the UT ânarcotics-freeâ.

âIt seems they were mixing several painkiller drugs to get the effect of heroin,â a police officer said, adding that abusers frequently use prescription medicines like Tramadol and Tapentadol, which they refer to as âTapalâ in their local slang.

Investigations have so far led to the recovery of 2,19,425 tablets and capsules of pharmaceutical drugs, as well as 3.830 kg of codeine-containing liquid, including the storage containers, police said.

Since its launch on April 11, Nasha Mukt Abhiyaan has resulted in over 4,000 arrests, the seizure of 288 properties, and registration of 3,257 cases under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act. The campaign includes awareness programmes, the destruction of illicit poppy crops, and random urine drug testing for drivers.

On Thursday, Srinagar police arrested eight people after busting a major network involved in the procurement, transportation, storage, distribution, and financing of banned pharmaceutical products, with supply lines extending well beyond J&K.





Among those arrested was Haris Hameed Malla, a Srinagar resident identified as a key accused in the network allegedly headed by Waseem Ahmad Zargar. While Zargar claimed to operate a legitimate pharmaceutical business, Malla allegedly projected himself as an influential figure, frequently flaunting photographs with top police and civil officials.

His Instagram account featured photographs with Union ministers Nitin Gadkari and Chirag Paswan, as well as Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and National Conference MP Aga Ruhullah Mehdi.

On his social media profiles, Malla described himself as the editor-in-chief of the âIndia News Panelâ and a community journalist. Malla had also posted a letter on X, purportedly written by L-G Manoj Sinha, regarding the UTâs efforts to combat drug abuse.

World.title: PoK woman crosses LoC in Rajouri, detained
World.content:
JAMMU: A 19-year-old woman from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) was intercepted by Army personnel after she crossed the LoC in J&Kâs Rajouri district, officials said Saturday.

Nothing incriminating was found with Samiya Azeem when she was caught late Friday, the officials said, adding she is a resident of PoKâs Kotli district. âDuring preliminary interrogation, the girl maintained she had inadvertently crossed the LoC and entered Indian territory,â an official said.

Troops found Samiya in the border village of Pukherni in Rajouriâs Nowshera sector. The teenager was later handed over to J&K Police officers for further detention and inquiries, the officials said.

Inadvertent LoC crossings are not rare in J&K. Such intruders are often intercepted by Army troopers and handed over to local cops for identity verification before being repatriated through designated checkpoints following special flag meetings with Pakistani counterparts.

Checks followed, and he was later handed over to Pakistani Rangers by BSF personnel at Golpattan outpost.

World.title: 1 dead, 55 hurt in J&K as Bengal bus hits hillside, vehicle sent for rescue overturns
World.content:
(Representative image): A QRT vehicle dispatched from Ramban police lines for the rescue overturned around 9.15 am, injuring nine personnel on board,â an official said.

JAMMU: A tourist died, and 55 others were injured in two separate but related accidents on Jammu-Srinagar NH in Ramban district on Saturday morning. The incidents involved a tourist bus returning to West Bengal and a speeding quick response team (QRT) vehicle that was dispatched for the rescue and evacuation efforts.âThe tourist bus reportedly lost control and hit a hillside around 8.30am. Jamuna, a resident of West Bengal, died and 46 others were injured. A QRT vehicle dispatched from Ramban police lines for the rescue overturned around 9.15 am, injuring nine personnel on board,â an official said.J&K lieutenant governor Manoj Sinha and Union minister Jitendra Singh expressed grief over the loss of life and prayed for the speedy recovery of the injured. Sinha assured that the best possible medical treatment would be provided to the seriously injured.

World.title: Road injuries 10th leading cause for deaths in India: WHO report
World.content:
NEW DELHI: âRoad injuriesâ was the eighth leading cause of deaths among males in India in 2023, and in the case of females, âfallsâ was the eighth biggest cause of deaths, as per the latest WHO Global Health Estimates (GHE).

Overall, road traffic injuries ranked the 10th leading cause of death for both males and females in India, while fatalities due to falls ranked 9th.

India, which has recorded the maximum road deaths since such global data compilation started, registered 1.74 lakh such fatalities in 2023, and this was a little over 14% of the 12.2 lakh people who lost their lives in road crashes across the world. This has only increased in the past two years to reach 1.83 lakh in 2025.

The figures underline the continuing scale of the road safety challenge in the country, where road crashes claim 500 lives daily.

Falls in India claimed 25,150 lives, as per the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) data, which was around 3% of the total 8.42 lakh lives lost in such incidents. Most of the deaths due to road crashes and falls are preventable. The data also highlights the significant burden of injuries that can result in loss of life and have wider social and economic consequences for families.





As per the WHO report, globally, road traffic injuries were the 8th biggest cause of death in low-income countries and the 10th biggest in middle-income countries. Globally, it was ranked 11th, indicating that the high number of such deaths not only has a huge burden on low- and middle-income countries but also a major concern for the global community, despite many developed nations having been successful in bringing down fatalities due to road crashes.

The differences in rankings across income groups also reflect the varying burden of road injuries across countries and regions.

They said addressing the problem would require greater attention to the safety needs of different categories of road users and a stronger focus on preventing crashes and reducing their consequences.

World.title: Russia to take 70,000 Indian skilled workers this year, Jaishankar tells panel
World.content:
NEW DELHI: External affairs minister

on Saturday briefed a parliamentary consultative committee on India's "multifaceted" engagement with Russia, covering bilateral trade, investment and energy cooperation as well as New Delhi's diplomatic efforts to contribute towards ending the Ukraine conflict.

Chairing the meeting on India-Russia relations, Jaishankar also informed members that Russia has agreed to take around 70,000 Indian skilled workers this year, particularly in construction and logistics, people familiar with the discussions said, according to news agency PTI.

Jaishankar said India and Russia share an ambition to expand bilateral trade in a more balanced manner, including by increasing Indian exports to Russia across seven sectors â automobiles, pharmaceuticals, food, marine products, engineering goods, chemicals and textiles.

Trade, connectivity and energy cooperation

The minister highlighted various areas of bilateral engagement, including trade, investments, energy, connectivity, culture and people-to-people ties, according to a social media post by Jaishankar.

The discussions also covered an India-Eurasian Economic Union Free Trade Agreement, the Chennai-Vladivostok corridor, the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) and the Northern Sea Route.





On energy cooperation, Jaishankar said India's priority was to safeguard the interests of Indian consumers.

"Our approach is to maintain multiple sources of supply," he said, according to people familiar with the meeting.

The government has also been seeking to expand opportunities for Indian workers in Russia.

Ukraine conflict and India's diplomatic efforts

The Ukraine conflict also featured prominently in the discussions, with Jaishankar apprising the panel of India's position and recent diplomatic efforts to support dialogue and diplomacy.

In his social media post, Jaishankar said he highlighted India's "active support to dialogue & diplomacy to end the Ukraine conflict".

The minister referred to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's August 31 meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Bishkek, where the PM said that "endless war must now give way to end of war".

Jaishankar travelled to Ukraine last month and subsequently met the foreign ministers of Ukraine and Russia in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

During those engagements, he conveyed India's readiness to assist efforts to bring the conflict to an end, people familiar with the meeting said.

"If India can be of any help in any manner to bring the war to an end, it is ready to do so," Jaishankar said in his conversations.

Putin's recent remarks at the Valdai Club in Moscow were also discussed. He had said Prime Minister Modi "has very good ideas for finding mutually acceptable solutions" to bring peace.

Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha's remarks appreciating India's efforts were also noted during the meeting.

Efforts to secure Indians in Russian military

Jaishankar also briefed the committee on the government's efforts to secure the release of Indian nationals serving in the Russian military.

The government has engaged with Russian authorities, including at the highest levels, for the early discharge of such individuals, the people cited above said.

So far, around 140 Indian nationals have been discharged, while India is in touch with Russian authorities regarding the whereabouts of 55 Indian nationals who are reportedly working for the Russian Arm.

The government has also been taking action against agents who recruit Indians for such roles, with members being briefed about the risks faced by Indian citizens joining the Russian Army.

The parliamentary committee meeting thus covered India's economic and energy engagement with Russia alongside its diplomatic efforts on Ukraine and its continuing efforts to secure the release of Indian nationals serving in the Russian military.

World.title: India summons Pak envoy over 'cross-border infiltration', rejects Ferozepur claims
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Saturday summoned the ChargÃ© d'Affaires of the Pakistan high commission to lodge a strong protest over what it described as the continued facilitation of illegal cross-border infiltration from Pakistan.

It also rejected as âbaseless and motivatedâ Pakistanâs allegations over an October 2 incident in the Ferozepur sector of Punjab along the International Border.

MEA said that Pakistan was informed that three individuals had entered Indian territory and continued moving towards the border fence despite repeated warnings from the BSF to return. The force subsequently engaged them after they were assessed to pose an imminent security threat.

"The Pakistani side was informed that three individuals infiltrated into Indian territory and despite multiple warnings by BSF to return to Pakistan, continued to move towards the border fence. The BSF was compelled to engage them for posing an imminent security threat," MEA said in a statement.

MEA said the incident was part of a repeated pattern of cross-border movement by armed narcotics syndicates operating from Pakistan.





Islamabad was urged to investigate such infiltration and drug-smuggling activities, including the alleged involvement of Pakistani border forces, and take appropriate corrective measures.

"This incident highlights a clear pattern of repeated cross-border movement by armed narcotics syndicates operating from Pakistan. Government of Pakistan was urged to investigate these cross-border infiltration, drug smuggling activities and the complicity of Pakistan Border Guarding forces therein, and to take appropriate remedial measures," it said.

NEW DELHI: A local court on Saturday granted bail to six Congress workers arrested for allegedly defacing the outer wall of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's ancestral home in Agra during a protest against alleged manipulation of voter lists.The accused - Mukesh Dhangar, Anil Yadav, Rajesh Kumar, Manoj Gaur, Rajesh Gautam and Pankaj Chaudhary - were granted bail after furnishing surety bonds of Rs 20,000 each, advocate Santosh Dixit, who represented them, said.The six were arrested on September 29 and had been sent to jail following a case registered against them under several provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, including those relating to attempt to murder, rioting, wrongful restraint and assault or criminal force against a public servant.Dixit said the police had dropped Section 109(2) of the BNS, relating to attempt to murder, after failing to substantiate the charge in its submissions before the court.In an earlier hearing, the court had directed the police to conduct a detailed investigation into the invocation of Section 109(1), asking them to specify the facts, injuries, medical evidence, eyewitness testimony or other evidence supporting the charge.The court had also directed the investigating officer to complete the probe by October 3 and drop the section if the investigation did not establish the alleged offence.On September 28 protest in which some Congress workers allegedly wrote slogans with black paint on the gate and outer wall of Kumar's residence in the Vijay Nagar area of Agra.Police registered the case at Hariparvat police station on a complaint by a sub-inspector against eight named persons and 15-20 unidentified Congress workers.The other charges in the case include Section 121 of the BNS, relating to voluntarily causing grievous hurt to deter a public servant from performing his duty, Section 126 on wrongful restraint and Section 132 on assault or criminal force against a public servant. Provisions relating to rioting, house-trespass, criminal intimidation and intentional insult were also invoked.Congress Agra city president Amit Singh welcomed the bail order and said the party would continue its agitation against Kumar."The serious section imposed by the police has been removed by the court. This is a victory for democracy," Singh said, adding that the Congress would continue its campaign until Kumar resigns as Chief Election Commissioner.

World.title: Netanyahu invites ‘true hero’ Indian flydubai captain to Israel
World.content:
Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday (October 3, 2026) invited to Israel as a guest of honour the Indian captain of a Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight who offered a dramatic account of how he saved the plane after being attacked.

Mr. Netanyahu said he wanted Captain Smit Machchhar and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, one of Israel’s key international partners, to light a flame at a national ceremony for Israel’s Independence Day next May, saying the role was usually reserved for Israeli citizens.

“You are a true hero of the brave peoples of India and Israel and you are a hero of the entire world,” Mr. Netanyahu said in a video his office released of his telephone conversation with the hospitalised captain.

UAE investigators have said that the co-pilot planned the “terrorist act” by attacking Mr. Machchhar with an axe.

Asked how the attack unfolded, Mr. Machchhar said the co-pilot had asked to take time to pray, as devout Muslims do five times a day.

“A lot of locals, they do pray, which is not out of the ordinary. While he was praying, out of respect, I was just looking at the front and not at the back,” Mr. Machchhar said.

“Suddenly after I think I would say about four to five minutes, there was a big blow to the back of my head. My first thought was that there was catastrophic damage to the aircraft and something is not right.

“But then after that the blows kept coming one after the other. That’s when I realised that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”

While saying his memory was not entirely clear due to his injury, Mr. Machchhar said he managed to pull open the cockpit door “but I think he shut it back closed.”

“I had that one last fight left in me,” Mr.Machchhar explained, saying he knew he faced certain death if not.

“That’s when I pushed against everything. I gave everything that I had and just went for the door and opened the door and thankfully people were waiting.”

World.title: CM lays foundation for waste processing, biogas plants in city
World.content:
Chief Minister Rekha Gupta on Saturday virtually laid the foundation stones for new waste processing plants at Okhla, Singhola and Ghazipur, as well as a 300-tonne-per-day biogas plant at Ghazipur for processing biodegradable waste, the Chief Minister’s Office (CMO) said in a release.

According to a separate release issued by the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD), the waste processing plants will have capacities of 1,400 tonnes per day (TPD) in Okhla, 700 TPD in Singhola and 800 TPD in Ghazipur.

‘100 acres freed’

Earlier in the day, Ms. Gupta visited the Okhla landfill site and said that over the past 18 months, 217.17 lakh metric tons of waste had been disposed of at the Okhla, Bhalswa and Ghazipur landfill sites, freeing nearly 100 acres of land.

As per the CMO release, Ms. Gupta told officials that merely removing the waste lying on the surface would not be enough. She said along with scientifically disposing of the old waste accumulated underneath, the system for processing the fresh waste must also be strengthened immediately.

World.title: CaRWAN protests ‘unlawful’ arrests of Noida workers, activists near Jantar Mantar, 70 detained
World.content:
Amid the ongoing protests over the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, the Campaign for Release of Workers and Activists of Noida (CaRWAN) on Saturday staged a separate protest near Jantar Mantar seeking the release of workers and activists jailed in connection with the April 13 Noida workers’ protest.

More than 100 protesters marched from Patel Chowk towards Jantar Mantar, and Delhi Police detained at least 70 of them before releasing them later in the day. The protesters alleged that the police forcefully detained and manhandled them, with female protesters allegedly being held by male officers.

‘Unlawful detention’

CaRWAN demanded that workers and activists who had been “unlawfully held by Uttar Pradesh Police and incarcerated for over five months” be released immediately.

“While there are protests going on against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, his daughter Medha Roopam, who is the District Magistrate of Gautam Buddha Nagar, issued NSA detention orders against Satyam Verma and Akriti Chaudhary,” CaRWAN member Anjali said during the protest.

Ms. Anjali said that while Mr. Verma, a translator and former journalist, continues to be detained under the National Security Act (NSA), 1980, Ms. Chaudhary remains in jail despite the Allahabad High Court quashing her detention under the NSA on September 2.

Six others, including activist Aditya Anand, workers Manisha and Rupesh, student leaders Yogesh Meena and Himanshu Thakur and artist Srishti Gupta are also in jail. The police have registered 11 FIRs against them.

“The Allahabad High Court called the police investigation on the basis of which the order was issued a ‘concocted story’ while quashing Ms. Chaudhary’s detention. The Uttar Pradesh government and police have been acting unlawfully since day one and people who have been working for social causes on the ground have been facing the brunt of it,” Ms. Anjali said.

For a cause

The protesters sat down near Jantar Mantar after the police asked them to clear the site. The police then allegedly forcefully took them into three buses, where female protesters were held by male officers and others were pushed and pulled by police personnel. Two buses were taken to Sector 23 Dwarka police station and one to Kapashera, where the detainees were later released, Ms. Anjali said.

“Female protesters were detained after 6 p.m.,” said Chitranshu, a protester.

Naureen, another member of CaRWAN, said the Uttar Pradesh police had tried to fabricate evidence and plant a mobile phone at Ms. Gupta’s house. “The police, working in alignment with the government, do not have any real evidence against them. We demand that they be released immediately,” she said.

Delhi University Professors Nandita Narain and N. Sachin were also part of the protest.

“Journalists like Satyam Verma and activists who are role models for all citizens have been held illegally and put behind bars. Regressive laws like the NSA have been imposed on them. These show the brutalities of both the police and those in power,” Ms. Narain said.

World.title: ‘AI’s success is based on effective bundling of technology with human judgment, leadership, execution’
World.content:
Project success in the artificial intelligence era will increasingly depend on how effectively organisations combine technology with human judgment, leadership and execution, said Amit Goyal, managing director, South Asia, Project Management Institute (PMI) at the institute’s annual conference, PMSAC26, held here on Saturday.

As artificial intelligence reshaped jobs, business models and technology delivery, India’s strong technology ecosystem and its ability to adopt and scale new technologies were expected to position it well for the next phase of growth, he observed.

Quoting McKinsey’s State of AI report, Mr. Goyal, however, said only 39% of organisations report an enterprise-level EBIT (earnings before interest and taxes) impact from AI, underscoring the challenge of translating adoption into measurable business outcomes.

PMI is a Pennsylvania-headquartered not-for-profit organisation that serves millions of project professionals and changemakers globally by providing them standards, certifications, resources, and networking opportunities to help them advance in their professions.

A wide spectrum of global industry leaders who spoke at the conference, themed around ‘Future-Ready Leadership in the Age of AI’, shared practical perspectives and strategies to collaboratively examine what it would take to turn the AI ambition of businesses globally into meaningful outcomes.

Business leaders also dealt around topics including how AI was reshaping project success and project execution and also the growing importance of combining technology with strategic thinking, human judgment, adaptability, leadership and strong execution capabilities.

Speaking at an interactive session, Johannes Heinlein, interim president and CEO of PMI, said having technical knowledge alone won’t make a professional unique. “What is critical today is learning, updating constantly and learning to stay relevant in the job market,” Mr. Heinlein said, adding, “While AI taken away certain kinds of coding jobs, it also created newer kinds of career opportunities.”

World.title: AUD students allege campus gates shut amid ongoing sit-in protest; university denies claim
World.content:
Ambedkar University Delhi (AUD) students on Saturday alleged that the university had closed the gates of its Kashmere Gate campus to students as their indefinite sit-in entered its seventh day. The protest is against two notices issued on July 31 mandating permission for gatherings and attendance requirements for PhD scholars.

Students and parents said no one was allowed inside the campus on Saturday, including some students who were scheduled to appear for an internal examination. The situation escalated late on Friday night after students alleged that security personnel restricted the delivery of food and water. According to the students, three of them remained inside the campus on Saturday of their own accord, while nine others continued their protest outside the gates.

Meanwhile, the university said in a statement that students had been informed in advance that its library, laboratories and certain blocks had been closed for maintenance and upkeep.

“One of the demands of the students was related to infrastructural issues on the campus, and in this connection, the university has been carrying out maintenance and upkeep on a regular basis,” the statement read.

World.title: Police inspector Mahesh Kumar placed on vacancy reserve
World.content: Inspector C. Mahesh Kumar, who was serving as an investigating officer with the Immoral Trafficking Prevention Unit (ITPU) of the Chennai Police when a complaint was filed against Gem Granites chairman R. Veeramani, has been placed on Vacancy Reserve with immediate effect on administrative grounds, sources said. Mahesh Kumar served as an inspector with the ITPU in 2025 when the complainant had submitted a pen drive containing a video clip of the businessman allegedly sexually assaulting a minor girl.

World.title: Trust undertakes traffic management and cleanliness drive to mark Gandhi Jayanthi
World.content:
Amba Maheshwari Seva Trust undertook traffic management around Mangaladevi Temple and cleanliness drive around Gujjarkere in Jeppu under its “Awake Kudla” initiative on the occasion of Gandhi Jayanti on Friday.

Trust volunteers helped the traffic police in regulating traffic on Mangaladevi Car Street between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. as there was a huge influx of devotees on a Friday.

They ensured cars and two wheelers were parked in an orderly manner, on the centre line of the road while leaving the sides of the road for unobstructed movement of vehicles. The trust has been carrying out this work for the past many weeks to ensure traffic orderliness on Fridays and other festival days. Inspired by the volunteers, a few local residents too joined hands in regulating traffic.

In the evening, trust volunteers and residents of Gujjarkere area undertook a mega cleanliness drive around the lake. They cleaned the surroundings, removed plastic waste and trimmed grass and other vegetation. The volunteers also created awareness among residents and visitors about maintaining the area clean, while educating them to segregate waste at source in homes. The trust has been undertaking regular cleanliness and maintenance work of Gujjarkere area for the past three years.

World.title: Fire breaks out at defunct building near Teynampet signal
World.content:
A fire broke out at a defunct four-storey building near Teynampet signal on Saturday afternoon, and destroyed garbage piled up on the premises. The fire also damaged the exterior of an adjacent building complex.

The building, which is reportedly involved in a legal dispute, is located between Guna Complex and another private building. A large quantity of garbage had accumulated in the space between the two buildings.

Fire and Rescue Services personnel went to the spot and brought the blaze under control.

The police are investigating the cause of the fire. Preliminary investigation revealed that it could have been caused by a lit cigarette being thrown into the garbage, though the possibility of an electrical trigger is also being examined. Further investigation is under way.

World.title: Official outcome of govt-opposition talks awaited after hours-long meeting
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: There was a flurry of activity at Parliament House on Saturday night as a second round of talks between the government and opposition extended past midnight, with discussions including the PTI’s planned Oct 4 march to Islamabad.

The meeting at Parliament House, which began shortly before 5pm, went on for over four hours. However, with both sides seemingly agreeing not to speak to the media before matters conclude, official details on the outcome are still awaited.

Visuals broadcast by DawnNewsTV after 9:30pm showed Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi — part of the government delegation — departing Parliament House with a document in his hand, with media reports suggesting he was likely to consult the president.

More than an hour later, footage showed Naqvi returning to Parliament House, with the interior minister maintaining his silence as reporters swarmed him for queries.

The meeting, chaired by National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq, was aimed at defusing the country’s ongoing political crisis. The PTI’s planned Oct 4 protest march, aimed at demanding the release of party founder Imran Khan, has emerged as the latest point of contention between the party and the federal government.

Even as extended talks kept hopes for an agreement alive, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi remained adamant on proceeding with PTI’s march to Islamabad.

After voicing his determination on Saturday afternoon — which irked government representatives — the KP CM again took to X at 12:46am to detail the itinerary for the protest march.

Laying out the journey plan, Afridi said PTI supporters from the districts of Tank, Dera Ismail Khan, South Waziristan, North Waziristan, Bannu, and Lakki Marwat will join the long march from Lakki Marwat’s Gandi Chowk Lakki Marwat at 1pm on Oct 4.

The caravan will halt for the night near Karak, from where people will depart at 12:30pm the next day and stay overnight near Kohat.

Then, at 12pm on Oct 6, protesters from Kohat, Hangu, Kurram, and Orakzai will join the convoy, which will move towards Peshawar and spend the night near Mattani.

The KP CM’s post went on to say that the caravan will depart from Budh Bair in Peshawar on Oct 7 afternoon. “The remaining constituencies of Peshawar will join us at Kohat Road Bridge and the Motorway Toll Plaza. And we will spend the night near Charsadda Interchange.”

They would then depart the Charsadda Interchange at 12:30pm on Oct 8 after people from Charsadda and Mohmand join them.

Refraining from detailing the final leg of the trip to the federal capital, Afridi said the people “of entire KP” would gather at Khairabad on Oct 8 and spend the night there. “God willing, the plan for the next phase will be announced there.”

NA speaker hopes for ‘cordial’ talks

When the huddle began, the NA speaker expressed his hope that the talks would proceed in the same “cordial atmosphere” as Friday’s, according to a post on the NA’s X account.

The government side included Naqvi, Minister for States and Frontier Regions Amir Muqam, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah and Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry.

Senator Sherry Rehman, along with MNAs Syed Naveed Qamar and Aijaz Hussain Jakhrani, represented the PPP.
