Open the government website and look at the prime minister and his deputies: we have five deputy prime ministers, 15 ministries, and so on down the list. As a practitioner, I can tell you that when a minister is granted the title of deputy prime minister, it signifies that the domain they oversee is top priority—meaning it receives more attention and carries greater authority.

Now look at who our five deputy prime ministers are today. Some of them, in my opinion, still don’t understand why they hold those positions, other than perhaps meeting ethnic or quota criteria. I am not speaking about them specifically, but take the Ministry of Internal Affairs: in my view, the law enforcement situation is a complete failure. Take your own Gagra District—you know what has been happening there recently. And it isn’t limited to Gagra District; criminal clashes continue unabated. Yet the primary task of a law enforcement system is prevention. I consider it a total failure.

Another example is the Committee for Youth and Sports. Yes, youth and sports are important to develop, but in my view, the state’s paramount priority must be education.

Georgi Berzenia: Isn’t there a deputy prime minister for education?

Adgur Ardzinba: No, there is a minister. Following that logic, I believe the Minister of Education should be the First Deputy Prime Minister. That is how priorities are defined. What happens instead? This might sound a bit dry, but it’s practical reality: the Minister of Education has to go to her deputy prime minister, and then together they must go to the prime minister.

Georgi Berzenia: Setting aside those details, what do you dislike on a global level?

Adgur Ardzinba: There are no clear priorities, and I see no development plan. A year ago, the president issued specific directives that were widely publicized. I have a report here on the execution of those directives, and the majority remain unfulfilled, while another portion was completed merely on paper. In my view, even this short one-year timeframe has been squandered. I have always said, and will continue to say, that we need a development plan, reforms, and defined priorities.

Today, the long-term priority must be education and enlightenment. Enormous focus needs to be directed here.

On a positive note in this regard, I recently spoke with the Minister of Education, and she shared very good news that you may have heard as well: the Primakov School in Moscow Oblast—in my view, one of the best schools in Russia, if not the best, because it combines modern foreign educational methods with our Soviet system—is a unique, elite institution in the Odintsovo District. They have agreed to build a branch here in the city of Sukhum. That is fantastic news. Furthermore, from what I gathered in my conversation with the minister, this school will adhere to those high standards while accommodating our local features and mentality—incorporating Abkhazian culture, language, and customs. That is precisely what we have all dreamed of. A state that fails to cultivate its own elite is doomed to failure, so this is a wonderful development. I hope it materializes quickly.

Otherwise, regarding general priorities, they remain absent.

Finally, regarding agriculture: there is talk about the “Year of the Village”—the current year was declared the Year of the Village, which is a good idea in itself. But what is happening in practice? Once again, decorative steps are taken that won’t yield long-term results. Agriculture requires a multi-year strategy. Without science, there is nothing to be done in agriculture or anywhere else.

How can we talk about developing the agricultural sector when the Institute of Agriculture is left to fend for itself? It’s simply impossible.

Adgur Ardzinba: I will also tell you something else that, in my view, illustrates this lack of systemic structure. Returning to the Ministry of Agriculture, the Ministry of Economy ought to be involved in these processes. We speak about cultivating certain crops. Yet there is such a concept as marketing, market analysis. Now, the potential target market is the Russian Federation, correct? Accordingly, economists should be tasked with analyzing the Russian Federation market to identify which crops imported into Russia—potentially adjacent ones, if working with agricultural institutes—could realistically grow in Abkhazia and yield the maximum added value. Do you understand what I am saying? Moreover, benchmarking needs to be conducted. Benchmarking means evaluating competitors. We would look foolish if, for instance, we were to visit a megamarket in Moscow, spot a particular variety of persimmon, and say, “Oh, how wonderful, a new persimmon, it costs 600 rubles, let’s plant it.” We will look foolish if, at that very same moment, tens of thousands of hectares had already been planted in Azerbaijan three or four years prior. And by the time we gather ourselves to enter the market, that product will already be right here. In other words, that is competitor analysis. It is an engaging, creative effort. That is precisely the work I do not see happening.

Handing out a million rubles to every village based on mere intuition—sure, that is better than nothing. Of course, anyone listening right now might say, “Well, at least something is being done there, it’s better than nothing.” I agree, that is also fine. But if we are talking about systemic work aimed at serious, long-term results, then without new technologies, without new crops, and without new approaches to the economy, there will be no serious results.

Georgi Berzenia: Right now, you are speaking about agriculture, providing specific examples, discussing what you dislike about education, and so forth. I just caught myself thinking how much I miss the debate format we used to have. The kind that existed previously. You are addressing each sphere now. We cannot and should not discuss every single detail. However, it seems to me it would be right if opposition figures today could sit in a single studio, for example, and discuss every topic with government representatives, where they could defend their point of view while the opposition presented theirs. Overall, that would have a positive effect.

Adgur Ardzinba: It would not have an effect, and I will explain why.

Alkhas Gagulia: We used to have that.

Adgur Ardzinba: If you recall our famous broadcasts where we debated energy policy and debated apartments. On energy, do you remember our discussions on Afganskaya’s airwaves? Where we were told, “That’s it, you were worrying over nothing.” In the end, everything we warned about occurred in the worst possible form, without them even acknowledging it.

Georgi Berzenia: That was un-systemic back then.

Adgur Ardzinba: A real application would follow the results of such a debate. But what if the state apparatus, the executive branch, completely refuses to see public opinion?

Georgi Berzenia: We are talking about a new stage now. We are talking about a new stage. I am asking what you like and what you dislike, and you are delving into details that we, as laypeople in this matter…

Alkhas Gagulia: I would like to add something regarding agriculture. There is a program in the Ministry of Agriculture…

Adgur Ardzinba: There is a subsidy program within… It is a good, decent program. But that program is insufficient. There is no science in that program. If there is no science, there will be no result. That is what I am trying to convey. First, there is no consistent, systemic work. Second, simply distributing money—yes, that too is better than nothing when people’s costs are subsidized. That is also good. But my concern lies elsewhere. I want a maximum long-term effect to be achieved. Without making our countryside competitive, we will not make this sector profitable. Consequently, we will always have a negative balance sheet. Why do we speak so much about the countryside? Because it is a cornerstone. We all say that the countryside is the cradle of our traditions. It is not merely an economic category; it is also a social, political, and cultural one. That is why we dedicate so much attention to it here.

Georgi Berzenia: Yes. That is a very interesting topic. A topic about which, truly, a great deal can be said. I simply brought it up because I asked you to provide an overall assessment. It feels to me as though, judging by what you are saying, you concentrate heavily on certain critical moments and specific details, whereas you haven’t touched upon the positive aspects at all.

Adgur Ardzinba: No.

Georgi Berzenia: You simply stated that the president does not divide people, broadly speaking, and that was essentially all.

Adgur Ardzinba: I focused on certain details because I… I articulated the premise that work is being conducted in an un-systemic manner, and I provided a series of examples. I could cite a great many such examples.

Georgi Berzenia: Perhaps you could name some positive aspects after all? For instance, even with agriculture, my association—I understand a deep conversation is one thing, but as an example—they opened a dairy plant in the Ochamchira District. That is agriculture, and as I understand it, it is a high-tech facility.

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, that is the agro-industrial complex.

Georgi Berzenia: Which also engages local villagers, provides jobs, and allows us to consume local produce, even if the raw material isn’t local. Just to give such an example, broadly speaking. And if we look back at the past, Abkhazia previously had much less to take pride in and showcase. Today, there are also things that can be highlighted.

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, an economic forum was held. A rather interesting event. A great number of people came to Abkhazia—top officials, bureaucrats, ministers. I cannot recall anything like it since the time of recognition. We hosted an economic forum. That is wonderful. We introduced many people to the country and drew attention, including media coverage. Following that attention, when an ordinary Russian citizen watches the news on the Rossiya television channel and sees several federal ministers and the First Deputy Chief of the Presidential Administration in Abkhazia discussing the development of this country’s economy, a desire arises in some to go and do business there. Upon arriving here, he does not see the Deputy Chief of Staff or our president. He goes to the Technical Inventory Bureau, he goes to the district administration. And there, he gets caught in such a whirlpool that, God willing, he might escape from it only after several years. That is what needs to be addressed immediately.

Alkhas Gagulia: Back in 2024, you stated that relations between Russia and Abkhazia were at their lowest point. A couple of years—a year and a half—have passed since then. How do you assess these relations now?

Adgur Ardzinba: The most interesting part is that the very same thing was voiced on March 7 of this year during a concert here in our capital. A representative of the Presidential Administration, one of the department heads, spoke there. I cannot recall his surname at the moment, but he was a rather pleasant person. He mentioned that…

Georgi Berzenia: The Russian Administration?

Adgur Ardzinba: Yes, the Russian Administration. He mentioned that our relations had cooled somewhat over the recent period, but that we need to fix all of this. By the way, I was pleasantly surprised by such a sober assessment. However, a whole host of factors contributed to that state of affairs. Without speaking of oneself, one cannot speak of others. To a greater extent, it was the activity of the ex-president, who attempted to resolve his own economic matters and tried to smear everyone opposing him as pro-Western and so forth. Naturally, when an official of such stature writes briefing notes on his fellow citizens, that information is examined at a serious level, to say the least. And when the head of state visits a district and tells people that their pensions will stop being paid unless we vote for the Pitsunda state dacha, and so on—how can that not reflect in the minds and hearts of the people? Those errors were committed. Now, over this period of time, I see that in Russia, with the arrival of a new team of individuals responsible for our direction, they have drawn the correct conclusions from what occurred previously. Once again, as we discussed above, far from everything has been rectified yet.

Alkhas Gagulia: And what specifically needs to be rectified?

Adgur Ardzinba: The persecution of citizens. That is what causes harm. On the whole, however, the agenda has shifted. All those harmful initiatives have receded into the background. Incidentally, they themselves acknowledge that those were not beneficial. Right now, as I see it, very broad opportunities are open before us, before our small country. By the way, similar opportunities were open to us right after recognition, during that flourishing period. Later, to some extent, everything experienced a slight decline, but now there is such a surge. We cited the economic forum as an example. Several federal ministers, governors, heads of republics, and the First Deputy Chief of Staff came to Abkhazia, to the city of Sukhum, to discuss the development of our economy. Those are enormous opportunities. In other words, a tremendous amount of attention is being paid to our relatively small country in this regard. And that ought to be capitalized on in the best sense. I do not see that same level of initiative from our side—from the authorized bodies and structures—to make full use of all this. Because such chances may not present themselves again in the future. Russia is a vast country. It is navigating a very complex period right now. Further escalation could follow, and people will focus on solving their own problems. Why should they travel with entire government delegations to Abkhazia, sit with us here in Sukhum, and try to help us figure out how to make our lives better? That is primarily our own responsibility. There is transportation infrastructure—the train has started running, work is underway at the border, the airport has begun operations. Most importantly, what genuinely pleases me is that very positive information about Abkhazia is circulating across the Russian Federation’s media space. There is outright promotion of Abkhazia as a resort destination. That provides a huge impetus for the growth of our tourism sector and the overall economy.

Yet, returning to those matters: when such promotion is taking place and top officials are calling Abkhazia an ally, prioritizing it, we must work proactively right here on the ground. Do you understand? Rather than simply trailing behind, picking up scattered initiatives, and failing to carry even those through to completion. That is what I am concerned about. And I will tell you why I am so concerned, Georgi. Alkhas, 2008 brought recognition. Following that, starting in 2010, Abkhazia was provided with financial assistance. Substantial financial assistance—exceeding one billion dollars. However, those funds dissolved across various projects. Back then, too, there were no clear priorities or plans. As a result, where we had the opportunity to completely resolve the situation—at least within the energy sector, given the possibilities that opened up at the time—we would not be facing these problems today. We would not be talking about a deficit today had we utilized that opportunity wisely back then. Therefore, I simply do not want history to repeat itself this time, which is why I am so concerned. The fact that there is a warming of relations, a mutual understanding, and that people are frankly paying far more attention to Abkhazia than before—that is a reality. That is a fact. The other question is what we ourselves are capable of proposing and what we ourselves are capable of achieving; that is where the problem lies.

Georgi Berzenia: And what role do you see for Sergei Vladimirovich Kiriyenko?

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, I already noted above that he is a person… First of all, let us be frank. Every official possesses a certain degree of capability. There are a number of leaders in the Russian Federation, and they all have differing levels of capability. As far as I can see, this individual possesses quite substantial capabilities. Within the scope of those capabilities, he is doing everything possible to assist Abkhazia and to involve as many federal leaders in this work as possible. Let us recall—we live here after all—past periods. Let us recall the period from 2020 to 2025. How many federal leaders visited Abkhazia over those five years? The Minister of Sports came. The Minister of Economic Development came a couple of times. To my memory, that was all. Yet now, in a span of a year and a half… Again, when these people visit, our officials and top leaders have the opportunity to sit down over a cup of coffee and discuss specific issues. I assure you, I know the situation in Russia: not every governor or regional leader has the opportunity to sit down with ministers and drink coffee whenever they wish. Yet we have that opportunity. And all of this is thanks to this new team.

At the same time, I cannot fail to mention our people here. Had our people not stood up in 2024—and throughout the period leading up to November 2024—to defend their core interests, none of this would exist. Absolutely no changes would have occurred. Had that entire proposed agenda passed quietly and silently, no one would have given us a second thought. The Abkhazian people courageously defended their interests, their core interests. And the Abkhazian people—who, by the way, are exceptionally friendly toward the Russian people—stood up, protected their interests, and drew attention to themselves. That commands respect, and I observe that respect coming from these leaders.

Georgi Berzenia: Speaking of the development of relations between Abkhazia and Russia, I have also recalled with several guests in this studio the 2014 treaty. It was signed more than 12 years ago now, back in 2014, so ten years have passed. Political events were taking place back then as well, yet no review was conducted, no outcomes were summarized, and it was extended automatically. How would you evaluate these 10 to 12 years of that treaty, and where do we go from here? Does it require refinement, or is a new treaty or a new phase in relations with Russia needed?

Adgur Ardzinba: The treaty is quite thoroughly developed. Moreover, when it was adopted, as you remember, there was a certain degree of opposition here as well. The very people who in the recent past accused us of being pro-Western and anti-Russian were themselves blocking the border to prevent that treaty from being signed, to speak specifically. But the treaty itself became a foundational document following the 2008–2009 post-recognition agreements. Coming after them in 2014, it served as a foundational document that touched upon economic forms of interaction, social matters, and other areas.

Of course, time moves forward. It keeps moving forward. And I am certain that we have not fully realized the potential of that agreement. There is still much to discuss within it. However, Georgi, we can also recall other agreements. We have a whole host of agreements that remain unfulfilled. If we return to defense and security, within the framework of signed agreements regarding joint efforts to strengthen the state border along the Ingur River, nothing has been done—neither from our side nor from the side of the Russian Federation. Furthermore, matters regarding the joint group of forces in that direction remain poorly developed.

If we speak about the economy, we have an agreement on the mutual protection of investments. In that direction, too, we need to look at what genuinely concerns investors from the Russian Federation—not those who sought to create a tailored, exclusive climate for themselves, but regular businesspeople. And they do not necessarily have to be billionaires; they can simply be people capable of investing 10 million rubles, or 20 million rubles, conditionally speaking. We need to communicate with them and examine the rules and standards that exist in the Russian Federation. They could be implemented here. For instance, the public service system in the Russian Federation—the MFC system, “My Documents”—which several years ago was announced to start operating here, has seen nothing done. That system is objectively considered one of the best and most efficient in the world. So, please, let us integrate it here.

Georgi Berzenia: In Russia, which…

Adgur Ardzinba: Yes, in Russia. We all use it, as we are Russian citizens. It is an incredibly convenient system. As for tax administration, one of the most effective systems has been established in Russia. That is a reality; you can see it in all surveys. Russia has specific criteria for evaluating the investment attractiveness of various regions. At the St. Petersburg forum every year, if memory serves, a specific rating and classification is assigned to one region or another. That, too, is a positive thing. Well, as I mentioned above, the entire local economy resides in the districts.

Georgi Berzenia: In September, elections to the State Duma will take place in the Russian Federation. These elections will also be held on the territory of Abkhazia, allowing citizens of Abkhazia who are simultaneously citizens of Russia to participate. What is your view on the significance of these elections for citizens of Abkhazia, and should citizens take part in them?

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, look, posters reading “Abkhazia’s Voice Matters to Russia” are currently hanging all across Abkhazia, right? If Russia, which has provided us with such immense support all these years, sends a message that our voice matters to Russia, is it really that difficult to go and vote if it truly is so important? And it is important, first of all because we are almost all Russian citizens, for the most part, when provided with such an opportunity… I remember in past periods there were issues with the number of polling stations and so forth; as far as I can see, it is being approached more systematically now. Of course, people should go and vote. Why not? It isn’t that difficult to do. If people say it is important, and one can demonstrate civic engagement in that sense, I believe one should go and vote.

As for whom to vote for, that is a separate question. I do not have the right to engage in campaigning here right now, but one should also look at the retrospective. Various political forces have existed throughout Abkhazia’s history; you are younger, but Alkhas and I remember the blockade times and the post-blockade period when the new team came in. We must also understand for ourselves which political force is minded to help Abkhazia, and which political force recognized Abkhazia’s independence. These are different teams with different viewpoints, so here too, I believe our choice is straightforward; we simply need to understand it all.

Alkhas Gagulia: We have spoken at length about relations with Russia—it is our strategic partner—but an event took place in the Turkish parliament recently. People view it in different ways, and opinions vary. In my view, it is a very landmark event when 30% of the Turkish parliament raised the issue of ending the isolation of Abkhazia. Recognition was not on the table, and there were differing opinions regarding the motives behind that speech. It turned out to be primarily the opposition party. But anticipating your answer, I would say—as one Chinese sage or general secretary put it—it doesn’t matter what color the cat is, as long as it catches mice. What is your view on this initiative, and what, in your opinion, actually happened there?

Adgur Ardzinba: Alkhas, your late relative Gennady Leonidovich Gagulia once told me a story about cats and mice too. He said that when you try to play political cat-and-mouse, make sure that you are not the mouse. Yes, of course, it is a positive signal. Incidentally, our organization issued a statement on this matter. The signal itself is positive, even if, as some note, it represents an element of internal political struggle to attract our large diaspora and secure votes. Even if that is the case, it remains positive. It shows the role and significance of our diaspora, which we utilize very weakly—and not only in Turkey. But that is a vast, separate topic. Therefore, it is a positive signal, and that is how we assess it. However, actions and deeds matter most. Words are fine—we approve and welcome them—but deeds are what count. Russia went ahead in 2008 and established diplomatic relations with Abkhazia, recognizing our independence. Those are real actions.

Alkhas Gagulia: There was a caveat there, if I am not mistaken, that there was no question of any recognition.

Adgur Ardzinba: When politicians speak about it to attract votes, again, it is still a good thing that the topic of Abkhazia and ending its isolation is being discussed, forming a positive agenda to attract votes. But I very much hope it will not remain mere words.

Alkhas Gagulia: Adgur Ardzinba of 2024 and Adgur Ardzinba of 2026. What advice would you give today to the person you were back then?

Adgur Ardzinba: That is a good question; I hadn’t thought about it. That is actually too short a time frame. I wouldn’t have changed much.

Georgi Berzenia: Significant events have occurred. First of all, the elections. They surely brought about some…

Alkhas Gagulia: Takeaways from the elections. What mistakes were made?

Adgur Ardzinba: Look, yes, of course, we made a whole host of mistakes. But it is not a given that if I had told my former self to avoid those mistakes, other mistakes wouldn’t have been made instead. Mistakes are part of any process.

Alkhas Gagulia: Nor is it a given that he would have listened?

Adgur Ardzinba: I will tell you this: it has been a rather interesting period of time. I consider myself fortunate. I feel fortunate in that—and I say this sincerely—the Abkhazian people, a portion of the Abkhazian people, and a substantial portion at that, entrusted me with this responsible mission. That is a great, immense honor. There is nothing above that, Alkhas. Any obstacles or hurdles are minor by comparison. When serving your people is not mere rhetoric but a reality—if done sincerely and from the heart—there are no obstacles. That is the highest honor.

Therefore, what would I advise my former self? I would advise him not to doubt, because a person always experiences doubt when faced with immense difficulties. Alkhas, we speak about this so casually now. For instance, when people entered the building in November 2024, some said they shouldn’t have entered, while others asked what would have happened had they not entered. Someone had to take responsibility. Other politicians were there; we were all together. While we achieved a certain goal on the one hand, on the other hand, during all those days—and I slept inside that building for three nights to ensure people wouldn’t clash with one another—it was a difficult period, followed by the election process.

Naturally, any person experiences doubt. Our recent presidential elections were unique—they were engaging and event-filled. But those elections were particularly interesting because our team faced such a formidable, serious opponent equipped with vast resources. When you have a very serious opponent, it mobilizes you immensely. I assure you, had that not been the case, the elections might have turned out very dull. Instead, they unfolded the way they did.

Alkhas Gagulia: To be honest, I dream of dull elections for all branches of power.

Adgur Ardzinba: We are speaking about personality and perception right now. Yes, I too dream that our country, like Switzerland, could have dull elections. But if we talk about what existed then versus now, it has been a very fascinating period during which I came to respect my people even more. I feel immense pride in being part of this nation—small in numbers perhaps, but possessing a grand spirit and a vast heart—a people that cannot be intimidated, no matter how hard anyone tries. And with such a spirit in our hearts, we are bound for success.

I am absolutely certain that we will succeed in everything. All those misunderstandings and unpleasantries, including those in relations between Abkhazia and Russia, are entirely surmountable. I am confident that… Look, we are talking about certain incidents right now, and they are indeed unpleasant. Yet we had a period when the entire country was under a blockade for six to seven years. We were under a blockade—the whole country. Now we are talking about a few individuals being unable to travel, whereas back then it was the entire country.

Even then… Vladislav Grigorievich Ardzinba—for which I will always be grateful to him—was a great, exceptionally wise man. He always maintained that we must orient ourselves toward a union with the Russian Federation; that time would pass, people would change, and understanding would arrive. And he was right. Although you remember, Alkhas, how many different proposals there were, delegation after delegation, yet we did not deviate from our path. All these misunderstandings taking place are simply part of the process. Just as there are mistakes on our side, there are mistakes on theirs as well.

I am confident that everything will be fine. The main thing is to remain vigilant. Times are very dangerous. I will repeat it endlessly: defense and security.

Alkhas Gagulia: Well, I want to say thank you for today’s broadcast, for coming to join us so that a thorough conversation could take place on all the questions that interested us. The only thing I would like to add, of course, is that while we spoke about priority tasks—about defense and education—all of this stems from a single overarching priority: our sovereignty and our independence. If that serves as the main guidepost, everything else is meant to serve that exact priority. There are no other options. You mentioned my age twenty times today; in any case, my generation accepts nothing less. We lost far too many people for this land, and it is thanks to them that we stand on this land today. That is what I want to say to every single politician, without exception, on both sides. Thank you for the broadcast and for coming. I look forward to our next meetings.

Adgur Ardzinba: Thank you, friends. I believe that while our conversation was lengthy, it was candid, and we answered a number of questions. If we missed anything, I think we will have another opportunity to meet. As for sovereignty, Alkhas, that concerns not only your generation. The younger generation and the youth—the rising generation with whom I interact—see no other path across all generations than the building of an independent, sovereign Abkhazian state in Abkhazia. If anyone thinks otherwise, that would be their mistake. All of us have stood, are standing, and will continue to stand for this. Fundamentally, our entire conversation has been dedicated to strengthening that sovereignty, to making our state less vulnerable.

Today, our state is vulnerable. Let us be frank. To eliminate these weak points, we need systemic work, the establishment of priorities, societal consolidation, and defense to preserve our territory, as well as our language—which you raised, Georgi—and our culture. All of this is vital, because knowing a language alone does not make you Abkhaz. The upcoming parliamentary elections are also crucial; the quality and substantive content of that body are of great importance. All of this, as was rightly stated, Alkhas, exists in order to preserve, strengthen, and pass down. Thank you.

Georgi Berzenia: Thank you for an engaging conversation.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: ‘We will decide in the coming months’: Pashinyan on choosing model for Armenia’s new nuclear power plant
World.content:
Pashinyan on building a new nuclear power plant in Armenia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has announced a change in the government’s position on the technology and design of a new nuclear power plant.

“I have said dozens of times before that we do not need anything more [powerful] than a modular nuclear power plant. That was our position. But now we have to understand that a modular plant will most likely not be enough to meet our needs,” Pashinyan said.

He explained that the government changed its position because of the construction of AI factories. Armenia now needs to import electricity to meet their power requirements.

Discussions continue over which technology would best suit the new nuclear power plant. The Armenian government expects to make a decision on the issue by the end of 2027.

A day earlier, the prime minister met a delegation led by Alexey Likhachev, director general of the state-owned Rosatom corporation. They discussed proposals from the Russian side.

Armenia is currently working to extend the operating life of the Metsamor nuclear power plant until 2036. Russia has taken part in efforts to extend the plant’s operating life and modernise it throughout this period. The plant originally entered service in 1977.

At the same time, Yerevan is discussing the construction of a new nuclear power plant with several countries, including the US. The prime minister has repeatedly said in recent months that the nuclear power issue is not a geopolitical choice for Armenia: “We will choose the proposal that serves us best.”

Pashinyan does not rule out accepting the Russian proposal

Speaking about the upcoming decision on the technology for the new nuclear power plant, the prime minister stressed that before Armenia signed memorandums of understanding with the US on 8 August 2025, Armenia had a surplus of electricity.

“We had to think about where to direct this surplus energy. A year later, Armenia had become a country with an electricity deficit,” he said.

According to Nikol Pashinyan, this resulted from the construction of two AI factories in Armenia during that period:

“The point is that, given the scale of the investment projects already approved, Armenia has faced an electricity deficit. In other words, these projects are fully absorbing the surplus we have. So we need to decide what to do next.”

The prime minister said the government would make a decision in the coming months. Pashinyan also said that Armenia could accept the proposal put forward by Russia:

“It is quite possible that building a 1,000 MW plant will prove to be the most logical solution. However, I cannot say for certain at this stage because experts are still assessing the issue.”

“The unit should be at least one, with a capacity of at least 1 GW” — Likhachev

Rosatom director general Alexey Likhachev told journalists some details of Russia’s proposal after talks in Yerevan. Likhachev said Armenia would continue to rely on nuclear energy for decades to come. Russia therefore plans to “formulate the most competitive proposal” for building a new reactor unit in the coming months.

“And in our view, this unit should be at least one, with a capacity of at least 1 GW,” Likhachev said.

According to him, the proposal involves a VVER-1000 reactor, a pressurised water reactor with a capacity of 1,000 MW.

The head of Rosatom stressed that this proposal is “the best currently available on the global market”. He added that Rosatom has built and continues to build VVER reactors of this type in India and Iran:

“They combine very high economic efficiency, namely a low cost of electricity, with all the necessary Generation III+ safety systems.”

Details of talks with Rosatom director general in Yerevan

The Armenian prime minister’s office said Pashinyan and Likhachev discussed:

work to extend the operating life of the existing second reactor unit at the Armenian Nuclear Power Plant;

Russia’s proposals for building a new reactor unit.

At the same time, the prime minister told Likhachev that the Armenian government was continuing to consider proposals from other international partners.

Pashinyan stressed that the final decision would depend solely on economic considerations. These would include price, quality, safety, construction timelines and guarantees.

The statement also said Alexey Likhachev described cooperation with Armenian partners as constructive. The Rosatom chief also provided detailed information about the construction of not only large VVER reactors, but also small and medium-sized reactors.

World.title: Azerbaijan marks 6th anniversary of Jabrayil's liberation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 4. Six years have passed since the liberation of Jabrayil city from occupation.

As a result of the Azerbaijani Army's counteroffensive launched on September 27, Jabrayil city was liberated from occupation on October 4.

On the first day of the fighting, the Azerbaijani Army broke through the front, forcing the opposing forces to retreat. Over the following days, many villages in the Jabrayil district were liberated.

On October 4, President of Azerbaijan and Supreme Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev announced in an address to the nation that Jabrayil city had been liberated.

In his address, the President noted that, along with Jabrayil city, nine more villages in the district – Karkhulu, Shukurbeyli, Yukhari Maralyan, Charakan, Dashkasan, Horovlu, Dejal, Mahmudlu and Jafarabad – had also been liberated.

Jabrayil became the first district to be liberated during the 44-day Patriotic War. A significant amount of the opposing forces' personnel and military equipment was destroyed during the Jabrayil operation. October 4 went down in history as the day of Jabrayil's liberation.

The "For the Liberation of Jabrayil" medal was established in Azerbaijan.

By order of President Ilham Aliyev, servicemen of the Azerbaijani Armed Forces who participated in combat operations to liberate the Jabrayil district and demonstrated personal courage and bravery were awarded the "For the Liberation of Jabrayil" medal.

By another order of President Ilham Aliyev, October 4 was designated as Jabrayil City Day.

The Jabrayil district was occupied by the Armenian armed forces on August 23, 1993. During the occupation, the city of Jabrayil and its villages were destroyed, while cultural, historical and religious monuments and cemeteries were damaged or destroyed, according to Azerbaijani authorities.

World.title: Harvest starts on SA crops that 'have not had a setback all season'
World.content:
The harvesters have started rolling in South Australia for one of the most eagerly anticipated crops in years.

Jesse Chandler was the first to front up to the silos at Thevenard with a load of Commodus barley on September 24.

He farms with his brother Harlee, father Milton and mother Tracey at Charra, halfway between Penong and Ceduna on South Australia's west coast.

Robin Schaefer's wheat ripened well this year. (Supplied: Robin Schaefer)

Milton Chandler said it was the earliest they had ever harvested.

"I think it was 14 or 15 [2014 or 2015] we reaped the Friday before the AFL grand final and delivered on the Monday and this year we reaped on the Thursday so we're a day in front," Mr Chandler said.

"Earliest wheat we put in was on the 8th of April and I was nervous about that, but we've got quite a bit of heavy country and when it gets wet we've just got to go."

Mr Chandler has estimated they would harvest about 4 tonnes to the hectare with their barley.

" Normally even in our good years we'll have a period during the growing season when the crop will have a bit of a moisture check but this year it's almost been textbook. "

"I've been farming here since 1980, and this is the best it's ever looked. It's great, and it's fantastic that it's statewide so it's a real positive for everyone.”

Crop estimate increased

Primary Industries and Regions SA's (PIRSA) crop and pasture report has revised up the state's crop yield forecast again.

The September report found all regions of South Australia had average to above-average winter rainfall with August being the fourth wettest on record.

Disease pressure has increased under the wet conditions with rusts, powdery mildew, net blotch, black leg and sclerotinia reported across several regions.

Overall PIRSA now believes the area sown this year was 4,234,000 hectares and estimates 11,591,000 tonnes will be harvested.

Growers have said they will need every tonne to make up for low grain prices and high input costs.

Robin Schaefer's lentil crop has put on a lot of biomass thanks to early season rainfall. (Supplied: Robin Schaefer)

"We did buy a little bit of diesel through seeding at $3.27; that hurt a little bit, that was a bit of a wake-up call," Mr Chandler said.

"Even though the [grain] prices aren't great hopefully we can [compensate] that with some big yields.

"Logistically it's going to be difficult to deal with it [the size of the crop], but what a great problem."

The September 24 delivery was not the earliest crop that has been harvested in South Australia.

Records show grain has been received as early as September 19 in the past.

Bunge director of industrial management Gavin Cavanagh said the bulk grain handler had been planning for harvest to be two to three weeks earlier than normal.

"We are expecting that we will receive more than we normally would in October given the good start the farmers had and the early plant on the back of those good opening rains," Mr Cavanagh said.

Bunge does a big recruitment drive each year for harvest, putting on an extra 1,500 jobs each year, including overseas workers.

Mr Cavanagh said the changes to visa requirements had not affected its ability to fill roles.

"It hasn't impacted us directly; the majority of travellers we recruit are already in the country.

"From our point of view, we're confident that we've got the right amount of people in the right locations to support our farmers in their delivery pattern."

Perfect timing for storms

With warm, dry weather in SA in recent weeks, the recent storms that delivered about 15 to 40 millimetres of rain across the state were very welcome.

Loxton grain grower Robin Schaefer said he thought he was going to get only a couple of millimetres but ended up tipping 17mm out of the gauge on Friday, October 2.

Robin Schaefer welcomed rainfall across South Australia. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

"It was a lovely surprise," Mr Schaefer said.

"Some of our very early barley is pretty close to going now so that won't benefit, but the majority, I'd say at least two thirds or more of our crop would still benefit".

With so much moisture early in the season the plants have put on a lot of vegetable matter.

" The lentils up here, the biomass is amazing, hopefully that will translate into grain but there's certainly lots of pods on them "

"It does vary a little bit from farm to farm with a number of drought years in a row and the price of fertiliser people couldn't put as much as they would have liked in a year like this to take advantage of it but we're thankful for what we've got.

"It's just wonderful compared to a drought and I think there will be some very tidy yields around right through the Mallee."

World.title: SA's first musical theatre company brings talent home in debut stage
World.content:
When Joey Haenen graduated with a music theatre degree in Adelaide, he knew he had to move states.

"There is no work here and so you've got to move over east, that's where most of the agents are," he said.

"You do all your auditioning over there and hopefully you'll land a gig."

Haenen moved to Melbourne, like Jazz Garcia who spent a year getting her name known while paying for her passion through a day job in speech pathology.

"There's just a lot more musical theatre opportunities in Melbourne, we don't really have anything in Adelaide," she said.

The exodus from South Australia to the east coast has been happening for decades, a talent drain Jo Casson was determined to stop.

Jo Casson says South Australia has been crying out for a professional musical theatre company. (Supplied)

The arts veteran joined forces with others to form Full Circle, the state's first-ever professional music theatre company.

"I just decided it's now or never, no-one's getting any younger," she said.

"I discovered in the middle of last year that every other major city has a professional local theatre company and Adelaide didn't."

Ironically, it's a full circle moment for the company's choreographer Zoe Komazec-Kermond, who returned from the east coast after a career performing in shows including Cats, Matilda and Mary Poppins.

"There is so much talent in South Australia, so much talent and we do sometimes feel like we have to go away in order to achieve what we want to achieve," she said.

Zoe Komazec-Kermond says a new SA musical theatre company will convince performers to come home. (Supplied)

With such a rich vein of talent, Casson said forming the new company made sense.

It has the backing of well-known arts lover and philanthropist Pamela Wall AO, but the company is seeking more support, as well as applying for grant funding.

'Catch Me if You Can' to premiere

Full Circle will stage the musical Catch Me If You Can as its opening number, a stage version of the story that Leonardo DiCaprio took to the big screen and earned rave reviews.

When the company held auditions, it attracted more than 100 performers for the 25 roles.

Haenen was working and had to push his case with an audition video he sent to producers.

The 21-year-old rising star's absence from the auditions did not stop him from landing the lead role of Frank Abagnale Jr.

"What I love is just being able to get little bits of Joey in each of the characters every time and that's such a great joy," Haenen said.

Garcia, who earned a contract among the show's ensemble, said the three-day auditions were exhausting.

"The dance call was extremely strenuous, I'd say that was one of the longest kind of dance audition processes I've ever been in," she said.

Jazz Garcia (middle) would love to travel back to South Australia to perform with Full Circle. (Supplied)

More than 30 creatives and technical crew have been hired with the final cast a mix of South Australians and others returning to the state.

"Everyone could sing, everyone could dance and everyone could act, so it made our job really hard to pick our final cast," Komazec-Kermond said.

Hope amongst industry pressure

Beetlejuice, Waitress, Back to the Future and Dear Evan Hansen were major musicals which cancelled shows recently, with one producer citing increased cost pressures from "touring across vast distances between Australian cities".

Full Circle said it was different because it would not have the high costs of touring a show nationally, like many others.

"Take a little show out into the regional areas if we can, but we won't be going beyond South Australia, it's designed to be a local professional theatre company," Casson said.

However, Casson said getting productions into the country was a goal in future years.

Full Circle wants to stage two musicals a year for the next two years, before increasing to three after that.

Jazz Garcia believes more performers will build careers in South Australia after a new musical theatre company was formed. (Supplied)

Those both on and off the stage realised the importance of pulling off the show and demonstrating the company should be here to stay.

"It's a huge responsibility and I think we're going to do a really good job," Garcia confidently predicted.

Zoe Komazec-Kermond has no doubts.

"There's so much buzz in Adelaide at the moment around Full Circle, so it's really up to us to produce the very best version of this show that we can," she said.

Catch Me If You Can is at Futures Theatre in Paradise from November 5-7.

World.title: Aussie duo and new world number one fall at China Open
World.content:
Australian women's involvement at the China Open is down to just one singles player after Kimberly Birrell and Storm Hunter were both second-round casualties.

World number 41 Birrell suffered a 6-4, 6-4 loss to Czech Marie Bouzkova at the WTA 1000 event in Beijing on Saturday night.

Birrell, 28, who won the Korea Open last Sunday with a win over compatriot Maya Joint in the final, raced out to a 3-1 first-set lead before dropping serve twice to lose it in 42 minutes.

Down 3-0 in the second, Birrell lifted and won the next four games but was broken twice more to see her involvement in the Chinese capital come to a premature end.

For Bouzkova, the 28-year-old 18th seed, a meeting with China's Zheng Qinwen awaits.

The 2024 Olympic champion was leading Anna Kalinskaya 6-7 (4/7), 6-4, 3-0 when the Russian retired.

Earlier, Queensland veteran and former doubles world number one Storm Hunter was beaten 6-2, 6-2 by Maria Sakkari in just 73 minutes.

The 182nd-ranked Hunter failed to join 20-year-old fellow Aussie Taylah Preston in round three, losing serve six times in her latest hardcourt tournament clash in Asia.

Next up for Sakkari, the Greek 25th seed and former world number three, is Elina Svitolina.

The sixth-seeded Ukrainian came from a set down to eliminate Czech Katerina Siniakova, 1-6, 6-4, 6-2.

Shock of the day came with newly crowned world number one Elena Rybakina crashing out ‌3-6, 6-4, 6-3 to unseeded Alina Charaeva in the second round.

It couldn't have been a worse start to her reign as the number one as Rybakina lost in her first match since defeating four-times major winner Aryna Sabalenka to capture the US Open title last month.

Charaeva, a 24-year-old Russian-born Armenian ranked 118th ​in the world, etched her name into the record books by becoming the lowest-ranked competitor since the introduction of the WTA rankings in 1975 to rally from a set down to defeat a world number one.

Elsewhere, there were wins for third seed Coco Gauff, eighth seed Iga Swiatek, 21st seed Ann Li and 24th seed Jelena Ostapenko.

World.title: Quit says tobacco ads slipping through cracks on social media
World.content:
Public health organisation Quit says the federal government is barely scratching the surface in its battle against illegal tobacco advertising on social media.

The ABC has seen examples of illegal tobacco s on Facebook, which were reported by a user but were not taken down.

Facebook only removed the s after ABC enquiries. (Supplied)

However, after ABC enquiries, a Meta spokesperson said it had removed the content.

"We've removed this content and taken action against the accounts and pages behind them for violating our policies," a Meta spokesperson said.

"We encourage people to report content that may breach our rules so we can review and take appropriate action."

A Quit spokesperson said social media advertising for tobacco was becoming more common and the Australian government was struggling to manage it.

'Tip of the iceberg'

Under the Public Health Act, it is illegal to advertise or promote smoking or the use of tobacco products, including on social media platforms.

As of July 1, the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) had 200 active investigations into online s, enforced the blocking of 436 websites, and issued 505 advertising warnings and $1.51 million in fines.

Quit director Rachael Andersen said those numbers were "just the tip of the iceberg".

Rachael Andersen says illegal tobacco s are also seen through influencer marketing. (Supplied)

"A lot of this advertising is happening subconsciously, and people may not be aware that it's illegal for tobacco companies to be advertising," Ms Andersen said.

Ms Andersen said stronger action on illegal advertising was needed to protect the public from the harms of the tobacco industry.

"What we need to see is this federal government exercising its powers under these laws and being able to act on these complaints when they're raised, and compelling social media giants to remove illegal tobacco or vaping ad content from their platforms," she said.

"Social media platforms can't be passive bystanders to this problem. They have got significant influence and reach and therefore responsibility to address this when it's being raised with them."

It is illegal to advertise or promote smoking or the use of tobacco products in Australia. (Supplied)

Ms Andersen said accountability was needed, including from social media giants.

"What we've seen is examples of where this advertising has been raised directly with these businesses, and they haven't removed the ads," she said.

" It's brazen illegal activity, it's happening in plain sight and we're seeing too few repercussions for retailers and for these commercial operators. "

Normalisation of tobacco consumption

Ms Andersen said illegal tobacco s were playing a role in normalising tobacco consumption.

"We know smoking tobacco is incredibly addictive," she said.

"It causes 16 types of cancer and addiction is really hard to break, so what we really don't want to be seeing is reinforcing messaging popping up on people's social media platforms."

Rachael Andersen says social media ads play a role in normalising smoking and vaping. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

A Department of Health, Disability and Ageing spokesperson said all alleged breaches of non-compliance were taken seriously.

"The Australian government is concerned about any advertising that encourages tobacco and nicotine use," the spokesperson said.

"This is why the government has taken strong action to strengthen legislation, enforcement, education and support to protect Australians from the harms of tobacco and e-cigarettes.

"Material may be assessed on a case‑by‑case basis, including whether it has the effect or likely effect of encouraging or normalising smoking behaviour."

World.title: Victorian Liberals promise to slash surgery waitlist while Labor backs land tax cuts
World.content:
The Coalition has promised to halve Victoria's waitlist for elective surgery if victorious in the upcoming state election.

The state's elective surgery waitlist has continued to climb over the past year, with about 68,730 Victorian patients across urgent and non-urgent categories still waiting for a procedure in June.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said her party would establish a program giving public patients the choice to undergo their surgery at a private hospital at no cost.

"The program will deliver an extra 25,000 surgeries a year," Ms Wilson said.

"For those people who are languishing on the elective surgery waitlist at the moment, putting their life on hold, I know they are looking for a government that is prioritising their needs."

The policy mirrors a similar program introduced by the Queensland government, which resulted in a small drop in surgery waiting lists, according to ABC analysis.

Ms Wilson said the $1.27 billion program would be wholly funded by winding up government investment fund Breakthrough Victoria.

"Victorians deserve a government that isn't playing venture capitalist but is instead delivering the health services that Victorians desperately need."

Jess Wilson says the Coalition will facilitate an additional 25,000 surgeries a year. (ABC News)

Breakthrough Victoria, currently valued at $600 million, recorded losses of $5.7 million in the 2025 financial year, and losses of $3 million in 2024.

The Breakthrough Victoria fund has already undergone consolidation after being merged with startup agency LaunchVic earlier this year.

The announcement has been backed by the private hospital sector, which would sign four-year contracts under the deal to treat public patients, with spare capacity.

Australian Private Hospitals Association chief executive Brett Heffernan said both the official and unofficial waiting times for surgeries were becoming a major problem.

"We're looking in the tens of thousands of patients who are stranded on longer and longer lists," he said.

"There's also an unofficial list and that is a multitude of patients, probably more than the official list, who are waiting for consultations with specialists to get onto the list in the first place."

The waitlist for elective surgeries in Victoria's public hospitals has continued to grow in the 12 months to June this year. (ABC News)

Mr Heffernan called the proposed program a "win-win" for patients and said the use of private hospitals had improved wait times in Queensland.

"They saw about 8,000 people in 18 months drop from their waiting lists, which may not sound dramatic, but it is because … when people come off the waiting lists, more people go onto the waiting list," he said.

The ABC guide to the 2026 Victorian election To learn more about the key electorates, candidates and swing seats in the coming election, head to this guide from the ABC's Chief Elections and Data Analyst Casey Briggs.

The Carroll government has backed its own record on surgeries, saying Victorian public hospitals had delivered a record 218,000 planned surgeries over the past year.

The government said 100 per cent of the most urgent patients, dubbed category 1, were treated within 30 days.

The government previously announced a $50.1 million investment towards 4,000 additional planned surgeries for children in the 2026/27 budget.

Labor to wind back land tax changes

The Carroll government has promised to reverse course on land tax if re-elected, scrapping changes it made to the threshold in 2023.

Under the changes, the threshold for paying land tax was lowered from a site value of $300,000 to $50,000, meaning 250,000 more Victorians were subject to the tax.

Victoria's election is nearly here — it's time to have Your Say Before Victorians head to the polls on November 28, we want to hear about what matters to you most.

The government said the proposed changes would be implemented progressively over the course of several years, with the threshold increasing by $25,000 a year.

The changes will cost $230 million over five years, which the government says it will pay for by consolidating the government car fleet and delaying level crossing removals.

"Lower land tax, more cost-of-living relief, and a responsible way to pay for it," Premier Ben Carroll said.

"Im a new premier and this is my new direction."

The announcement mirrors Coalition and One Nation policies, with both parties committing to also reversing the 2023 land tax changes.

World.title: NRL and NRLW grand final day has arrived. Here's what you need to know
World.content:
The final day of the NRL and NRLW seasons is here. The grand finals for the men and women will be held today.

In the women's decider, the Sydney Roosters and Brisbane Broncos face off in a rematch of last year's grand final.

In the men's grand final, the Sydney Roosters are facing the Newcastle Knights.

Here's everything you need to know about NRL and NRLW grand finals day.

What time are the NRL and NRLW grand finals?

The NRL and NRLW grand finals will be held on Sunday, October 4, the first day of daylight saving time in many states and territories across the country.

Here is when each grand final begins in each state and territory.

NRL grand final

7:30pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania

7pm ACDT: South Australia

6:30pm: Queensland

6pm: Northern Territory

4:30pm: Western Australia

NRLW grand final

4pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania

3:30pm ACDT: South Australia

3pm: Queensland

2:30pm: Northern Territory

1pm: Western Australia

How can you watch and listen to the grand final?

The game will be on Channel 9 and 9Now, but be aware that it will not be shown on Kayo or Fox Sports. It is the only game of the entire NRL season that is exclusive to Channel 9.

To listen to the grand final, join your local ABC Sport radio team, and follow along with the ABC Sport live blog at abc.net.au.

Where are the NRL and NRLW grand finals being played?

The NRL and NRLW grand finals are being played at Stadium Australia in Sydney.

Stadium Australia has hosted every NRL grand final since 1999, with the exception of the 2021 decider which was played at Brisbane's Lang Park during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Since the NRLW's inception in 2018, all grand finals have been played at Stadium Australia, again with 2021 being the exception. That decider was played at Dolphin Stadium in Redcliffe.

Who is playing in the NRL grand final?

The Sydney Roosters face the Newcastle Knights for the NRL premiership.

The Roosters finished the season fourth on the ladder, and lost their opening match of the finals before victories over Cronulla and the Dolphins.

The Newcastle Knights finished seventh on the ladder. After defeating Souths in the first week of the finals, the Knights went to Auckland and defeated the Warriors, then beat Penrith while being down to 12 players for all of the second half.

What pre-match entertainment is taking place at the NRL grand final?

After talks between the NRL and Australian artist Tones And I, the grand final appeared set to take place without any pre-match entertainment.

However, on Friday it was revealed that an all-star ensemble of Australian musicians, led by Amy Shark, will lead a tribute to recently retired player Jai Arrow, who was diagnosed with MND earlier this year.

Shark will be joined by members from Newcastle favourites and Better hit-makers The Screaming Jets, electronic duo Peking Duk, plus rock groups Grinspoon, and Teen Jesus and the Jean Teasers.

Shark previously performed at the 2020 NRL grand final, and is set to perform a series of cover songs, including the Gerry and the Pacemakers' song and Liverpool FC anthem You'll Never Walk Alone.

Each musician's appearance fee is reportedly being donated to motor neurone disease causes.

World.title: 'Flying boat' history behind Sydney's first international airport
World.content:
Some may assume the new terminal in Western Sydney is the city's second international airport, but it is historically the third.

Almost a century ago, Sydney experienced its golden age of aviation via flying boats.

By the end of 1934, the first regular air mail service between Australia and England began.

Flying boats were the chosen mode of transport as they could carry much larger freight loads than the land-based aircraft of the time, and had cheaper operating costs.

Two Qantas Empire Airways flying boats at Rose Bay in 1939. (Supplied: Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales)

That same year, Qantas Empire Airways was established as an international airline joint venture by Australia's Qantas and Britain's Imperial Airways.

In 1938 the airline moved its operations from Brisbane to Sydney, settling on Rose Bay in the east thanks to its calm waters and central location.

And so began the Rose Bay Water Airport.

While Rose Bay's airport was mostly used for mail services, expensive travel also became a commodity for wealthy travellers.

Flights travelled along the east coast to Singapore then via stops at Bangkok, Calcutta, Karachi, Alexandria, Basra, Marseilles and onto Southampton.

Rose Bay became home to Sydney's first international airport in the 1930s. (Supplied: Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales)

First class travel 'cream on the cake'

While air mail was the financial basis for the Qantas Empire Airways flying boats system, "the cream on the cake" was its first class offerings for passengers.

The Qantas Empire Airways route map. (Supplied: Qantas Empire Airways)

David Crotty, former curator of the Qantas Heritage Collection, who still does consulting work with Qantas, said the return fair from Sydney to Southampton was about £342.

"In those days it was a heck of a lot of money, considering you could buy a new Chevrolet car at that time in Sydney for about £330," he said.

The air trip would take approximately nine and a half days, compared to a five week ship journey.

"It was quite luxurious, it was unlike anything Australia had seen before," Mr Crotty said.

"The flying boats typically took somewhere up to 15 passengers, and there were a series of cabins. In one cabin you could smoke … there was room to wander around and the seats could be reclined back."

A Qantas promotional image of passengers. (Supplied: Qantas Heritage Collection/Museums of History NSW)

It was the first time Australia had in-flight service, with Qantas employing stewards who had worked on ships.

"They didn't cook on board but they had a little galley kitchen where warm meals could be served," Mr Crotty said.

It was a brief but "romantic period" for aviation, because when World War II heightened, the service's travel offering ended so the flying boats could assist with military activities.

How flying boats supported the war effort

The flying boats played a number of roles during World War II.

Civil Aviation Historical Society president Phil Vabre said this included shifting military equipment in Darwin to running services to Nouméa, which served as a base for the United States in the war.

"Later on they were largely employed up and down the east coast ferrying personnel, cargo and mail up into New Guinea in support of the war," he said.

"One by one they either were crashed, a couple were shot down … the air force had also taken some Empire flying boats early on in the piece."

Flying boats played a vital role in World War II. (Supplied: Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales)

It was not until after World War II that commercial land airports and their aircraft became more widely used.

"Flying boats were commercially difficult to operate … there's a lot of difficulty operating off water for various reasons," Mr Vabre said.

"During the war lots of big airports had been built all over the world and land planes had developed to a significant degree."

Rose Bay's enduring legacy

A commemorative plaque remains at Rose Bay's waterfront promenade. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Rose Bay Water Airport had quite an impact on Sydney.

The first scheduled commercial passenger flight directly between Auckland and Sydney took place in 1940 on a Tasman Empire Airways Limited flying boat landing into Rose Bay.

In its later years, the flying boats at Rose Bay were used for passengers travelling to and from Lord Howe Island until the island's land airport was built in 1974.

Rose Bay Water Airport then closed that same year.

Rose Bay today still has seaplanes for scenic trips around Sydney. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Today, Sydney Seaplanes has a base in Rose Bay, and there is a plaque nearby to mark the area's legacy.

Sydney Airport in Mascot became the city's primary aerodrome, with its international terminal officially opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 1970.

Almost 60 kilometres away in Badgerys Creek in Sydney's west, Western Sydney International Airport will open to commercial passenger flights from October 25.

Sydney Airport's international terminal was opened in 1970 by Queen Elizabeth II. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Western Sydney International Airport has been decades in the making. (ABC News: Therese Banna)

Mr Vabre reflected on the importance of Sydney's first international airport.

"Rose Bay was important; it was the headquarters of our connection to Britain and the rest of the world by air," he said.

"Rose Bay is probably associated with the romance of the flying boats. There's just something about those graceful, old aircraft that are half boat, half airplane."

World.title: Newcastle's joy tempered by heartache on NRL grand final day after car crash
World.content:
Newcastle has woken with a heavy heart on NRL grand final day, its excitement tempered by concern for those injured when a car hit a crowd of Knights fans farewelling the team yesterday morning.

Multiple people were injured when a car crashed into a crowd of supporters about 9:30am at a roundabout on Newcastle Link Road, in Newcastle's west.

The 18-year-old driver, Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, has since been charged with multiple driving offences, including dangerous driving, negligent driving occasioning bodily harm and causing bodily harm by misconduct.

New South Wales Police said in a statement Mr Samarasinghe's P1 Provisional licence has been suspended and the vehicle has been seized prior to undergoing forensic examination.

Two other teens, present in the vehicle with Mr Samarasinghe, were unharmed according to police.

The crash injured 10 people, including a five-year-old girl who remains in a critical but now stable condition, the statement continued.

Police said the 67-year-old man who was initially in a critical condition is currently reported to be in a serious but stable condition.

Four other people – a second five-year-old girl, a two-year-old girl, a 31-year-old woman and a 48-year-old man – remain hospitalised in stable conditions.

Three men – aged 24, 25 and 27 – along with a 63-year-old woman have since been discharged from hospital.

Loading...

They were among thousands who had lined the streets to see off the Knights team bus, which was due to pass through the area as it left for Sydney ahead of the grand final match.

It comes after a week of celebration across the city, as Newcastle prepared for its first grand final in 25 years.

The driver was later released from hospital and taken to a police station where he was charged with nine offences including:

The car at the scene of the crash at a roundabout on Newcastle Link Road in Wallsend. (ABC News)

Widespread heartbreak

Many Novocastrians say they have felt the hurt of yesterday's crash deeply.

"It's really devastating," Newcastle man Anderson Dell said.

"It just goes to show one person's silly act can completely ruin something so great."

Knights supporters gathered on an oval where emergency services were transporting patients. (ABC News: Piper Duffy)

Mr Dell echoed how the region felt, saying he hoped those injured had a quick recovery.

"Best wishes to all of them [those injured] and their families," he said.

In hospital for grand final

One of those injured, Chris Clancy, posted on social media late yesterday saying he would be spending the grand final in hospital.

"I have a broken left collarbone which requires surgery and may have a possible sprained or broken right foot," his post read.

"I will be JJH [John Hunter Hospital] for a couple of days but will let you all know."

Chris Clancy was one of 10 people taken to hospital after the incident. (Instagram: Chris Clancy)

Knights captain Kalyn Ponga commented on the post.

"All the best with recovery mate! The team and community are with yas," his comment read.

In a statement, Newcastle Knights chief executive Peter Parr expressed his "deep concern and support" for those affected.

"Our thoughts and prayers are first and foremost with everyone who has been injured, their families and loved ones, and everyone who witnessed what occurred this morning," the statement read.

"What was meant to be a special morning for our community, thousands of Novocastrians coming together to farewell our team and show their support ahead of the Grand Final, has understandably turned into a distressing morning."

A GoFundMe for those affected by the tragedy has raised more than $17,000.

World.title: Former rugby league star once banned by corporate regulator lists $12m estate
World.content:
Exclusive PropertyNewsTitle Deeds Former rugby league star once banned by corporate regulator lists $12m estate Kristy Johnson October 4, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former rugby league star Lou (Lubo) Zivanovic and his wife Olivia Zivanovic have put their grand Dural estate on the market with a price guide of $12 million to $12.5 million, local sources say. Lou was banned by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) for three years from 2016 to 2019 over the collapse of 18 building and construction companies he operated, as previously reported by this masthead. Former Penrith Panthers star Lou (Lubo) Zivanovic and his wife Olivia are offloading their Dural estate that they renovated. Domain Records show the Zivanovics purchased the six-bedroom, four-bathroom property for $11 million in October 2021, with settlement in February the following year. The pool was already there, but substantial renovations have been made, including a new kitchen, painting, wall panelling and landscaping improvements, local sources say. The single-level house is designed for entertaining with a new kitchen, pool and games room with bar and wine cellar. Domain



The single-level house has a porte-cochère entrance, travertine floors, a Calacatta marble kitchen, cinema, gym, games room with bar and wine cellar, and bi-fold doors that lead to an al fresco zone with a pool, spa and outdoor kitchen. Lou (Lubo) Zivanovic. ASIC initially banned Lou in February 2016, but this announcement was suppressed while the former Penrith Panthers star appealed the decision. A Federal Court decision in 2018 lifted the suppression order, revealing that Lou lost his appeal to the Administrative Appeals Tribunal. He was disqualified from managing corporations until 18 February 2019. ASIC stated that all 18 companies were allegedly “insolvent and had failed to keep books and records”. According to the corporate regulator, creditors were left with unpaid debts totalling $26.8 million from the collapse.



Lou said in 2018 that $24.5 million of this amount was owed to him via intercompany loans; the remainder was owed to the Australian Tax Office. He claimed that every other creditor was paid in full. After the ban expired in 2019, Lou became the sole director of various companies, including Cabe Developments, a property development firm which he founded in 1999. The price guide is $12 million to $12.5 million, local sources say. Domain Lou played 116 games for Penrith between 1979 and 1986, and still has strong ties to the NRL club. Cabe is the developer behind a $500 million development called ESQ 1818 (East Side Quarter), an 850-apartment project within the Panthers precinct. William Brush of Manor Real Estate, who holds the Dural listing, declined to comment on the listing, vendors’ identities and decision to sell when contacted by this masthead.



Inner-city living Angela Fleming, widow of supermarket tycoon Jim Fleming, has splashed millions on two units in the CBD. Pictured is an entirely different unit that’s available to rent. Colliers/Domain Angela Fleming, wife of the late Jim Fleming, who launched the Jewel supermarket chain, has bought into the new residential development at Castlereagh Street in the CBD, the former site of the David Jones menswear store. Settlement documents that emerged last month reveal Angela bought two four-bedroom, five-bathroom units, one for $15,215,000, and the other for $4.2 million. Both apartments were purchased off the plan in 2021.



Angela and other residents can enjoy this pool. Hugo Agency Angela Fleming Belinda Rolland The development includes one, two, three and four-bedroom residences, and architecture and interiors are by fjcstudio. Design details include hand-finished stone, marble and floor-to-ceiling windows. Communal areas include an outdoor pool, terraces, fitness studio with yoga deck, a private dining room and wine cellar. Angela sold her four-bedroom, three-bathroom abode in Bellevue Hill for $10.25 million in March this year. She bought it for $6.5 million in 2015 and made some modern updates.



The Bellevue Hill property was sold by Adam Reichman of Ray White Double Bay and Paul Langsam of Raine & Horne Double Bay. Both declined to comment on any aspect of the sale. Jim, who died in 2007, bought NSW grocery chain Warman’s Stores and relaunched the business as Jewel Food Stores in the 1970s before selling it to Davids Holdings in 1995 for $59 million. The buyers paying for multiple Sydney CBD homes In his later years, he was involved in the racing industry, becoming chairman of the Sydney Turf Club from 1983 to 1990. Designer pad for sale An eye for design may prove handy for celebrated interior designer Greg Natale and his partner, Jason Greenhalgh, as they list their Darlinghurst apartment with a price guide of $4 million. Acclaimed interior designer Greg Natale is saying goodbye to his Darlinghurst unit, listed with a price guide of $4 million.
