World.title: ‘Let’s get back to real food’: Adam Liaw’s new show is a long way from MasterChef
World.content:
Adam Liaw and Pia Miranda host the new ABC cooking show Recipe of the Year, with Ellice Schrader (left) as a judge.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the middle of a barn, on the edges of a farm on Sydney’s south-western fringe, chef, author and TV producer Adam Liaw is biting into an Anzac biscuit. “Whoarrrh,” he says in delight. “Excellent crunch.” Editor's pick Streaming Wild, profane and heartbreaking: A guide to Anthony Bourdain’s best TV I take a biscuit too, freshly baked by contestants on the ABC’s new seven-part cooking show Recipe of the Year. The show is being filmed all around us at handmade wooden benchtops stationed against a backdrop of green pastureland beyond the barn’s wide open doors. Liaw takes my phone and films me breaking the golden, oat-flecked biscuit in two. “Good?” he says. It is. Perfectly crisp and, after a bite, nicely chewy. I explain my love for Anzac biscuits that are more chewy than crispy, but Ellice Schrader, a judge on the series and a member of the Country Women’s Association of NSW, overhears. “It needs to snap,” she says of the biscuit being broken apart. She also confirms that the CWA advises Anzac biscuits must never, ever, be called “cookies”.



“Ellice is formidable,” Liaw says. It’s a label he also gives her in the series’ first episode to which Schrader replies: “I’m a pussycat.” Ellice Schrader had never done TV before. The show’s director now calls her “the Margaret Pomeranz of cooking”. Geoff Magee Photography Recipe of the Year features 10 home cooks, drawn from 20 hopefuls in the show’s first episode, competing to achieve Australia’s “recipe of the year”. Hosted by Liaw and actor and food-lover Pia Miranda, it’s created and produced by i8 Studio, the Sydney production company Liaw runs with co-executive producer and director Josh Martin. Liaw and Martin, whose company is known for shows such as Tonight at the Museum, The Cook Up with Adam Liaw and Adam & Poh’s Great Australian Bites, say this series is a departure from the usual competitive cooking TV show. Not only do contestants bring their own recipes to cook, they share the meals cooked in each episode around a table together. Liaw says they wanted to “make the show feel accessible and more like cooking feels at home”. Geoff Magee Photography “It’s a really familiar space for a lot of viewers, and we’re genuinely trying our hardest to do things that are different,” Liaw says. “Not just for the sake of being different, but because we felt there were important reasons to make the show feel accessible and more like cooking feels at home.” Those reasons include the current cost of living, time constraints for everyday cooks and how and why people cook for themselves, friends and family. Unlike shows like MasterChef Australia (which Liaw won in 2010) or My Kitchen Rules, Recipe of the Year’s focus is on recipes rather than cooking.



“[Australians] love recipes,” Liaw says. “We love them in the newspaper, online and in books. We were really thinking through what’s the experience with somebody when they’re making a recipe? And, when they choose to cook something, is it a recipe that makes sense for the purpose that is being set for it? “Then, when you actually make it, what’s the process of eating? There aren’t many circumstances in home cooking where three members of your family stand there in front of you and taste it, give stern expressions and then give you feedback. Even though it is a competition, there’s also an atmosphere of home cooking on the show around the way we instruct the challengers and the way we judge.” “Everybody’s opinion on food matters – not just the expert.” Adam Liaw, on the judging criteria for his new series. Pia Miranda, a passionate cook and food lover, says making the show inspired great warmth and conviviality. “It’s one of the best experiences I’ve ever had, and I’m not just saying that because it’s about to come out,” she says. “It really was. “Everyone who was there just had a great time … It felt like a fourth or fifth season, not like the first season of a TV show. It was a real celebration of life.” “It’s one of the best experiences I’ve ever had”: Recipe of the Year co-host Pia Miranda. Geoff Magee Photography Adam Liaw and Pia Miranda host the new ABC cooking show Recipe of the Year. Geoff Magee Photography



The show’s location also resulted in a passing parade of animal life beyond the barn’s doors. “We had cows,” she says. “We had kangaroos. There were deer and beautiful, beautiful birds. Adam’s so cute: every time kangaroos went past, he got misty-eyed. He gets so excited by kangaroos. We had to stop and just look at them.” Josh Martin believes the show’s focus on recipes, along with the contestants’ stories about their recipes’ origins and histories, will inspire a broad range of viewers. “We love MasterChef. We love Bake Off … But we thought, let’s just get back to real food that people cook.” Josh Martin, executive producer and director of Recipe of the Year “Adam and I have made a lot of food shows,” Martin says. “And don’t get me wrong: we love MasterChef, we love Bake Off. Six hours for a challenge to do something? That’s great. But we thought, let’s just get back to real food that people cook. In the second episode, the very first challenge they do is make a sandwich. But it really works.” Recipe of the Year’s format features three challenges: the blue ribbon, the gold ribbon and a feature recipe section. The first is about creativity; the second focuses on precision and is judged by the CWA, with recipes ranging from a jam roll to scones and Anzac biscuits; the third is a recipe brought in by competitors. Across the series, themes include comfort food, budget cooking, the big barbecue, weekend brunch recipes and more. Adam Liaw, Pia Miranda and Ellice Schrader at the barbecue on new ABC cooking show Recipe of the Year. Geoff Magee Photography



“The final challenge is the only one with stakes on it,” Martin says. “They all bake a dish and at the end, rather than the judges tasting and judging like a lot of other shows, everybody sits around the table and votes for their favourite to least favourite. Then we tally the votes. Because everybody’s opinion on food matters – not just the expert.” Today, contestants are getting ready to bake more Anzac biscuits. They stand at benchtops fitted with ovens, cooktops and kitchen equipment while crew members bustle around them. Editor's pick Streaming Why TV is full of celebs eating chicken and doing Tim Tam slams Rustic wooden walls display retro tea towels, souvenir teaspoon displays, hanging copper pans and ceramic jugs filled with eucalyptus and banksia branches. Contestants have been given tea towels printed with the Anzac biscuit recipe (“Bake at 175 degrees for 15 to 20 mins or until golden brown”). The contestants – who have a wide variety of ages, experience and cultural and geographical backgrounds – include a 19-year-old aspiring chef who experiments passionately with cannoli, and a builder from Sydney celebrating his mother’s cooking. There’s also a Malaysian-born home cook sharing flavours of her homeland, and a teacher who, expressing the importance of connecting with family via food, shares her late mother’s recipes. Schrader, decked out in pearls and a total natural in front of the cameras, judges the gold ribbon category with warmth, generosity and strict CWA criteria. As with food competitions at major Australian agricultural shows, judging cakes, slices, biscuits and other baked goods is not done lightly. Do not call Anzac biscuits “cookies” in front of this woman. Geoff Magee Photography

World.title: Tim had never been on a jury. This TV experiment left him ‘gobsmacked’
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV Tim had never been on a jury. This TV experiment left him ‘gobsmacked’ Nicole Elphick October 4, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tim had been called up for jury duty four times, but the 29-year-old musician had always been unavailable due to his former career in the busy advertising industry. However, when a friend who worked at SBS suggested he apply to be part of TV experiment The Jury, his interest was piqued. “God, I had nothing better to do,” he says. “I’d gotten out of rehab a couple of months before that, so I was just chilling, and I was like, ‘Why not? Let’s do some reality TV.’” The experience ended up significantly changing his perceptions of the justice system. The show’s creators describe Tim as a “powerhouse” in the jury room – logical, articulate and intellectually agile. SBS Tim is one of the 12 everyday Australians taking part in season two of The Jury, where viewers are taken inside the usually off-limits world of the jury room. As in the first season, which came out in 2024, the series follows a real case, the details of which have been anonymised. The 1700-page transcript of the real criminal trial is condensed to a 500-page script (created to very closely reflect the original testimony) and the new jurors are left to find their own verdict. For the show’s legal consultant Simone Quinn, a solicitor who has been practising law for nearly 30 years, it’s a unique insight for audiences. “[The jury room] is completely secret and closeted,” she says. “It is an extremely sacred space and the confidentiality of those deliberations and the jurors is critical to ensuring that justice is dispensed properly.”



The trial this season covers the disappearance of a woman whose remains are found when the defendant’s former backyard is dug up for construction a decade later. Quinn says it’s a trial that would have been particularly challenging for jurors to navigate. Editor's pick Australian TV He respects Hughesy’s ‘passion’, but Peter Helliar is staying on the silly side “I thought it was a really tricky case to put in front of a jury,” she says. “Having a woman’s remains dug up in a residential backyard points to something very sinister, yet the case or the evidence before them really was circumstantial. There was no direct evidence of a killing.” This season was a massive undertaking, with 16 actors and dozens of crew working together for a two-week shoot at the 172-year-old Justice and Police Museum in Sydney. “There was a court officer who took you in, every detail was as it would be if you were experiencing it in real life,” Tim says. “So it wasn’t hard to pretend. Everything felt completely real.”



Sixteen actors performed from scripts that closely resembled the original trial transcripts. SBS As in an actual jury, the 12 participants also brought a range of life experiences to the table. Throughout the episodes, they candidly shared their own personal histories of crime, tragedy and hardship. For Tim, who has experienced substance addiction, he felt reasonably able to park his biases and aim for objectivity on the case, though he admits that was not always 100 per cent possible. Editor's pick Streaming Netflix’s new Wonka series is bonkers. It was even crazier in real life “Having experienced drug addiction and seeking treatment with other people who are drug addicts, I think you really sharpen this sense of empathy for people that you did not have,” Tim says. “My sense of empathy is almost the biggest bias that I brought into it. Some of the people in this case acted very irrationally, but I can understand why.” He says his experience on the show has completely flipped his thoughts on juries. Tim now believes the system used in most of Europe, where a judge or panel of judges determines guilt or innocence, seems the best option.



The front row shows Tim alongside 38-year-old business analyst Sahar, and 75-year-old hairdresser, Sue. SBS “This is like the digestive part of our legal system that you don’t see. It’s kind of gross,” he says. “Everyone knows it’s a jury of your peers. In a criminal trial, they need to prove beyond reasonable doubt. You hear those as sound bites. But when you’re really there, to me, it didn’t make a damn bit of sense to have 12 people plucked off the street who have no legal experience actually having to grapple with some pretty serious legal concepts. “I thought everything would be explained, but they just plonk you in a room and say, ‘Figure it out for yourself.’ I was gobsmacked at how much faith they put into 12 random people that may or may not have any experience with the legal system. I think it’s to its detriment, honestly.” The Jury: Skeleton in the Garden premieres at 7.30pm on Monday October 5 on SBS and SBS On Demand.

World.title: After an unforgettable career, Kate Ceberano has few regrets – but there is one big one
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After more than four decades on stage and screen, singer Kate Ceberano has few regrets. She’s crafted 31 albums (11 platinum, eight gold), won five ARIA awards and been inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame for her performances, which span rock, soul, jazz, pop and classical. In the 1980s, she won three Countdown awards, in the 1990s she played Mary in a record-breaking run of Jesus Christ Superstar and won a Logie for the video clip for the song Everything’s Alright. She was the first woman inducted into the Australian Songwriters Association Hall of Fame in 2014. On top of that, in 2007 she won Dancing with the Stars, and portraits of her have been chosen as finalists in the Archibald three times, with two winning the Packing Room Prize (in 1994 and 2021). From fronting the band I’m Talking in 1984 to her successful solo career, for which she was made a member of the Order of Australia in 2016, Ceberano is one of the best-known voices and faces of the Australian entertainment industry. Kathrin Longhurst’s portrait of Kate Ceberano won the 2021 Archibald Packing Room Prize. AGNSW, Jenni Carter “I’ve come to an age where I can’t be ‘un-Kate Ceberano’,” she says. “Like Chrissy [Amphlett], Renee [Geyer], Kylie [Minogue] and Delta [Goodrem], we’re all on a one-name basis with our audiences. That’s quite a rare and privileged place to get to in Australia and you only get there by being yourself.” But there is one missed opportunity that hounds her still. It was during her serious flamenco phase, a dance form she took up at the age of 12 to understand more of her Filipina/Spanish origins. Her Filipino/Hawaiian father Tino was known as “the father of Australian karate” after his 1970s morning-TV appearances teaching self-defence. “My dad is the highest-ranked of his style in the world. He’s not just a karate master, he’s like Kung Fu Panda,” she jokes.“I first found out about fame and being in the public eye thanks to my dad.” Her mother Cherie, whose ethnicity is Swedish and Welsh, was also one of the first women to hold a black belt in karate in Australia.



“At our house, at any given time, there was anywhere between 50 to 100 black belts. The only reason I didn’t do it was because I didn’t love the sound of women sparring. I found it very unfeminine.” Instead of karate, the youngest of three, and only girl in her family, took up singing and dancing. At about the age of 12 she joined a dance group with the Filipino Association – “flamenco without the frilly dresses” as she calls it – and became obsessed. So much so that a young filmmaker called Baz Luhrmann approached her in the early 1990s to become involved in a film he was making about ballroom dancing. “To my absolute shame, I declined the offer to be part of Strictly Ballroom because I didn’t know what the film was about. I didn’t understand that it was actually going to be exactly about the very thing that I was being a purist about,” she says. Ceberano decided not to join the Strictly Ballroom cast. Steven Siewert She now realises how wrong she was. Steven Siewert “I found ballroom’s version of flamenco to be kind of like an aberrant version of flamenco because it wasn’t the true ethnic flamenco that I was into. But as it turns out, that was a lost opportunity of the highest degree. When the film came out I just wanted to bite my arm off.” So since then she’s said ‘yes’ to everything, which is one of the main reasons she’s headed back on tour for the Australian Made encore tour. It began in London on August 8 and will end in Shepparton, Victoria, on November 20. It will take her to venues throughout regional Australia, as well as the Sydney Opera House (October 11) and Melbourne’s Hamer Hall (October 23), on the back of her 2025 21-date Australian Made tour, 2024’s Superstars Live with Jon Stevens, and the 2023 orchestral collaboration with the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, My Life Is a Symphony. All three tours were sell-outs.



The Australian Made tour of 1986-87 was a watershed moment in Australian music, showcasing local talent in major stadiums and acting as a precursor to festivals like the Big Day Out. Ceberano was barely 20 that summer when, as lead singer of I’m Talking, she joined the stellar line-up of INXS, Jimmy Barnes, Divinyls, Models, The Saints and The Triffids. The idea for a 2025 tour and live album came after a discussion with her husband and manager Lee Rogers after the 2016 re-release of Richard Lowenstein’s film Australian Made: The Movie. Some of the 1986 Australian Made line-up (left to right): Jon Farriss, Michael Hutchence, Jimmy Barnes, Reg Mombassa, Wayne DeLisle, Kate Ceberano, Greedy Smith, Martin Plaza, Warren McLean and Gary Beers. Rick Stevens/Fairfax Media “We bemoaned the fact that almost all of the performers are now dead,” she says, listing the tally of fallen fellow musos, from INXS’ Michael Hutchence to Divinyls’ Chrissy Amphlett, The Saints’ Chris Bailey, Models’ James Freud and now James Valentine. “I was kind of like the last of the Mohicans, along with Jimmy Barnes and Sean Kelly from Models.” She felt it was time to tell her old friends’ stories to new audiences (or old ones keen for a dose of nostalgia). Looking back, she remembers she was slightly terrified by the Australian Made cohort, especially Amphlett. “What she taught me was you need to be bold enough to be yourself,” Ceberano says. “I wasn’t sidling up to any of my peers, like Renee Geyer or Chrissy Amphlett, for any badge of approval. But what they did teach me is that if you come too close to imitating or trying to become your idol, you have to pay the price … No one wants a poor imitation of another person.”



For a girl who left school at 15, whose band won the Victorian Battle of the Bands at 16 and who not long after opened for Vince Jones, jazz was a focus of her early career – thanks in part to Melbourne restaurateur Mietta O’Donnell. “She saw me as a sort of Josephine Baker singer and put me on her menu at [the restaurant] Mietta’s as a dessert – a warm chocolate tart.” Ceberano credits her love of singing back to a childhood illness. “I got a very severe case of glandular fever around 13 and I sat and watched midday movies for about three months, and mostly they were musicals. And then I reckon I just started sort of hallucinating with fever and imagining I was singing in musicals.” Like it or not, she is best known as a rock singer whose name will be eternally linked to those giddy days of Oz-rock in the 1980s. Ceberano’s name will be forever linked to the ’80s rock scene but her repertoire spans rock, soul, jazz, pop and classical. Steven Siewert “I always really loved the entourage of the bands that were on the Australian Made stage,” she recalls. “Michael Hutchence was going out with [model] Helena Christensen. Backstage there were a lot of his beautiful acolytes who were beautiful spirits as well. Among them was Jane Barnes, who had baby Mahalia on her hip through most of Jimmy Barnes’ wild gigs.” That baby, Mahalia Barnes, has since gone on to play Mary Magdalene in Jesus Christ Superstar, the same role Ceberano played next to John Farnham in the 1990s, and Ceberano’s own daughter, Gypsy, has also gone into a career in music, as next-gen Australian Made offspring. Ceberano welcomes the fact there are more professional female musicians than when she began. “Barbara Hogarth, who was the first woman that I’d ever worked with or had known of in the music business, was on bass in I’m Talking, When you consider that of all of the bands on that tour, there were only two bands with women in them, you can see how far we’ve come in the music industry.”



Despite early warnings that “girls don’t play the drums” (“The Go-Betweens’ Lindy Morrison was the first woman I’d ever seen on drums”), for this tour, like the last one, she plays the drums. “The reason why I drum on this particular tour was because we wanted to travel light in two cars with [support acts] Kathleen Halloran and Dusty Lee and our crew as well, and we wanted to be able to be very nimble when coming into regional gigs,” she said. Related Article Tina Arena says it's harder for female singers to make it in Australia “I also wanted the sounds to be big and I wanted that to be rock, so it has the same visceral impact. The body has to feel like you’re shaking, and the roof is shaking, and you need to be able to make it big.” Ceberano developed a passion for sewing during the COVID lockdowns and has a clothing line she sells online, including flamenco-like frilly skirts that she embroiders with song lyrics. In between songs in the show she will tell anecdotes about her former 1980s muso friends, but insists it is not a tribute show; just an old friend singing songs to remember an amazing time in Australian rock history. As a prelude to the show she uses the same music INXS used to come on stage to every night during the original Australian Made tour. “It’s fantastic warm-up music,” said the singer, who will turn 60 in the final month of this tour. “The minute it starts I feel like the child that I was at 20, watching at the side of the wings for Michael and the boys to launch into their first hits. I hope my own enthusiasm and nostalgia for this era can bring the audiences along with us.”

World.title: A ski town that’s not like most others – it has a soul
World.content:
InspirationSki holidays A ski town that’s not like most others – it has a soul Jim Darby October 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You can thank Lord Revelstoke for all the puns and the bumper stickers – “get Stoked”, “feel the Stoke”, and even “ride the Stoke chair”. His Lordship arranged the finance to get the railway through here in the late 1800s and the town beneath the mighty Selkirk and Monashee mountain ranges in Canada’s British Columbia was named after him as a tribute. Nat Segal skiing fresh snow at Revelstoke, with the Columbia River valley below. Ryan Collins A century or so on, Revelstoke has grown somewhat, and there are no signs of the peerage, for here you have all the attributes of a mountain town – full of youth and energy and shops and services dedicated to outdoor pursuits. In summer, it’ll be buzzing with hikers and mountain bikers and all sorts of water lovers on the lakes and the Columbia River that runs right alongside. In winter, you’ll find skiers and snowboarders hopping aboard one of the dozen or so heli-skiing operations to get their thrills in the hills or making the short trip up the road to the Revelstoke Mountain Resort.



The Resort itself is a work in progress, as far as its base area goes – there are hotels and apartments established and under construction, cafes and bars for the hungry and thirsty, and excellent ski/board retail and rental outlets. 



“My first time skiing at Revelstoke Mountain Resort was in 2013 when I was competing on the Freeride World Tour. I just remember having my mind blown, like I’d never skied trees like that or found pillow lines [mounds of snow covering logs or rocks] like that in bounds”, Segal says. Australian Nat Segal on her new home mountain. Ryan Collins She returned several times and used it as a location for the feature-length documentary she made with her sister Anna – Finding the Line. “So I had some connections through that and a few friends who had moved here, and I moved to Revelstoke in 2018”. By now, she knows the mountain well. The main drag, as she calls it, is the gondola, with some long blue (intermediate-level) groomed runs “if it’s a little busier, I’ll just do laps on the gondola, just fast. It’s the best place to get your legs going because they’re such long runs. When my parents come to visit me and I do it with them, we have to stop all the time and I’m just like ‘oh come on you two, you haven’t done your training’.” The Stoke Chair gives access to some of the mountain’s bigger bowls – North Bowl and Greely Bowl and if you don’t mind a hike you can head up to the sub-peak area below Mackenzie Peak. “There’s amazing access all through there. A lot of the areas off the Stoke Chair are ungroomed, off-piste. It’s the more challenging terrain, but they’re really fun runs and it’s a great place for stepping up into harder and harder terrain.”



Then there’s the Ripper Chair, lower in elevation but offering entertaining blue and green (easiest) groomed runs and if you want to head off those runs, “there’s some tree skiing that’s not too steep but still really fun and playful. “Some people on a powder day will go straight to the Stoke Chair and other people go straight to the Ripper. It’s all to do with style. I like the steeper terrain, I like a little bit more open terrain, whereas I have friends that all they want to do is ski the trees.” One of the “Art Alleries” – street art in downtown Revelstoke. Rob Buchanan Another measure of the area relates to the company you’ll keep. Revelstoke has the highest concentration of Association of Canadian Mountain Guides members in the country (you’ll see the ACMG status with their signature). Many work as heli-ski or cat-ski guides and backcountry ski touring guides. It also has a healthy community. “One of the reasons I moved to Revelstoke and I’m staying, is the community. I live in the downtown area, just a few blocks from the main street. And it feels so lovely – so much art and culture and some amazing nonprofits.



“If you stick around for a season you can be really involved in the town, but even if you’re just there for a visit, there’s always stuff going on. A classic is going to the Grizzlies [ice] hockey games. There are local kids playing and you have people who have lived there all their lives to people who have been for a week all cheering for the same team.” Revelstoke town at night. Tom Poole “From my house downtown to the resort parking lot is seven minutes if I time it. And there are buses and shuttles, so if you’re staying at one or the other you can easily get between the two. “You can stay at the resort and get that resort feeling, but then if you want to go downtown and have a walk around a cozy town, you can do that as well. There are lots of options for accommodation in the town and the resort. Sutton Place Hotel – a stroll away from the lifts at Revelstoke Mountain Resort. Royce Sihlis



“One thing I really appreciate is that there isn’t a divide, there are lots of residents living in the areas where tourists stay, but at the same time, the tourist accommodation isn’t crowding out the town, the town still has soul.” Given its deep-in-the-mountains location, outside winter, Revelstoke still draws in the visitors and has plenty to entertain the locals. Related Article Ski holidays If you wanted to create the ultimate ski resort, this place would be the template That might be hiking or mountain biking, or spending time on the river or lakes. Those waterways are mountain-fed though. “It’s funny, as someone who loves the water and grew up by the beach, it doesn’t replace the beach, but Canadian lakes are lovely in their own right. So there’s a whole experience out there. But the water is freezing!



“Later in the summer it does warm up, so at the end of September it’s just like March in southern Australia. But yeah, early season, you’re not staying in the water very long,” Segal says. THE DETAILS STAY + SKI

Two choices in location and then many choices for accommodation. Stay at the resort base, at the likes of the Sutton Place Hotel (suttonplace.com rooms from $C469/$470 a night in winter), and you can wander out the door and straight on to the lifts. Stay in town, a few minutes’ from the skiing, and you get all the accommodation, cafes, bars and shops of Revelstoke township. The lift pass is part of the Ikon and Mountain Collective networks, which will suit some season pass holders from Mount Buller and Thredbo. See revelstokemountainresort.com FLY + DRIVE

Air New Zealand (airnewzealand.com.au) flies daily to Vancouver where there are onward connecting flights to Kelowna (about an hour in the air). Revelstoke is about a two-and-a-half hour drive from Kelowna, with hire cars and regular shuttle services available. A tip in winter is to come via Kelowna, rather than Calgary on the Alberta side, as snow is more likely to interrupt access if you’re coming in from Alberta. The writer flew to Canada as a guest of Air New Zealand and visited Revelstoke as a guest of Destination British Columbia (supernaturalbc.com) and Revelstoke Mountain Resort.

World.title: Queenstown crash leaves one dead, three injured
World.content:
One person died after a single-vehicle crash on State Highway 6 near Kawarau Falls in Queenstown on Sunday morning.

Police said the crash happened shortly before 4am, between the intersections of Peninsula Road and Boyd Road.

Fire and Emergency said the vehicle left the road and hit a tree, with four people needing to be rescued.

Two people in the car had serious injuries, while another had critical injuries, police said.

World.title: Job seeker calls for ban on 'ghost' interviews that harvest data for AI
World.content:
Sitting across from the AI interview agent, Charlie Maclean tried to put her best foot forward, but it was awkward.

"It had specific questions," she said, but it was nothing like connecting with a potential employer face-to-face.

"It would sort of pick up on a key word or something that you've said, [like] 'Hey, that's good experience in project management - tell us more about it'."

Answers were timed, Maclean told RNZ, leaving little room to consider a response.

"You're not really able to take a second to think mid-sentence because it will just assume that you're finished and then cut you off and on to the next bit."

It was a jarring experience, which became more strange after the initially very eager company ghosted her.

Do you know more? Email: mary.argue@rnz.co.nz

Maclean is now sounding the alarm about companies that post prolifically on sites such as LinkedIn, advertising remote roles with attractive salaries.

Charlie Maclean fears she unwittingly handed over her data to a company that used it to train AI. Supplied

After some digging online, she fears the company that sent an AI agent to interview her was simply after her personal data to train artificial intelligence - a potential scam or so-called "ghost" job, a scenario where a company advertises for a role it has no intention of filling.

The experience has prompted Maclean to launch a petition to Parliament explicitly banning such job s.

'Data is king'

Senior lecturer in organisational psychology at Victoria University Ben Walker doesn't have "case-closed" evidence of phantom job listings but feels there is enough online commentary to suggest advertised roles by certain companies were spurious.

Companies under fire in online message threads for suspected data harvesting have not responded to RNZ's requests for comment.

While recruiters RNZ contacted had not come across ghost jobs in New Zealand, they had heard of such practices.

One recruiter, with almost 20 years experience, said companies posting fake jobs to harvest candidate data was a new con for the industry and had been a topic of discussion among colleagues overseas.

Chief executive of Tribe Group recruitment agency Bruce Pilbrow found the scenario plausible, and said it would be an effective way to gather core information.

"There's a lot happening in the AI space and the online space in the sense of harvesting information," he said. "Data is king."

Andrew Lensen, senior lecturer in artificial intelligence at Victoria University. Supplied

Fake job listing or not, Victoria University senior lecturer in artificial intelligence Andrew Lensen said there was growing concern about where personal information ended up.

CVs and cover letters contained potentially valuable data, he said, including a person's name, educational background and even an address.

"It's your career history, it's what you've learned, the skills you have, and we often don't think about it that carefully but that is a lot of information.

"If it is going into any sort of database or system that could be used for things like AI in the future, then I think people are quite rightfully getting more and more concerned about how the data is being used and where it's going."

Rapid recruitment a red flag

In her months-long search for work, Maclean said she came across a handful of companies on LinkedIn - a professional networking platform - advertising remote jobs with inflated salaries that seemed to "go nowhere".

According to Walker, an intense recruitment drive could be a red flag.

"Where it's a company that you've never heard of suddenly doing those sorts of things, it potentially raises a few question marks and alarm bells about whether the jobs are legitimate or whether they may be a cover or some means to another end."

As a global platform, LinkedIn differed greatly from job sites such as SEEK and Trade Me, he said, and in his opinion it had undergone a transformation in recent years: "People talk about the slopification of LinkedIn."

In response to questions from RNZ, a LinkedIn spokesperson said the company was investing in free verifications for jobs, recruiters and company pages, and that every job must be authentic and accurately represented.

Neither SEEK nor Trade Me considered ghost jobs to be a material issue on their sites, citing the financial commitment to advertise a role, verification processes, and the ability for job seekers to report suspect listings.

A petition and a warning

Maclean has since found work but the process was demoralising to the point that she almost forgot what she was good at.

"Jobs that I was really keen on I even took to sending people cupcakes with a little QR code in the icing, literally just to cut through the noise to get a phone call."

The exhausting process, in addition to her experience with the suspect company, has prompted a petition to Parliament to see ghost jobs explicitly banned, in line with crackdowns overseas.

"It's incredibly difficult out there.

World.title: Whistleblowers offer to aid Education Ministry probe
World.content:
Education Ministry whistleblowers, who contacted RNZ in the past week, plan to add their voices to an investigation by the Office of the Ombudsman.

The investigation was announced after publication of a video showing a ministry manager asking staff not to mention contact with the Education Minister's office in writing.

Nine people with inside knowledge of different parts of the ministry subsequently contacted RNZ to corroborate claims that ministry managers routinely asked staff not to write down sensitive information, least it be discovered through the Official Information Act.

Some were from the ministry's curriculum centre, which was the subject of a negative report about workplace culture published last week.

Others said that a culture of secrecy and avoidance of written records was common in other parts of the organisation.

The Education Ministry said the comments made in the leaked video did not meet its expectations, but it would not comment on claims made by the people who contacted RNZ.

It initially said it was investigating whether there was a wider problem, but told RNZ it had dropped plans for an internal inquiry in light of the Ombudsman's investigation.

Three of the sources confirmed they would contact the Ombudsman to make a protected disclosure and others said they were likely to do so.

A 10th person - former ministry staff member Claire Coleman - told RNZ she had already offered to participate in the Ombudsman's investigation.

This week, Chief Ombudsman John Allen said he had formally notified the ministry of the investigation.

"I will be looking at various practices, including whether the ministry's curriculum centre staff have either deliberately failed to make records or have been told not to do so," he said.

Chief Ombudsman John Allen Supplied

"My investigation will concentrate on administrative conduct, and whether the Ministry has met its legal obligations under the Official Information Act and the Public Records Act.

"I will not be considering any substantive advice or decision making relating to the curriculum itself."

Coleman, who has been a strong critic of the government's approach to the curriculum rewrite, said she hoped the Ombudsman "might get to the truth of things".

"I hope we can hold some people responsible and any future processes are transparent."

Coleman also hoped the Ombudsman's work might lead to a wider inquiry into the curriculum rewrite.

"There were far too many things that were done in a secretive and unethical way," she said. "Too many financial interests that have no business in that space."

Coleman previously claimed work on the curriculum was heavily politicised and several of the ministry insiders who contacted RNZ made similar allegations.

One source told RNZ the new curriculums felt like a step back in time.

"It felt like I was taken right back to the 80s of 'we don't let brown people have any rights' and 'we're going to whitewash everything,' and 'we're going to make sure that this is back to how things should be'," they said.

They said the curriculum was too directive of what teachers must teach.

"Some of the prescribed nature is needed, in order to be consistent and to make sure that children have all got equity wherever they are," they said. "I get that, but not to the extreme this is.

"New Zealand is innovative, creative... yet we're just throwing it all down the tubes."

Another source said schools could teach the new curriculums with resources left over from 20 years ago.

"It misses how young people learn today and it misses what's important for young people today," she said. "It's such a missed opportunity for what a good curriculum could look like.

"It's devastating, actually."

Another source said: "I think the public deserve to know, in no uncertain terms, that the quality of primary and secondary education in this country is being directly compromised and coloured by the government's ideological position, that the people responsible are consciously aware of it and that the minister, ministry and related parties have taken steps to circumvent proper protocol, and intentionally obscure the truth about how they have been operating."

Minister of Education Erica Standford RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Foreign influence

Several of the nine whistleblowers said the Australian firm Learning First had a major hand in draft curriculums and some ministry staff were flown to Melbourne to work with the company.

One said the primary school maths curriculum was completely rewritten by Learning First and other learning areas were heavily influenced by the company.

"The general feeling amongst internal staff was that the work being produced by Learning First was bad and unnecessary," they said. "There was a lot of confusion about why they were involved at all."

Another said Learning First wrote a lot of curriculum content, but ministry staff were told not to imply or say that the ministry was not the author of the curriculum.

"Learning First replaced everything we had done," they said.

They also said Learning First's understanding of the Treaty of Waitangi was "completely wrong".

A third source said Learning First provided a lot of content for some curriculums, but not for others, and ministry staff rewrote much of it.

"A lot of it was wrong, literally wrong," they said.

However, Learning First chief executive Ben Jensen denied the allegations.

He said the claim Learning First wrote most of the content for several curriculum drafts was not true.

"We did lots of research, benchmarking, provided advice and so on, but this is just completely false," he said.

Jensen said his company did not write the revised version of the maths curriculum

"We provided comparisons with other systems and made suggestions," he said. "We do a lot of work on how to sequence foundational learning in maths and what this means for the curriculum, but as above, we were not even doing this work when the draft was written.

"A lot of the feedback we provided was rejected by the ministry, so the idea that we wrote most of it is simply not true.

"When we finished, a lot of writing was still taking place, so just don't know how people can say it was mainly written by us."

Jensen said he was not aware of Learning First content being rewritten due to errors, and the company was up front about not having expertise on local knowledge and history, such as the treaty.

The Education Ministry also defended the process, and said it was responsible for all final content and decisions.

"Characterisations of the curriculum process based on individual recollections or particular examples do not necessarily reflect the full context of how curriculum content was developed, reviewed, and finalised," it said.

"The ministry develops and writes the curriculum, drawing on input from teachers, subject matter experts, stakeholders and external advisers throughout the process.

"As previously outlined publicly, including during the Education and Workforce Select Committee scrutiny examination, external advisers may contribute specialist expertise and international perspectives.

"For example, ministry officials have previously explained that Learning First helped identify relevant international curriculum content, while the curriculum itself was written by the ministry."

123RF

No written records

The Ombudsman's investigation was sparked by a video showing a principal seconded to the ministry to lead work on the secondary school curriculum, warning staff not to mention in writing feedback from the Education Minister's office.

The source of that video said they were outraged by the attempt to circumvent the proper processes for recording and providing information.

"These rigorous processes are put in there exactly to serve the children and to serve the schools, and us bypassing them is not okay," they said.

They said they heard similar requests almost once a month.

Other sources who contacted RNZ shared similar stories.

"Verbal instructions were given for changes that were controversial and come directly from the minister's office," one ministry insider told RNZ.

Another source said the comments made by the ministry manager in the leaked video were not an isolated case.

"This was a routine and extensive problem before she was seconded," they said. "The problem did not walk in the door with her."

Another ministry insider told RNZ: "We have been told many times not to write things down."

As RNZ reported last week, a person present at a ministry-run curriculum hui said ministry staff were present to take notes and one of those staffers revealed that they had been told to be very careful about what they wrote down.

"The things that they weren't writing down were pretty obviously things that they didn't want to be recorded as part of the feedback we were giving," she said.

She said, later at the same hui, a ministry manager instructed their staff to stop recording what was being said, because it was beyond the scope of the meeting and because it could be discovered through the OIA.

An established culture

Several sources told RNZ they witnessed repeated attempts to keep information off the record prior to the change of government in late 2023, but it became worse after the election.

One said ministry managers would respond to complaints or potentially critical queries with face-to-face meetings, a tactic that appeared aimed at avoiding a written email response.

"The whole 'have meetings, keep things off paper' is deliberate," they said.

The source said there were frequent meetings where nothing was written down.

"It didn't feel like there was any integrity."

A separate source said they commonly heard "that you shouldn't write things down, because they would then be OIA-able" prior to the 2023 election.

"Recording discussions and notes was sometimes discouraged, with people encouraged to have conversations instead," they told RNZ.

Another source said, prior to the change in government, reminders about the OIA and putting things in writing were light in tone and emphasis, but after the election, the term "OIA-able" was frequently used and, in 2024 meetings, became the preferred mode of communication.

Banned words

A learning lesson from a book for teaching te reo Māori. RNZ / Te Aniwa Hurihanganui

Most of the sources told RNZ they were told to remove Māori words from curriculum documents or noticed that others had done so.

They said the word "Aotearoa" was used as a synonym for or alongside New Zealand in original curriculum drafts, but was later removed.

"This instruction was never written down and, in some cases, senior staff made the changes themselves, rather than relay this change to the writing teams," one source said.

Another said Aotearoa New Zealand was the blanket term used in the curriculum, often shortened to ANZ, but proofreaders and editors were told to replace it with New Zealand.

One source said the push to remove Māori words began before the new coalition government had even taken office, with some managers indicating they wanted to make the change because "it was in the pipeline".

Two other sources said some English words were also apparently unwelcome, with instructions to remove words including "culture", "identity", and "wellbeing".

The Education Ministry had previously denied that it sought to remove Māori language from the curriculum.

Bullying and fear

The source of the video said ministry staff were being asked to behave dishonestly.

"We're public servants and we're being bullied, which I would say strongly, we are being bullied," they said. "The majority of people in the ministry are under a toxic environment."

They said nobody felt safe to complain.

"If you speak up and ask a professional, polite question of 'is this okay?', you very quickly have your fixed-term contract ended," they said.

Another ministry insider said staff felt they had to comply with government demands or lose their jobs.

"There was a lot of fear within the ministry that our jobs were now at risk, due to the change in government, and this contributed to what I experienced as an overall feeling that we had to say yes to everything and not question whether proper process was being followed," they said.

World.title: Cost of fixing storm-damaged Whangārei roads balloons to more than $23m
World.content:
The cost of fixing storm damage inflicted on Whangārei district roads earlier this year has risen to more than $23 million - of which almost $11m has been spent clearing one giant landslide.

The almost week-long January storm cut off coastal settlements at Ōakura and Whangaruru, swept away a bridge approach, damaged dozens of homes and destroyed others, and triggered a huge number of slips on the coastal road between Whangārei and Russell.

One section of road at Helena Bay Hill was only re-opened on Friday, after an eight-month effort to remove almost 100,000 cubic metres of soil, boulders and trees.

Further storms in March and April added more damage.

A report prepared for Whangārei District Council said the initial estimate for repairing storm-damaged roads was $16.5m, but that had now increased to $23.2m.

The report, by transportation manager Greg Monteith, sought councillors' approval for the extra $6.7m.

The NZ Transport Agency was expected to contribute $16m, leaving Whangārei ratepayers to pick up the remaining $7.2m.

The $23.2m total included $10.9m for emergency works at the massive Helena Bay Hill slip on Russell Road, the main connection between Whangārei and coastal communities at Ōakura and Whangaruru.

Almost $11 million has been spent repairing Russell Road, in the Whangārei District, after a massive slip on 21 January. Supplied / Ngātiwai Trust Board

The council previously described the slip repair as one of the biggest and most complex projects it had ever undertaken.

About 93,000 cubic metres of soil, boulders and downed trees had to removed - reduced from the initial estimate of 110,000 cubic metres - and the 35m-high slip face had to be stabilised.

The cost of fixing the slip had previously been put at $7.5m.

The council would fund its share of the extra costs by borrowing, to avoid major delays or cuts to existing roading projects.

The report stated the original cost estimate for the Helena Bay Hill slip was based on a completion date of mid-2026.

Since then, however, persistent wet weather, difficult ground conditions, giant basalt boulders, fill site constraints and further slip movement had delayed work and increased costs.

Some boulders were so big, they could not be broken up, even with a 50-tonne breaker, and instead required blasting or a specialist rock-breaking crew.

The report stated there had also been delays due to health and safety issues, such as near-misses involving trucks and local residents, and unauthorised entry into exclusion areas.

Aerial view of the cleared slip on Russell Road’s Helena Bay Hill. Supplied / Whangārei District Council

Once the slip had settled, which was expected to take about a year, more funding would be needed to repair the road below the slip and along the 2km route to the clean-fill site.

The estimated road rehabilitation cost was $2.3m.

During the road closure, the Whangārei District Council operated a convoy, via steep, narrow and unsealed Kaiikanui Road, to allow continued access from the south.

Piloted convoys left every 35-40 minutes from 6.30am to 6.30pm, seven days a week.

The cost of operating the Kaiikanui Road detour was put at $2.1m.

According to claims recorded by the Insurance Council, the total nationwide cost of the January storm, was $75.9m.

More than 5000 claims were lodged including $54.5m for damage to homes, $13.7m to commercial property and $4.6m for vehicles.

According to the Insurance Council, the most costly event of the past decade in terms of insurance claims was the 2023 Anniversary Weekend storm, which totalled $1.98 billion nationwide.
